titre: The 7 "I Am" Statements of Jesus — Day 1
texte:
Day 1. I Am the Bread of Life.

Today's reading : John, chapter 6, verses 26 to 40.

Jesus answered them, “Most certainly I tell you, you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled. Don’t work for the food which perishes, but for the food which remains to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For God the Father has sealed him.” They said therefore to him, “What must we do, that we may work the works of God?” Jesus answered them, “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.” They said therefore to him, “What then do you do for a sign, that we may see and believe you? What work do you do? Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness. As it is written, ‘He gave them bread out of heaven to eat.’” Jesus therefore said to them, “Most certainly, I tell you, it wasn’t Moses who gave you the bread out of heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread out of heaven. For the bread of God is that which comes down out of heaven and gives life to the world.” They said therefore to him, “Lord, always give us this bread.” Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty. But I told you that you have seen me, and yet you don’t believe. All those whom the Father gives me will come to me. He who comes to me I will in no way throw out. For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me. This is the will of my Father who sent me, that of all he has given to me I should lose nothing, but should raise him up at the last day. This is the will of the one who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day.”

Key verses.

Exodus, chapter 3, verse 14. God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”

The Context.

The day before, Jesus fed over five thousand people with five loaves and two fish. The next day, the crowd searches everywhere for him and finally finds him on the other side of the lake. You might think faith is driving them. But Jesus reads hearts: "Jesus answered them, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, you are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves. '" (John, chapter 6, verse 26)

They want more bread. And they remind Jesus that their fathers ate manna in the desert, that bread God made fall from heaven every morning for forty years. In other words: "Do us a miracle like Moses did."

What Jesus Reveals.

That's when Jesus speaks the first of his seven great statements: "Jesus said to them, 'I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst.'" (John, chapter 6, verse 35)

To understand this "I am" properly, you need to go back to the burning bush. When Moses asks God his name, God answers: "God said to Moses, 'I AM WHO I AM.' And he said, 'Say this to the people of Israel: "I AM" has sent me to you.'" (Exodus, chapter 3, verse 14) In Jesus' mouth, "I am" is not an ordinary phrase. It is God's very name. John builds his entire Gospel around seven "I am" statements, like seven open windows into who Jesus is.

And the first thing he wants you to know is that he is bread. Not a dessert, not a supplement, not an option for special occasions: bread, basic food, the kind you need every day to live. Manna nourished the body for one day; it spoiled the next. Jesus nourishes the soul for eternity.

Moses had already announced this: manna was just a lesson. "And he humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna, which you did not know, nor did your fathers know, that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the Lord." (Deuteronomy, chapter 8, verse 3) Jesus is that Word that came from God's mouth, made flesh. In fact, he will answer the devil with this very verse in the desert.

Notice also the two verbs: come and believe. "Whoever comes to me... whoever believes in me." You don't eat bread by looking at it or reading the label. You have to take it and eat it. Many people know Jesus from a distance, admire his words, respect his miracles, but have never truly eaten. Jesus doesn't want to be admired: he wants to be received.

And he adds a magnificent promise, for you who may fear rejection: "All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out;" (John, chapter 6, verse 37) Nobody is too far away, too broken, too complicated. The one who comes is never cast out.

For Your Life.

Ask yourself honestly: what am I feeding my soul with? Our souls are hungry, and if they don't eat real bread, they fill themselves with something else: the approval of others, screens, success, pleasures. Isaiah already said it: "Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy? Listen diligently to me, and eat what is good, and delight yourselves in rich food." (Isaiah, chapter 55, verse 2)

These things calm hunger for an hour, then leave it stronger. Only Jesus truly satisfies. And like bread, you need him every day. You don't live today on last week's meal. Your relationship with Jesus needs its daily portion: time with his Word, time in prayer, time in his presence.

That's exactly what you're doing right now with this plan. Don't see it as a religious chore, but as a meal. Today, come to the table. He's waiting for you.

Put it into practice.

One. Take Stock of Your Plate. Write down on a piece of paper what has nourished your soul this week: screen time, conversations, music, reading, prayer. Look at the list honestly: what leaves you satisfied, and what leaves you even more hungry?

Two. One Meal Before All Others. Tomorrow morning, before you open your phone, spend five minutes with Jesus: a verse, a sentence of prayer. If you have children, do it with them at breakfast; if you work early, do it on the bus or while walking.

Three. If You're Going Through a Season of Emptiness. Don't try to feel better right away. Simply say to Jesus: "I'm hungry; feed me." Then read John 6:35 three times during the day, like having three meals.

To reflect on. What am I currently feeding my soul with, and what is taking the place of the "bread of life" in my days?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you are the bread of life. Forgive me for seeking to satisfy my soul anywhere but in you. Today, I come to you and I believe in you. Feed me with your presence and your Word every day. Amen.

Key takeaway. Jesus is not an option in my life: he is my daily bread.

titre: The 7 "I Am" Statements of Jesus — Day 2
texte:
Day 2. I Am the Light of the World.

Today's reading : John, chapter 8, verses 12 to 20.

Again, therefore, Jesus spoke to them, saying, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.” The Pharisees therefore said to him, “You testify about yourself. Your testimony is not valid.” Jesus answered them, “Even if I testify about myself, my testimony is true, for I know where I came from, and where I am going; but you don’t know where I came from, or where I am going. You judge according to the flesh. I judge no one. Even if I do judge, my judgment is true, for I am not alone, but I am with the Father who sent me. It’s also written in your law that the testimony of two people is valid. I am one who testifies about myself, and the Father who sent me testifies about me.” They said therefore to him, “Where is your Father?” Jesus answered, “You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father also.” Jesus spoke these words in the treasury, as he taught in the temple. Yet no one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come.

Key verses.

John, chapter 1, verses 4 to 5. In him was life, and the life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.

The Context.

Jesus speaks this statement in Jerusalem during the Feast of Tabernacles. Each evening of this feast, in the Temple courtyard, they lit massive lampstands. Their light was so bright they say it illuminated the entire city. These flames recalled the pillar of fire that had guided Israel at night in the wilderness.

It's probably before these lights that Jesus stands up and declares: "Then Jesus again spoke to them, saying, 'I am the Light of the world; he who follows Me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the Light of life.'" (John, chapter 8, verse 12)

Imagine the effect. Like someone standing up during fireworks and saying: "The real light—that's me."

What Jesus Reveals.

The entire Bible begins with light. Before the sun, before the stars, God speaks: "And God said, 'Let there be light,' and there was light." (Genesis, chapter 1, verse 3) And John opens his Gospel in echo of that first day of creation: "In him was life, and that life was the light of all mankind. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it." (John, chapter 1, verses 4 to 5)

Jesus is not a light among others, one more wisdom beside the philosophers. He is "the Light of the world," the one who reveals the truth about God, about us, and about the path to follow.

Light does three things. First, it reveals. In darkness, you see neither the dirt nor the danger. When Jesus enters a life, he brings to light what was hidden. That can hurt, but it's always to heal, never to shame. Just before this statement, John tells of the woman caught in adultery: Jesus exposed the sin of all her accusers, then he said to the woman: "Go, and do not sin again." His light unveils, then it restores.

Next, light guides. Notice the promise: "he who follows Me will not walk in the darkness." Light is not made to be admired from a distance, but to walk by. You don't need to see your whole life's path; you need to see the next step. "Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path." (Psalm, chapter 119, verse 105) A lamp lights your feet, not the entire horizon. Jesus gives you light for today.

Finally, light gives life. Jesus speaks of "the Light of life." Without light, nothing grows. Right after this, in chapter 9, Jesus gives sight to a man born blind. This man can't explain everything, but he has an unbeatable testimony: "He answered, 'Whether he is a sinner I don't know. One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see.'" (John, chapter 9, verse 25)

For Your Life.

There may be dark areas in your life: a sin you're hiding, a fear that paralyzes you, a decision where you can't see clearly. Darkness pushes us to hide; Jesus invites us to come out. Don't run from his light. Let it enter those closed rooms of your heart. What he illuminates, he wants to heal.

And don't forget what comes next. The one who said "I am the Light of the world" also said to his disciples: "You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden;" (Matthew, chapter 5, verse 14) The moon has no light of its own; it shines because it reflects the sun. Neither do you have to produce your own light: you have to stay turned toward him. The more you walk close to Jesus, the more your life reflects something of him around you, in your family, at work, on social media.

Today, open the shutters of your heart.

Put it into practice.

One. Open One Closed Room. Choose just one dark area of your life (a hidden habit, a fear, a lie) and name it before God in writing. What is named in the light already loses some of its power.

Two. Talk to Someone You Trust. If this dark area has held you for a long time, share it with a brother, a sister, or a mature leader. James 5:16 invites us to confess our faults to one another so we can be healed.

Three. Reflect Light Where You Are. At work, at school, or in your family, make one luminous gesture today: a word of encouragement, a truth spoken gently, a quiet help. Like the moon, you shine by reflecting, not by forcing.

To reflect on. Is there an area of my life I'm keeping in shadow and don't dare expose to the light of Jesus?

Prayer. Jesus, you are the Light of the world. Come and illuminate every corner of my heart, even those I prefer to hide. Guide my steps today, and make my life a reflection of your light for those around me. Amen.

Key takeaway. Jesus doesn't show me the entire path, but he always lights my next step.

titre: The 7 "I Am" Statements of Jesus — Day 3
texte:
Day 3. I Am the Door.

Today's reading : John, chapter 10, verses 1 to 10.

“Most certainly, I tell you, one who doesn’t enter by the door into the sheep fold, but climbs up some other way, is a thief and a robber. But one who enters in by the door is the shepherd of the sheep. The gatekeeper opens the gate for him, and the sheep listen to his voice. He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. Whenever he brings out his own sheep, he goes before them; and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice. They will by no means follow a stranger, but will flee from him; for they don’t know the voice of strangers.” Jesus spoke this parable to them, but they didn’t understand what he was telling them. Jesus therefore said to them again, “Most certainly, I tell you, I am the sheep’s door. All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep didn’t listen to them. I am the door. If anyone enters in by me, he will be saved, and will go in and go out and will find pasture. The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.

The Context.

To understand this image, you need to picture a sheepfold from Jesus' time. In the evening, the shepherds would gather their sheep into a stone enclosure with a single opening. Often there wasn't even a real wooden door: the shepherd would lie down across the entrance himself. No sheep could leave, no wolf could enter, without passing over his body.

Jesus takes this simple image and declares: "I am the door. If anyone enters by Me, he will be saved; and will go in and out and find pasture." (John, chapter 10, verse 9)

What Jesus Reveals.

A door is both an opening and a protection. In these words, Jesus reveals three truths.

First: there is a door. God hasn't remained locked away from us. Heaven isn't an impossible fortress to reach. There is a way in, and it's not a system, a technique, or a religion: it's a person. Jesus doesn't say "I'll show you the door," but "I am the door."

Second: there is only one door. That's not very popular today, when people like to say all paths are equal. But the apostles preached it with confidence: "Nor is there salvation in any other, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved." (Acts, chapter 4, verse 12) That's not arrogance: it's good news. If salvation depended on my efforts, my morality, or my knowledge, I'd never be sure I'd done enough. But the door is Jesus, and He is open to everyone: "If anyone enters by Me..." Anyone at all. Including you.

Third: behind the door is life. Notice everything Jesus promises: to be saved, to enter, to go out, to find pasture. Entering means security, rest, belonging. Going out means freedom, growth, purpose. Pasture means food and abundance. Jesus didn't come to lock you down with rules; He came to open you up to a full life.

He says it with incredible force: "The thief does not come except to steal, and to kill, and to destroy. I have come that they may have life, and that they may have it to the full." (John, chapter 10, verse 10)

Two forces are at work. The thief, the enemy, comes for only three things: to steal your joy and peace, to kill your dreams and faith, to destroy your relationships and your future. But Jesus came for the exact opposite: life, and life overflowing. The word translated "to the full" means something that spills over, something in excess.

For Your Life.

Maybe you've felt like you're living a cramped Christian life: effort, guilt, little joy. That's not the life Jesus promises you. Identify what the thief is trying to take from you right now, and shut the door on him in Jesus' name. You don't have to put up with it: you're in the sheepfold, and your Shepherd is lying across the entrance.

And if you've never really entered, if you've been standing on the threshold for years, watching, hesitating—today the door is open. All you have to do is enter: tell Him that you receive Him as your Savior and Lord. He will not cast out anyone who comes to Him.

Put it into practice.

One. Identify the Thief. What is stealing your joy, peace, or faith right now? Write it down. Then pray out loud: "In Jesus' name, I shut the door to this thief. Jesus is my door."

Two. If You've Been Standing at the Threshold. If you've been watching faith from a distance for a long time, take ten minutes today to tell Jesus, in your own words, that you receive Him as your Savior and Lord. Then tell someone about it this week.

Three. For a More Abundant Life. Choose one thing that could make your life with God more alive this week: a worship service, a home group, a time of praise, serving. An abundant life grows in the sheepfold, not alone in your corner.

To reflect on. What is the thief trying to steal from me right now (peace, joy, faith, relationships), and how will I shut the door on him?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, You are the door. Thank You for opening the way to the Father for me. I refuse to let the enemy steal what You've given me. I choose to enter fully into the abundant life You've planned for me. Amen.

Key takeaway. The thief comes to take; Jesus came to give life in abundance.

Jesus takes this simple image and declares: "I am the door. If anyone enters by Me, he will be saved; and will go in and out and find pasture." (John, chapter 10, verse 9)

What Jesus Reveals.

A door is both an opening and a protection. In these words, Jesus reveals three truths.

First: there is a door. God hasn't remained locked away from us. Heaven isn't an impossible fortress to reach. There is a way in, and it's not a system, a technique, or a religion: it's a person. Jesus doesn't say "I'll show you the door," but "I am the door."

Second: there is only one door. That's not very popular today, when people like to say all paths are equal. But the apostles preached it with confidence: "Nor is there salvation in any other, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved." (Acts, chapter 4, verse 12) That's not arrogance: it's good news. If salvation depended on my efforts, my morality, or my knowledge, I'd never be sure I'd done enough. But the door is Jesus, and He is open to everyone: "If anyone enters by Me..." Anyone at all. Including you.

Third: behind the door is life. Notice everything Jesus promises: to be saved, to enter, to go out, to find pasture. Entering means security, rest, belonging. Going out means freedom, growth, purpose. Pasture means food and abundance. Jesus didn't come to lock you down with rules; He came to open you up to a full life.

He says it with incredible force: "The thief does not come except to steal, and to kill, and to destroy. I have come that they may have life, and that they may have it to the full." (John, chapter 10, verse 10)

Two forces are at work. The thief, the enemy, comes for only three things: to steal your joy and peace, to kill your dreams and faith, to destroy your relationships and your future. But Jesus came for the exact opposite: life, and life overflowing. The word translated "to the full" means something that spills over, something in excess.

For Your Life.

Maybe you've felt like you're living a cramped Christian life: effort, guilt, little joy. That's not the life Jesus promises you. Identify what the thief is trying to take from you right now, and shut the door on him in Jesus' name. You don't have to put up with it: you're in the sheepfold, and your Shepherd is lying across the entrance.

And if you've never really entered, if you've been standing on the threshold for years, watching, hesitating—today the door is open. All you have to do is enter: tell Him that you receive Him as your Savior and Lord. He will not cast out anyone who comes to Him.

Put it into practice.

One. Identify the Thief. What is stealing your joy, peace, or faith right now? Write it down. Then pray out loud: "In Jesus' name, I shut the door to this thief. Jesus is my door."

Two. If You've Been Standing at the Threshold. If you've been watching faith from a distance for a long time, take ten minutes today to tell Jesus, in your own words, that you receive Him as your Savior and Lord. Then tell someone about it this week.

Three. For a More Abundant Life. Choose one thing that could make your life with God more alive this week: a worship service, a home group, a time of praise, serving. An abundant life grows in the sheepfold, not alone in your corner.

To reflect on. What is the thief trying to steal from me right now (peace, joy, faith, relationships), and how will I shut the door on him?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, You are the door. Thank You for opening the way to the Father for me. I refuse to let the enemy steal what You've given me. I choose to enter fully into the abundant life You've planned for me. Amen.

Key takeaway. The thief comes to take; Jesus came to give life in abundance.

titre: The 7 "I Am" Statements of Jesus — Day 4
texte:
Day 4. I Am the Good Shepherd.

Today's reading : John, chapter 10, verses 11 to 18.

“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. He who is a hired hand, and not a shepherd, who doesn’t own the sheep, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees. The wolf snatches the sheep and scatters them. The hired hand flees because he is a hired hand and doesn’t care for the sheep. I am the good shepherd. I know my own, and I’m known by my own; even as the Father knows me, and I know the Father. I lay down my life for the sheep. I have other sheep which are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice. They will become one flock with one shepherd. Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, that I may take it again. No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. I received this commandment from my Father.”

Key verses.

John, chapter 10, verses 27 to 28. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.

The Context.

In the same conversation, Jesus continues the sheepfold image, but this time He presents Himself not as the door but as the shepherd. And not just any shepherd: "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd gives His life for the sheep." (John, chapter 10, verse 11)

For His Jewish listeners, this word carried weight of history. Abraham, Moses, David had all been shepherds. And most importantly, God Himself had presented Himself as the shepherd of His people. David had sung it in the most famous psalm in the Bible: "The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want." And through the prophet Ezekiel, God had made a promise at a time when Israel's leaders were mistreating the people: "For thus says the Lord God: Behold, I Myself will search for My sheep and seek them out." (Ezekiel, chapter 34, verse 11)

By saying "I am the good shepherd," Jesus affirms: this promise is fulfilled in Me. The God who is a shepherd has come in person.

What Jesus Reveals.

Jesus contrasts the good shepherd with the hired hand. The hired hand tends the sheep for money; when the wolf comes, he runs away, because the sheep don't belong to him. The good shepherd does the opposite: he doesn't run from danger, he stands between it and his sheep. And Jesus takes the image all the way: he doesn't just risk his life, he gives it.

That's exactly what He will do on the cross. Isaiah had announced it centuries before: "All we like sheep have gone astray; We have turned, every one, to his own way; And the Lord has laid on Him the iniquity of us all." (Isaiah, chapter 53, verse 6) The sheep had strayed; the shepherd paid the price. And Jesus makes clear that no one takes His life from Him: He gives it willingly, and He has the power to take it back again. The cross isn't an accident; it's an act of love He chose.

He also reveals something very tender: relationship. "I know My sheep, and am known by My own." In the large flocks of the East, shepherds often gave each sheep a name. Multiple flocks might spend the night in the same enclosure; in the morning, each shepherd would call his own, and they would recognize his voice among thousands.

"My sheep hear My voice, and I know them, and they follow Me. And I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish; neither shall anyone snatch them out of My hand." (John, chapter 10, verses 27 to 28)

Read that promise carefully: no one will snatch you out of His hand. Your security doesn't rest on how tightly you're holding Jesus, but on how tightly He's holding you.

For Your Life.

The good shepherd knows your name, your story, your wounds, your needs. You're not a number in a crowd. You are known and loved personally.

The question is: do I recognize His voice? He speaks through His Word, through His Spirit, through the peace or unease He puts in your heart, through brothers and sisters. But there are many other voices around us: fear, guilt, opinions, social media. You learn to recognize a voice by spending time with that person. The more time you spend with your Shepherd, the more familiar His voice becomes, and the more power the other voices lose.

Today, if you feel lost, exhausted, or under attack, remember: you have a shepherd who doesn't run away. He came to find you, He gave His life for you, and He will not let you go.

Put it into practice.

One. Learn His Voice. This week, read a short passage from the Gospels each day and note one sentence that touches you. You learn to recognize the Shepherd's voice by spending time with Him.

Two. Sort Out the Voices. Each evening, ask yourself: what voices did I listen to today? Fear, guilt, social media, my family, God? Put the ones that don't come from the Shepherd back in their place.

Three. If You Are Responsible for Others. Parent, manager, church leader: you are also a shepherd to someone. Choose one person in your care and reach out to them this week, really listening to them.

To reflect on. What voices are taking up the most space in my thoughts right now, and how can I make more space for my Shepherd's voice?

Prayer. Jesus, my good Shepherd, thank You for giving Your life for me. Thank You for knowing my name. Teach me to recognize Your voice among all the others, and to follow You with confidence. I rest in Your hand. Amen.

Key takeaway. My security doesn't depend on how tightly I hold Jesus, but on how tightly He holds me.

titre: The 7 "I Am" Statements of Jesus — Day 5
texte:
Day 5. I Am the Resurrection and the Life.

Today's reading : John, chapter 11, verses 17 to 44.

So when Jesus came, he found that he had been in the tomb four days already. Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away. Many of the Jews had joined the women around Martha and Mary, to console them concerning their brother. Then when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary stayed in the house. Therefore Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died. Even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.” Jesus said to her, “Your brother will rise again.” Martha said to him, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day.” Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies. Whoever lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?” She said to him, “Yes, Lord. I have come to believe that you are the Christ, God’s Son, he who comes into the world.” When she had said this, she went away and called Mary, her sister, secretly, saying, “The Teacher is here and is calling you.” When she heard this, she arose quickly and went to him. Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was in the place where Martha met him. Then the Jews who were with her in the house and were consoling her, when they saw Mary, that she rose up quickly and went out, followed her, saying, “She is going to the tomb to weep there.” Therefore when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell down at his feet, saying to him, “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died.” When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews weeping who came with her, he groaned in the spirit and was troubled, and said, “Where have you laid him?” They told him, “Lord, come and see.” Jesus wept. The Jews therefore said, “See how much affection he had for him!” Some of them said, “Couldn’t this man, who opened the eyes of him who was blind, have also kept this man from dying?” Jesus therefore, again groaning in himself, came to the tomb. Now it was a cave, and a stone lay against it. Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha, the sister of him who was dead, said to him, “Lord, by this time there is a stench, for he has been dead four days.” Jesus said to her, “Didn’t I tell you that if you believed, you would see God’s glory?” So they took away the stone from the place where the dead man was lying. Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, “Father, I thank you that you listened to me. I know that you always listen to me, but because of the multitude standing around I said this, that they may believe that you sent me.” When he had said this, he cried with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!” He who was dead came out, bound hand and foot with wrappings, and his face was wrapped around with a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Free him, and let him go.”

The Context.

Lazarus, Jesus' friend, became ill. His sisters, Martha and Mary, sent word to Jesus. And Jesus... waited two more days before leaving. When He arrives in Bethany, Lazarus has been dead for four days. For the Jewish people of that time, four days meant all hope was gone: the body was already beginning to decay.

Martha comes to meet Him with a sentence many of us have spoken in sorrow: "Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died." Then she adds sincere but distant faith: she knows her brother will rise "on the last day."

That's when Jesus brings her into the present: "Jesus said to her, 'I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in Me, though he may die, he shall live. And whoever lives and believes in Me shall never die. Do you believe this?'" (John, chapter 11, verses 25 to 26)

What Jesus Reveals.

Martha believed in a future resurrection, a doctrine for the end of time. Jesus tells her: resurrection isn't just an event, it's a person, and that person is standing before you. He doesn't say "I will give resurrection," but "I am the resurrection." The life of God, the life that is stronger than death, is present in Him, now.

Then comes one of the shortest and most profound verses in the Bible: "Jesus wept." (John, chapter 11, verse 35) Jesus knows He's about to raise Lazarus in just a few moments, yet He weeps. He doesn't dismiss Martha and Mary's pain. He enters into their grief. Your God is not indifferent to your tears; He weeps with you before He acts for you.

Finally, He goes to the tomb and has the stone rolled away, despite objections: "He stinks by now." He prays to the Father, then: "Now when He had said these things, He cried with a loud voice, 'Lazarus, come forth!' And he who had died came out bound hand and foot with grave clothes, and his face was wrapped with a cloth. Jesus said to them, 'Loose him, and let him go.'" (John, chapter 11, verses 43 to 44)

Notice two details. First, Jesus calls Lazarus by name; some have said with a smile that if He had just said "Come out!" all the dead in the cemetery would have come out. Second, He gives a task to the witnesses: "Loose him." Jesus gives life, but He involves His community in removing the grave clothes.

For Your Life.

The raising of Lazarus was a sign. Lazarus would die again later. But it pointed to Jesus' own resurrection, just days later, and to ours. For the one who believes, death no longer has the final word. Paul could declare: "O Death, where is your sting? O Hades, where is your victory?" (1 Corinthians, chapter 15, verse 55)

And this power is not reserved for the afterlife. Paul affirms that the Spirit who raised Jesus dwells in those who believe: "But if the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, He who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through His Spirit who dwells in you." (Romans, chapter 8, verse 11) This is the same life that heals the sick, that lifts up the discouraged, that resurrects marriages, dreams, a faith grown cold.

There may be an area of your life you've buried: "It's too late, it's already decaying." Jesus is never too late. Let Him roll away the stone. And maybe around you, someone has come out of the tomb but is still bound by grave clothes: old habits, wounds, shame. God may be asking you to help loose them.

Jesus asks you the same question He asked Martha: "Do you believe this?"

Put it into practice.

One. Name What Seems Dead. A dream, a relationship, your faith, your joy? Write it down, then pray: "Jesus, You are the resurrection and the life, even here." Keep this paper in your Bible and note the signs of life God gives you.

Two. If You Are Grieving. Reread John 11:35 and 1 Thessalonians 4:13-14. You have the right to weep; Jesus wept. But weep with hope. If the sorrow is heavy, don't stay alone: call someone from your church today.

Three. For Someone Else. Think of someone who has lost hope. Send them a simple message with John 11:25, or invite them for coffee. Sometimes hope reaches someone through an outstretched hand.

To reflect on. What area of my life have I "buried" thinking it was too late, and will I let Jesus roll away the stone?

Prayer. Jesus, you are the resurrection and the life. Thank you for weeping with me in my grief. I believe you are never too late. I bring to you what I have buried: breathe life into it. And help me unbind those who are coming out of their tombs. Amen.

Key takeaway. Jesus is never too late: wherever he enters, death no longer has the final word.

titre: The 7 "I Am" Statements of Jesus — Day 6
texte:
Day 6. I Am the Way, the Truth, and the Life.

Today's reading : John, chapter 14, verses 1 to 14.

“Don’t let your heart be troubled. Believe in God. Believe also in me. In my Father’s house are many homes. If it weren’t so, I would have told you. I am going to prepare a place for you. If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will receive you to myself; that where I am, you may be there also. You know where I go, and you know the way.” Thomas said to him, “Lord, we don’t know where you are going. How can we know the way?” Jesus said to him, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me. If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on, you know him and have seen him.” Philip said to him, “Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us.” Jesus said to him, “Have I been with you such a long time, and do you not know me, Philip? He who has seen me has seen the Father. How do you say, ‘Show us the Father’? Don’t you believe that I am in the Father, and the Father in me? The words that I tell you, I speak not from myself; but the Father who lives in me does his works. Believe me that I am in the Father, and the Father in me; or else believe me for the very works’ sake. Most certainly I tell you, he who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do also; and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to my Father. Whatever you will ask in my name, I will do it, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If you will ask anything in my name, I will do it.

The Context.

We are at the evening of the Last Supper. Within a few hours, Jesus will be arrested. He has just announced that he is going away, that Peter will deny him, and the disciples are deeply troubled. It is in this moment of anguish that he speaks to them with immense tenderness: "Do not let your heart be troubled. Believe in God, believe also in me. In my Father's house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you? And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also." (John, chapter 14, verses 1 to 3)

Thomas, always direct, dares to say what everyone is thinking: "Lord, we do not know where you are going; how can we know the way?" And Jesus responds with the sixth "I Am" statement: "Jesus said to him, 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.'" (John, chapter 14, verse 6)

What Jesus Reveals.

Thomas asks for directions; Jesus gives him a person. When you ask for directions in an unfamiliar city, there are two types of people: those who explain "turn right, then take the second left...," and those who say "follow me, I'll take you there." Jesus doesn't give you a map: he is the guide, and he is the road.

He is the Way. The way to where? To the Father. The goal of the Christian life is not first to go to heaven as you would go to a place, but to know God as you know a Father. Jesus says this later in his prayer: "And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." (John, chapter 17, verse 3)

He is the Truth. Not just someone who speaks true things, but the truth in person: the truth about God, because "whoever has seen me has seen the Father"; the truth about you, about your worth and your sin; the truth that sets free. "So Jesus said to the Jews who had believed him, 'If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.'" (John, chapter 8, verses 31 to 32) In a world where everyone wants "their truth," Jesus is a fixed point, solid, unchanging.

He is the Life. Not a better version of your current life, but the very life of God, eternal, which begins right now.

Then he adds: "No one comes to the Father except through me." As with the door, this is not a word of exclusion; it is a word of clarity. Jesus does not say "no one comes to the Father without having lived well enough," but "through me." The way is narrow, but it is open to all.

And in this same passage, Jesus makes a stunning promise to his disciples: whoever believes in him will also do the works that he does, and even greater works, because he is going to the Father. Those who follow the way do not remain spectators: they continue his work through his Spirit.

For Your Life.

The disciples had troubled hearts because they saw their future growing dark. Perhaps your heart is also troubled: an exam, an illness, a loss, uncertainty about your future. Jesus does not say to you "everything will always be fine"; he says to you: "believe in me." You do not know the entire path, but you know the Way.

When you have to make a decision, before asking "which road should I take?", ask: "Am I walking with Jesus in this decision?" When you hear contradictory voices, return to the truth of his Word. And when you feel empty, return to the source of life.

He is preparing a place for you, and he will come back to get you. Your destination is sure, and so is your guide.

Put it into practice.

One. Before Making a Decision. If you have a choice to make, first write: "Am I walking with Jesus in this decision?" Then pray, look for what his Word says, and ask advice from a mature believer before you decide.

Two. When Your Heart Is Troubled. Learn John 14:1 by heart. Every time worry rises (an exam, a medical appointment, a bill, your children's future), say it out loud and give that specific concern to Jesus.

Three. Testify to the Way. Think of someone who is searching for his way. Without preaching, tell him in two minutes how Jesus showed you the way at a moment in your life.

To reflect on. In what situation in my life is my heart troubled, and how can I choose today to trust the Way rather than seek out the whole map?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you are the way, the truth, and the life. When my heart is troubled, teach me to believe in you. Lead me to the Father, keep me in your truth, and fill me with your life. I follow you. Amen.

Key takeaway. I do not know the entire path, but I know the Way.

titre: The 7 "I Am" Statements of Jesus — Day 7
texte:
Day 7. I Am the True Vine.

Today's reading : John, chapter 15, verses 1 to 17.

“I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer. Every branch in me that doesn’t bear fruit, he takes away. Every branch that bears fruit, he prunes, that it may bear more fruit. You are already pruned clean because of the word which I have spoken to you. Remain in me, and I in you. As the branch can’t bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me. I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing. If a man doesn’t remain in me, he is thrown out as a branch and is withered; and they gather them, throw them into the fire, and they are burned. If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, you will ask whatever you desire, and it will be done for you. “In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit; and so you will be my disciples. Even as the Father has loved me, I also have loved you. Remain in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love, even as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love. I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full. “This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you. Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. You are my friends if you do whatever I command you. No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you. You didn’t choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain; that whatever you will ask of the Father in my name, he may give it to you. “I command these things to you, that you may love one another.

The Context.

After the meal, Jesus and his disciples leave the upper room and cross Jerusalem toward the Mount of Olives. According to some accounts, they pass in front of the Temple, whose entrance was decorated with a great golden vine, a symbol of Israel. In the Old Testament, Israel is often compared to a vine that God planted with love, but which did not produce the fruit expected. Isaiah sang of it with sadness: "Let me sing for my beloved my love song concerning his vineyard: My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill. He dug it and cleared out its stones, and planted it with choice vines; he built a watchtower in the midst of it, and hewed out a wine vat in it; and he looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes." (Isaiah, chapter 5, verses 1 to 2)

It is in this context that Jesus speaks the last of his seven "I Am" statements: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser." The true vine, the authentic vine: where Israel had failed, Jesus succeeds. And all those who are attached to him become branches that bear fruit.

What Jesus Reveals.

"I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing." (John, chapter 15, verse 5)

The vine is the root stock, the trunk connected to the roots. The branches are the limbs. A branch makes no effort to produce grapes. It does not strain, it does not worry, it does not grit its teeth. It remains attached, and the sap does the work. The fruit is not the result of its efforts, but of its connection.

The key word of this chapter is "abide." Jesus repeats it about ten times. "Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me." (John, chapter 15, verse 4) To abide is to remain, to dwell, to make your home in him. This is not a visit on Sunday; it is a moment-by-moment relationship.

Jesus also explains the work of the vinedresser: he removes branches that do not bear fruit, and he prunes those that do bear fruit so that they may bear even more. Pruning looks like a loss, but it is an investment. When God removes certain things from your life, it is not to punish you: it is so that the sap flows to what matters most.

And what is this fruit? First, the character of Jesus formed in us: "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law." (Galatians, chapter 5, verses 22 to 23) Next, lives touched around us: Jesus speaks of fruit that remains. Finally, a life of answered prayer: "If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and so prove to be my disciples." (John, chapter 15, verses 7 to 8)

For Your Life.

Notice the most humble statement in the entire chapter: "apart from me you can do nothing." Not "not much": nothing. This is liberating. You do not have to produce the Christian life by your own strength. Your work is not to manufacture fruit, but to remain connected.

Concretely, abiding means keeping his words in you: reading them, meditating on them, obeying them. It means staying in his love, and Jesus clarifies that this comes through obedience and love for one another. It means speaking to him throughout the day, not just at the beginning.

And here is the purpose of all of this, the final word of this plan: "I have told you these things, so that in me you may have peace. In this world you will have trouble. But take heart! I have overcome the world." (John, chapter 15, verse 11)

In seven days, you have discovered that Jesus is your bread, your light, your door, your shepherd, your resurrection, your way, and your vine. The same "I Am" who spoke to Moses in the burning bush wants to dwell in you. Do not leave him again.

Put it into practice.

One. Set Your Appointment. Choose a specific time each day to stay connected to the vine: fifteen minutes of Scripture and prayer. Write it in your calendar as an appointment you do not miss.

Two. Pray as You Walk. Abiding is not just in the morning. Choose three moments in your day (your commute, a break, doing dishes) to say a sentence to Jesus. Little by little, the conversation becomes continuous.

Three. Keep the Fruit of These 7 Days. Write the 7 "I Am" statements on a card and place it on your fridge or as your phone wallpaper. When a situation comes, ask: which "I Am" do I need today?

To reflect on. What disconnects me most often from Jesus during my day, and what simple habit could help me "abide" in him?

Prayer. Jesus, you are the true vine and I am a branch. Apart from you I can do nothing. I choose to abide in you, in your Word and in your love. Father, prune in me what needs to be pruned, so that I may bear much fruit, and that my joy may be complete. Amen.

Key takeaway. My work is not to manufacture fruit, but to remain attached to Jesus.

texte:
Day 1. Lord, Teach Us to Pray.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 11, verses 1 to 13.

When he finished praying in a certain place, one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John also taught his disciples.” He said to them, “When you pray, say, ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. May your Kingdom come. May your will be done on earth, as it is in heaven. Give us day by day our daily bread. Forgive us our sins, for we ourselves also forgive everyone who is indebted to us. Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.’” He said to them, “Which of you, if you go to a friend at midnight and tell him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves of bread, for a friend of mine has come to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him,’ and he from within will answer and say, ‘Don’t bother me. The door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I can’t get up and give it to you’? I tell you, although he will not rise and give it to him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence, he will get up and give him as many as he needs. “I tell you, keep asking, and it will be given you. Keep seeking, and you will find. Keep knocking, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives. He who seeks finds. To him who knocks it will be opened. “Which of you fathers, if your son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, he won’t give him a snake instead of a fish, will he? Or if he asks for an egg, he won’t give him a scorpion, will he? If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?”

The Context.

The disciples saw Jesus walk on water, multiply loaves, heal lepers, cast out demons, raise the dead. And yet, they never asked him, "Teach us to do miracles." The only thing they ever asked him to teach them was prayer.

"One day Jesus was praying in a certain place. When he finished, one of his disciples said to him, 'Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples.'" (Luke, chapter 11, verse 1)

Why? Because they understood where everything else came from. They saw Jesus disappear before dawn: "Very early in the morning, while it was still dark, Jesus got up, left the house and went off to a solitary place, where he prayed." (Mark, chapter 1, verse 35) They watched him withdraw after long days of ministry. They had noticed that the power he displayed in public came from what he lived in secret.

What Jesus Teaches Us.

The disciples' request should already reassure you: prayer is something you learn. No one is born knowing how to pray. Even those who had grown up in the synagogue, who knew the Psalms by heart, felt something was missing.

Think of a baby learning to talk. He says "da… da…," he mixes up words, he makes mistakes. Does his father laugh at him? Does he wait for the child to speak perfectly before listening? No—every little word melts him. God isn't waiting to catch you out for fumbling with your words. He rejoices that you come.

Jesus then gives them a model, what we call the Lord's Prayer. It's not a formula to recite mechanically: just before, in Matthew, he warns against those who "use many meaningless words." Rather, it's a framework, like the load-bearing walls of a house. Each phrase opens a room: worship, the kingdom, God's will, our needs, forgiveness, spiritual battle. Over ten days, we'll visit these rooms one by one.

Then Jesus tells the story of a friend who knocks on his neighbor's door at midnight to borrow bread, and who insists until he gets it. And he concludes: "So I say to you: Ask and it will be given to you; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; the one who seeks finds; and to the one who knocks, the door will be opened." (Luke, chapter 11, verses 9 to 10)

Ask, seek, knock—three verbs of increasing intensity. Prayer is not religious politeness; it's an active, persevering, confident pursuit.

And he ends with a promise that reveals the Father's heart: What father would give his son a snake if he asked for a fish? How much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him! The greatest answer to prayer is not just something God gives—it's God himself giving himself.

Prayer is not learned from a book; it's learned on your knees.

For Your Life.

Many Christians live with silent guilt: "I don't pray enough. I don't know how to pray. I fall asleep, I get bored, I think of something else." If that's you, good news: you're exactly where the disciples were. And that's the best place to start.

For these ten days, I'm suggesting three very simple things. A time: choose a fixed slot, even ten minutes, rather than "a moment sometime" that never comes. A place: Jesus speaks of "going into your room and closing the door"; find your corner, your chair, your parked car, your walking route. An honest heart: start with the disciples' prayer: "Lord, teach me to pray."

It's not a small prayer. It's the beginning of a revolution.

Put it into practice.

One. A Fixed Time. Choose a specific time slot for the next ten days: ten minutes when you wake up, at lunch or before bed. Set an alarm. A moment "when you have time" never comes.

Two. Your Own Place. Your armchair, your parked car, your bedroom with the door closed, a walk around the neighborhood. If you have young children and no quiet space, pray during their nap or while pushing the stroller—God hears you there too.

Three. An Honest Prayer. Start today with just one sentence, the disciples' prayer: "Lord, teach me to pray." Then tell him simply what keeps you from praying. That's already a prayer.

To reflect on. What keeps me from praying the most: lack of time, lack of motivation, or feeling like I don't know how to do it?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, like your disciples, I ask you: teach me to pray. Forgive me for rushed and distracted prayers. During these ten days, draw me into the secret place, and let my prayer life become a real encounter with you. Amen.

Key takeaway. Prayer is not learned from a book; it's learned on your knees.

May your Kingdom come. May your will be done on earth, as it is in heaven. Give us day by day our daily bread. Forgive us our sins, for we ourselves also forgive everyone who is indebted to us. Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.’” He said to them, “Which of you, if you go to a friend at midnight and tell him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves of bread, for a friend of mine has come to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him,’ and he from within will answer and say, ‘Don’t bother me. The door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I can’t get up and give it to you’? I tell you, although he will not rise and give it to him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence, he will get up and give him as many as he needs. “I tell you, keep asking, and it will be given you. Keep seeking, and you will find. Keep knocking, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives. He who seeks finds. To him who knocks it will be opened. “Which of you fathers, if your son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, he won’t give him a snake instead of a fish, will he? Or if he asks for an egg, he won’t give him a scorpion, will he? If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?”

The Context.

The disciples saw Jesus walk on water, multiply loaves, heal lepers, cast out demons, raise the dead. And yet, they never asked him, "Teach us to do miracles." The only thing they ever asked him to teach them was prayer.

"One day Jesus was praying in a certain place. When he finished, one of his disciples said to him, 'Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples.'" (Luke, chapter 11, verse 1)

Why? Because they understood where everything else came from. They saw Jesus disappear before dawn: "Very early in the morning, while it was still dark, Jesus got up, left the house and went off to a solitary place, where he prayed." (Mark, chapter 1, verse 35) They watched him withdraw after long days of ministry. They had noticed that the power he displayed in public came from what he lived in secret.

What Jesus Teaches Us.

The disciples' request should already reassure you: prayer is something you learn. No one is born knowing how to pray. Even those who had grown up in the synagogue, who knew the Psalms by heart, felt something was missing.

Think of a baby learning to talk. He says "da… da…," he mixes up words, he makes mistakes. Does his father laugh at him? Does he wait for the child to speak perfectly before listening? No—every little word melts him. God isn't waiting to catch you out for fumbling with your words. He rejoices that you come.

Jesus then gives them a model, what we call the Lord's Prayer. It's not a formula to recite mechanically: just before, in Matthew, he warns against those who "use many meaningless words." Rather, it's a framework, like the load-bearing walls of a house. Each phrase opens a room: worship, the kingdom, God's will, our needs, forgiveness, spiritual battle. Over ten days, we'll visit these rooms one by one.

Then Jesus tells the story of a friend who knocks on his neighbor's door at midnight to borrow bread, and who insists until he gets it. And he concludes: "So I say to you: Ask and it will be given to you; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; the one who seeks finds; and to the one who knocks, the door will be opened." (Luke, chapter 11, verses 9 to 10)

Ask, seek, knock—three verbs of increasing intensity. Prayer is not religious politeness; it's an active, persevering, confident pursuit.

And he ends with a promise that reveals the Father's heart: What father would give his son a snake if he asked for a fish? How much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him! The greatest answer to prayer is not just something God gives—it's God himself giving himself.

Prayer is not learned from a book; it's learned on your knees.

For Your Life.

Many Christians live with silent guilt: "I don't pray enough. I don't know how to pray. I fall asleep, I get bored, I think of something else." If that's you, good news: you're exactly where the disciples were. And that's the best place to start.

For these ten days, I'm suggesting three very simple things. A time: choose a fixed slot, even ten minutes, rather than "a moment sometime" that never comes. A place: Jesus speaks of "going into your room and closing the door"; find your corner, your chair, your parked car, your walking route. An honest heart: start with the disciples' prayer: "Lord, teach me to pray."

It's not a small prayer. It's the beginning of a revolution.

Put it into practice.

One. A Fixed Time. Choose a specific time slot for the next ten days: ten minutes when you wake up, at lunch or before bed. Set an alarm. A moment "when you have time" never comes.

Two. Your Own Place. Your armchair, your parked car, your bedroom with the door closed, a walk around the neighborhood. If you have young children and no quiet space, pray during their nap or while pushing the stroller—God hears you there too.

Three. An Honest Prayer. Start today with just one sentence, the disciples' prayer: "Lord, teach me to pray." Then tell him simply what keeps you from praying. That's already a prayer.

To reflect on. What keeps me from praying the most: lack of time, lack of motivation, or feeling like I don't know how to do it?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, like your disciples, I ask you: teach me to pray. Forgive me for rushed and distracted prayers. During these ten days, draw me into the secret place, and let my prayer life become a real encounter with you. Amen.

Key takeaway. Prayer is not learned from a book; it's learned on your knees.

Day 2. Our Father.

Today's reading : Matthew, chapter 6, verses 5 to 9.

“When you pray, you shall not be as the hypocrites, for they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen by men. Most certainly, I tell you, they have received their reward. But you, when you pray, enter into your inner room, and having shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly. In praying, don’t use vain repetitions as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard for their much speaking. Therefore don’t be like them, for your Father knows what things you need before you ask him. Pray like this: “‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.

Key verses.

Romans, chapter 8, verse 15. For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!”

The Context.

In the Old Testament, God is sometimes compared to a father, but almost no one addresses him directly by that name. He is called the Lord, the God of Abraham, the Most High, the Lord of Hosts. And now Jesus opens his prayer with two words that must have surprised everyone: "Our Father."

"This, then, is how you should pray: 'Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name'" (Matthew, chapter 6, verse 9)

Jesus himself prayed by saying "Abba." It's a simple Aramaic word that a child uses when speaking to his father, with warmth and trust—something like "daddy," but with respect. And the most incredible thing is that he gives us the right to use it too: "The Spirit you received does not make you slaves, so that you live in fear again; rather, the Spirit you received brought about your adoption to sonship. And by him we cry, 'Abba, Father.'" (Romans, chapter 8, verse 15)

What Jesus Teaches Us.

There's a famous photograph taken at the White House in the 1960s: President Kennedy is working in the Oval Office, one of the most powerful rooms in the world, and his little son is playing under his desk. Ministers and generals waited for hours to get a few minutes with this man. The child walked in without an appointment. Why? Not because he was important, but because he was his son.

That's exactly what Jesus offers you. You don't enter God's presence like an employee asking for a raise, and not like a defendant before a judge. You enter like a child into his Father's house. Your place is not based on how well you performed this week, but on what Jesus did for you.

Notice too the first word: "our." Jesus doesn't begin with "my Father." Even in the secret place, when you pray alone, you're part of a family. You pray with millions of brothers and sisters around the world and throughout the centuries. The Lord's Prayer teaches us that prayer is never selfish—it carries others.

Maybe the word "father" is hard for you. Your father was absent, harsh, violent, or you never knew him. And when you hear "God is your Father," you imagine someone distant, cold, or dangerous. I want to tell you gently: God is not your earthly father on a larger scale. He is the perfect Father your heart has always needed. David, who knew what it was to be forgotten by his family, wrote: "Though my father and mother forsake me, the Lord will receive me." (Psalm, chapter 27, verse 10)

You don't have to fix your past to approach this Father. Let him—let him heal the picture you have of a father.

It's not your prayer that makes you God's child; because you are his child that you can pray.

For Your Life.

Today, before asking for anything, just take a moment to say: "Father." Repeat it slowly, without adding anything else. Let that word sink into your heart. You're not alone, you're not an orphan, you're not a number.

And if the word sticks, if it awakens pain, tell God honestly: "Father, I don't know what it means to have a real father. Teach me." That might be the most powerful prayer you pray this week.

Then think of "our": pray for a brother, a sister, someone in your faith family who is going through a hard time. You never pray alone.

Put it into practice.

One. Say "Father". Today, before any request, say "Father" slowly several times, pausing silently between each one. Let that word do its work in you.

Two. If the Word "Father" Hurts. If your father hurt, abandoned, or disappointed you, say it to God without holding back. Ask him to show you what a real father is. You might also talk about it with a pastor or trusted friend.

Three. Think of "Our". Today, pray by name for three people in your faith family. Send a message to one of them: "I prayed for you this morning."

To reflect on. What image do I naturally have of God when I pray: a judge, a boss, a stranger, or a Father?

Prayer. Father, thank you for calling me your child. Thank you for Jesus, who opened the door of your house for me. Heal the picture I have of a father, and teach me to come to you with confidence, like a child, without an appointment. Amen.

Key takeaway. I don't enter God's house like an employee—I enter like a child with his Father.

Day 3. Who Is in Heaven.

Today's reading : Psalms, chapter 8, verses 1 to 10.

For the Chief Musician; on an instrument of Gath. A Psalm by David. LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth! You have set your glory above the heavens! From the lips of babes and infants you have established strength, because of your adversaries, that you might silence the enemy and the avenger. When I consider your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have ordained, what is man, that you think of him? What is the son of man, that you care for him? For you have made him a little lower than the angels, and crowned him with glory and honor. You make him ruler over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet: All sheep and cattle, yes, and the animals of the field, the birds of the sky, the fish of the sea, and whatever passes through the paths of the seas. LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!

Key verses.

Psalms, chapter 115, verse 3. But our God is in the heavens. He does whatever he pleases.

Isaiah, chapter 55, verses 8 to 9. “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not my ways,” says the LORD. “For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.

The Context.

Yesterday, we saw that God is a close, tender, accessible Father. But Jesus doesn't stop at "Our Father." He immediately adds: "who is in heaven." These three words don't mean God is far away, somewhere above the clouds. In the Bible, "the heavens" refers to God's place, his reign, his sovereignty over all things.

"Our God is in heaven; he does all that he pleases." (Psalm, chapter 115, verse 3)

Jesus holds together two truths that we tend to separate: God is close enough that I can call him Father, and great enough to govern the universe.

What Jesus Teaches Us.

In 1990, the spacecraft Voyager 1, billions of miles away, turned around one last time to photograph Earth. In the image, our planet is just a tiny pale blue dot, barely visible in a ray of light. Everything we know, all of human history, fits in that pixel.

David didn't have a spacecraft, but he had looked up at the starry sky and felt the same thing: "When I consider your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have set in place, what is mankind that you are mindful of them, human beings that you care for them?" (Psalm, chapter 8, verses 3 to 4)

That's the wonderful tension of prayer. The God who created billions of galaxies knows the number of hairs on your head. The one who holds the universe holds your hand too.

If we forget that God is "in heaven," we turn him into a buddy, a personal assistant we call whenever we need something. Our prayer becomes small, centered on ourselves. If we forget he is "Father," we turn him into a distant, frightening being we don't dare speak to. Jesus keeps us from both mistakes.

Saying "who is in heaven" is also recognizing that God sees further than we do. "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, declares the Lord. As the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways and my thoughts than your thoughts." (Isaiah, chapter 55, verses 8 to 9) When a prayer seems to go unanswered as you hoped, it's not that God isn't listening; it's that he sees the whole picture, while you only see one piece of the puzzle. A four-year-old who asks for candy at breakfast doesn't always understand his father's "no." Later, he understands that the "no" was love.

My Father is close enough for me to hear him, and great enough to change everything.

For Your Life.

Before you present your problems to God, lift your gaze. Problems look enormous when you're close to them; they return to their true size when you place them before a God who is in heaven.

Today, if you can, pray outside or by a window. Look at the sky. Think about the greatness of the one who created it, then remind yourself that this same God calls you by name. Tell him: "You are great, and you are my Father. What worries me today is not too great for you."

And when you don't understand his answers, choose trust. He is in heaven—he sees what you don't yet see.

Put it into practice.

One. Pray While Looking at the Sky. Go outside for a few minutes, or sit by a window. Look at the sky, then present your main concern to God by saying: "This is not too big for you."

Two. Put Your Problems in Their Right Size. Write your biggest worry at the top of a page. Below it, write three things you know about God (he is all-powerful, he is faithful, he loves me). Read the list aloud.

Three. When You Don't Understand. If there's an answer from God you don't understand, write it down and tell him: "You see what I don't see. I choose to trust you." Psalm 8 can accompany you as you pray it.

To reflect on. Do I tend to make God a "buddy" who's too small, or a God who's too distant? How can I hold together both his closeness and his greatness?

Prayer. Our Father in heaven, you are greater than everything that worries me, and yet you remember me. Expand my vision. When I don't understand your ways, teach me to trust you, because you see what I don't yet see. Amen.

Key takeaway. My Father is close enough to hear me, and great enough to change everything.

texte:
Day 4. Hallowed Be Your Name.

Today's reading : Isaiah, chapter 6, verses 1 to 8.

In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple. Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings. With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew. One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!” The foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke. Then I said, “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips and I live among a people of unclean lips, for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of Armies!” Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with the tongs from off the altar. He touched my mouth with it, and said, “Behold, this has touched your lips; and your iniquity is taken away, and your sin forgiven.” I heard the Lord’s voice, saying, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” Then I said, “Here I am. Send me!”

Key verses.

Psalms, chapter 34, verse 4. I sought the LORD, and he answered me, and delivered me from all my fears.

The Context.

The first request of the Lord's Prayer is not about our needs. It's about God: "Hallowed be Your name." To hallow means to set apart, to recognize as holy, to honor as unique. In the Bible, a name is not just a label—it reveals who a person is.

The prophet Isaiah experienced what God's holiness means one day. In a vision, he sees the Lord on a throne, and seraphs crying out: "They were calling to one another: 'Holy, holy, holy is the Lord Almighty; the whole earth is full of his glory!'" (Isaiah, chapter 6, verse 3) The foundations of the Temple shake. And Isaiah, overwhelmed, realizes his own smallness—before God purifies him and sends him out.

What Jesus Teaches Us.

Jesus teaches us to begin prayer with worship. Not because God needs compliments, but because we need to put things back in their proper place.

Have you ever tried to look at a tiny pebble held right in front of your eye? It hides the entire mountain. Our problems do the same thing: stuck in front of our eyes, they hide God. Worship moves the pebble and helps us see the mountain again.

In the Old Testament, God revealed his name through concrete situations. When Abraham saw God provide the sacrifice on Mount Moriah: "Abraham called that place 'The Lord Will Provide.' And to this day it is said, 'On the mountain of the Lord it will be provided.'" (Genesis, chapter 22, verse 14) When Israel, thirsty in the desert, saw bitter waters become sweet, God said: "I am the Lord, who heals you." When Gideon, terrified, received God's peace, he built an altar and called it "The Lord Is Peace."

Each name of God is an answer to a human need. He provides, he heals, he gives peace, he is my shepherd, he fights for me. Hallowing his name means declaring: "You are all of this, and you are this for me today."

David understood this. He invited others to join him: "Glorify the Lord with me; let us exalt his name together!" (Psalms, chapter 34, verse 4) He wrote this psalm during one of the worst times of his life—he was fleeing from King Saul and had to pretend to be insane before a foreign king to save his life. And that's when he begins with: "I will extol the Lord at all times." Worship is not reserved for easy days. It is often the key that unlocks difficult days.

When God becomes great, my problems find their true size.

Put it into practice.

One. Five Minutes of Worship. Begin your prayer with five minutes without any requests: simply tell God who he is. You can use a psalm (Psalm 103 or 145) by reading it aloud.

Two. Pray His Names. Take three names of God (the One who provides, the One who heals, my peace) and connect each one to a situation in your life: "You are the One who provides, for this rent. You are the One who heals, for this knee."

Three. Honor His Name in Your Life. Choose one area where your life could better honor the name of Christ (the way you speak at work, your honesty, your patience at home) and take a concrete step today.

To reflect on. Which name of God (the One who provides, who heals, my peace, my shepherd) do I most need to proclaim in my current situation?

Prayer. Our Father, hallowed be Your name. You are holy, holy, holy. You are the One who provides, the One who heals, my peace and my shepherd. Before I ask you for anything else, I want to worship you for who you are. Let my entire life honor your name. Amen.

Key takeaway. When God becomes great, my problems find their true size.

With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew. One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!” The foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke. Then I said, “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips and I live among a people of unclean lips, for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of Armies!” Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with the tongs from off the altar. He touched my mouth with it, and said, “Behold, this has touched your lips; and your iniquity is taken away, and your sin forgiven.” I heard the Lord’s voice, saying, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” Then I said, “Here I am. Send me!”

Key verses.

Psalms, chapter 34, verse 4. I sought the LORD, and he answered me, and delivered me from all my fears.

The Context.

The first request of the Lord's Prayer is not about our needs. It's about God: "Hallowed be Your name." To hallow means to set apart, to recognize as holy, to honor as unique. In the Bible, a name is not just a label—it reveals who a person is.

The prophet Isaiah experienced what God's holiness means one day. In a vision, he sees the Lord on a throne, and seraphs crying out: "They were calling to one another: 'Holy, holy, holy is the Lord Almighty; the whole earth is full of his glory!'" (Isaiah, chapter 6, verse 3) The foundations of the Temple shake. And Isaiah, overwhelmed, realizes his own smallness—before God purifies him and sends him out.

What Jesus Teaches Us.

Jesus teaches us to begin prayer with worship. Not because God needs compliments, but because we need to put things back in their proper place.

Have you ever tried to look at a tiny pebble held right in front of your eye? It hides the entire mountain. Our problems do the same thing: stuck in front of our eyes, they hide God. Worship moves the pebble and helps us see the mountain again.

In the Old Testament, God revealed his name through concrete situations. When Abraham saw God provide the sacrifice on Mount Moriah: "Abraham called that place 'The Lord Will Provide.' And to this day it is said, 'On the mountain of the Lord it will be provided.'" (Genesis, chapter 22, verse 14) When Israel, thirsty in the desert, saw bitter waters become sweet, God said: "I am the Lord, who heals you." When Gideon, terrified, received God's peace, he built an altar and called it "The Lord Is Peace."

Each name of God is an answer to a human need. He provides, he heals, he gives peace, he is my shepherd, he fights for me. Hallowing his name means declaring: "You are all of this, and you are this for me today."

David understood this. He invited others to join him: "Glorify the Lord with me; let us exalt his name together!" (Psalms, chapter 34, verse 4) He wrote this psalm during one of the worst times of his life—he was fleeing from King Saul and had to pretend to be insane before a foreign king to save his life. And that's when he begins with: "I will extol the Lord at all times." Worship is not reserved for easy days. It is often the key that unlocks difficult days.

When God becomes great, my problems find their true size.

Put it into practice.

One. Five Minutes of Worship. Begin your prayer with five minutes without any requests: simply tell God who he is. You can use a psalm (Psalm 103 or 145) by reading it aloud.

Two. Pray His Names. Take three names of God (the One who provides, the One who heals, my peace) and connect each one to a situation in your life: "You are the One who provides, for this rent. You are the One who heals, for this knee."

Three. Honor His Name in Your Life. Choose one area where your life could better honor the name of Christ (the way you speak at work, your honesty, your patience at home) and take a concrete step today.

To reflect on. Which name of God (the One who provides, who heals, my peace, my shepherd) do I most need to proclaim in my current situation?

Prayer. Our Father, hallowed be Your name. You are holy, holy, holy. You are the One who provides, the One who heals, my peace and my shepherd. Before I ask you for anything else, I want to worship you for who you are. Let my entire life honor your name. Amen.

Key takeaway. When God becomes great, my problems find their true size.
