Day 5. Your Kingdom Come.

Today's reading : Mark, chapter 1, verses 14 to 28.

Now after John was taken into custody, Jesus came into Galilee, preaching the Good News of God’s Kingdom, and saying, “The time is fulfilled, and God’s Kingdom is at hand! Repent, and believe in the Good News.” Passing along by the sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew, the brother of Simon, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. Jesus said to them, “Come after me, and I will make you into fishers for men.” Immediately they left their nets, and followed him. Going on a little further from there, he saw James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, who were also in the boat mending the nets. Immediately he called them, and they left their father, Zebedee, in the boat with the hired servants, and went after him. They went into Capernaum, and immediately on the Sabbath day he entered into the synagogue and taught. They were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as having authority, and not as the scribes. Immediately there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit, and he cried out, saying, “Ha! What do we have to do with you, Jesus, you Nazarene? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God!” Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be quiet, and come out of him!” The unclean spirit, convulsing him and crying with a loud voice, came out of him. They were all amazed, so that they questioned among themselves, saying, “What is this? What can this new doctrine be? For with authority he commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him!” The report of him went out immediately into all the region of Galilee and its surrounding area.

Key verses.

Matthew, chapter 6, verse 33. But seek first God’s Kingdom and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.

The Context.

Jesus's very first message, at the beginning of his ministry, fits in one sentence: "The time has come," he said. "The kingdom of God has come near. Repent and believe the good news." (Mark, chapter 1, verse 15) The kingdom of God is the heart of all his preaching. And right after, Mark tells us that Jesus enters a synagogue, teaches with authority, and casts an unclean spirit out of a man. God's kingdom is not just an idea—it manifests.

When Jesus teaches us to pray "Your kingdom come," he invites us to ask that this kingdom expand: in our hearts, in our families, in our cities, and until the day it is fully established.

What Jesus Teaches Us.

God's kingdom is where God reigns, where his will is done, where his presence changes things. And this kingdom has something surprising about it: it is both here already and not yet complete.

It is already here. Jesus said so himself: "But if I drive out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you." (Luke, chapter 11, verse 20) Every time someone is healed in the name of Jesus, every time a person is set free, every time a heart is restored, every time a sinner returns to the Father, God's kingdom breaks into the earth. Paul sums it up: "For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit." (Romans, chapter 14, verse 17)

And it is not yet fully here. There is still sickness, injustice, war, death. One day, the kingdom will be fully established, and the Bible describes that moment with splendor: "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Messiah, and he will reign for ever and ever."

Think of an embassy. In a large foreign city, the embassy of a nation is a small territory where that nation's laws apply. You pass through the door, and you are, in a sense, "in that country." The Church is an embassy of God's kingdom on earth. And you are one of its representatives. Paul says we serve "as Christ's ambassadors." Wherever you go—at work, at school, in your family—the kingdom enters with you.

To pray "Your kingdom come" is therefore a dangerous prayer. It means saying: "Lord, reign first over me." You cannot ask God to reign over the world while refusing him the throne of your own heart.

Don't ask God to bless your kingdom; ask him to bring his.

For Your Life.

Jesus made a promise to those who put his kingdom first: "Seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well." (Matthew, chapter 6, verse 33) Notice the order: first. Not "also," not "when I have time left over." First.

Today, ask yourself: What areas of my life are still "my kingdom" instead of his? My money, my time, my relationships, my projects, my hobbies? Open them one by one in prayer: "Lord, may your kingdom come here too."

Then expand your prayer. Pray for your city, for the sick people you know, for those who don't yet know Jesus. Ask that the kingdom be manifested through conversions, healings, and deliverance. And be ready: often, God answers this prayer by sending you.

Put it into practice.

One. Open Your Domains One by One. List four areas: money, time, relationships, projects. For each one, pray: "Your kingdom come here too." Note which one resists the most—that's often where God wants to work.

Two. Pray for Your City. Take five minutes to pray for your city: its leaders, the schools, the hospitals, broken families, those who don't yet know Jesus. If you can, do it while walking through your neighborhood.

Three. Let the Kingdom Flow Through You. Ask God for one opportunity today: a sick person to pray for, someone to tell about Jesus, a chance to act justly. The kingdom comes through your hands too.

To reflect on. What area of my life is still "my kingdom" instead of God's reign, and am I ready to give it to him today?

Prayer. Our Father, Your kingdom come. Reign first over me: my heart, my time, my money, my projects. Make me an ambassador of your kingdom wherever you send me. Let lives be saved, healed, and set free in my city, for your glory. Amen.

Key takeaway. Don't ask God to bless your kingdom; ask him to bring his.

Day 6. Your Will Be Done.

Today's reading : Matthew, chapter 26, verses 36 to 46.

Then Jesus came with them to a place called Gethsemane, and said to his disciples, “Sit here, while I go there and pray.” He took with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, and began to be sorrowful and severely troubled. Then Jesus said to them, “My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death. Stay here and watch with me.” He went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.” He came to the disciples and found them sleeping, and said to Peter, “What, couldn’t you watch with me for one hour? Watch and pray, that you don’t enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” Again, a second time he went away and prayed, saying, “My Father, if this cup can’t pass away from me unless I drink it, your desire be done.” He came again and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy. He left them again, went away, and prayed a third time, saying the same words. Then he came to his disciples and said to them, “Are you still sleeping and resting? Behold, the hour is at hand, and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. Arise, let’s be going. Behold, he who betrays me is at hand.”

Key verses.

Romans, chapter 12, verse 2. Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.

The Context.

"Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven." In heaven, God's will is done perfectly, joyfully, immediately. Jesus teaches us to ask that earth resemble heaven.

But to understand what this phrase costs, you have to go to the Garden of Gethsemane, a few hours before the cross. Jesus knows what awaits him: betrayal, flogging, crucifixion, and above all the weight of the world's sin. He is so anguished that his sweat becomes like drops of blood. And he prays: "Then, going a little farther, he fell with his face to the ground and prayed, 'My Father, if it is possible, may this cup be taken from me. Yet not as I will, but as you will.'" (Matthew, chapter 26, verse 39)

What Jesus Teaches Us.

Jesus doesn't pretend. He tells the Father what he truly feels: "If it is possible, take this cup from me." Praying "your will be done" doesn't mean hiding your emotions or reciting a pious phrase through gritted teeth. You have the right to tell God what you want, what you fear, what hurts you.

But Jesus doesn't stop there. He adds: "Yet not as I will, but as you will." This is the most difficult and most liberating moment of prayer: when you place your will in the Father's hands.

And Luke tells what happens next: "Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me; yet not my will, but yours be done. An angel from heaven appeared to him and strengthened him." (Luke, chapter 22, verses 42 to 43) God didn't remove the cup, but he gave strength to drink it. Sometimes God changes the situation. Sometimes he changes the one going through it. Both are answers to prayer.

Have you ever used a GPS? When you miss an exit, it doesn't yell at you. It simply says: "recalculating route." God's will is a bit like that. Even when you've taken the wrong road, he doesn't abandon you: he redirects you. But for the GPS to work, you have to let it decide the destination.

Watch out for a misunderstanding: praying "your will be done" doesn't mean giving up by saying "anyway, God will do what he wants." The Bible shows that prayer truly changes things: "The prayer of a righteous person is powerful and effective." God's will is often to heal, to save, to deliver, to provide. Praying his will is therefore also claiming it with faith where he has already revealed it in his Word.

How do you know it? Paul answers: "Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what God's will is—his good, pleasing and perfect will." (Romans, chapter 12, verse 2) The more you fill your mind with his Word, the more you recognize his will.

Prayer doesn't serve to bend God to my will, but to align my will with his.

For Your Life.

Is there a situation where you're struggling with God right now? A project, a relationship, a decision where your will and his seem to pull in two directions?

Do as Jesus did. First, be honest: tell him what you really want, without filter. Next, if your request aligns with what God has promised in his Word (the salvation of a loved one, healing, peace, provision), pray with faith and perseverance. And finally, let go: "Yet not as I will, but as you will."

It's not a defeat. It's trust. The One to whom you entrust your will is a Father who wants only your good.

Put it into practice.

One. Be Honest. Write down the situation where your will and God's seem to oppose each other. Tell him without filter what you really want. Jesus did this in Gethsemane.

Two. Pray the Promises. If your request matches a clear promise in the Bible (a loved one's salvation, peace, provision, wisdom), find a verse that carries it and pray it with perseverance this week.

Three. Let Go of the Rest. End with Jesus' words: "Not as I will, but as you will." If it's too hard today, say: "Lord, help me be able to say this." That's a real beginning.

To reflect on. In what situation am I struggling to say "not as I will, but as you will," and why?

Prayer. Our Father, may your will be done on earth as it is in heaven, and first in my life. I tell you honestly what I want. I entrust it to you. Where your Word reveals your will, I claim it with faith; where I don't understand, I trust you. Strengthen me as you strengthened Jesus. Amen.

Key takeaway. Prayer doesn't serve to bend God to my will, but to align my will with his.

Day 7. Give Us Today Our Daily Bread.

Today's reading : Exodus, chapter 16, verses 11 to 21.

The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, “I have heard the murmurings of the children of Israel. Speak to them, saying, ‘At evening you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread. Then you will know that I am the LORD your God.’” In the evening, quail came up and covered the camp; and in the morning the dew lay around the camp. When the dew that lay had gone, behold, on the surface of the wilderness was a small round thing, small as the frost on the ground. When the children of Israel saw it, they said to one another, “What is it?” For they didn’t know what it was. Moses said to them, “It is the bread which the LORD has given you to eat. This is the thing which the LORD has commanded: ‘Gather of it everyone according to his eating; an omer a head, according to the number of your persons, you shall take it, every man for those who are in his tent.’” The children of Israel did so, and some gathered more, some less. When they measured it with an omer, he who gathered much had nothing over, and he who gathered little had no lack. They each gathered according to his eating. Moses said to them, “Let no one leave of it until the morning.” Notwithstanding they didn’t listen to Moses, but some of them left of it until the morning, so it bred worms and became foul; and Moses was angry with them. They gathered it morning by morning, everyone according to his eating. When the sun grew hot, it melted.

Key verses.

Exodus, chapter 16, verse 4. Then the LORD said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law or not.

Philippians, chapter 4, verse 19. My God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.

The Context.

After speaking about God's glory, his kingdom, and his will, Jesus teaches us to speak about… bread. Nothing is too small for God. The same lips that worship the Creator of the universe can ask him for food today.

This phrase refers to a story that all of Jesus' listeners knew: the manna in the wilderness. Israel had just left Egypt, there was nothing to eat, and the people grumbled. God responds: "The Lord said to Moses, 'I will rain down bread from heaven for you. The people are to go out each day and gather enough for that day. In this way I will test them and see whether they will follow my instructions. On the sixth day they are to prepare what they bring in, and that is to be twice as much as they gather on the other days.'" (Exodus, chapter 16, verse 4) Each morning, manna covered the ground. Everyone gathered enough for the day. Those who tried to save some for the next day discovered it was full of maggots.

What Jesus Teaches Us.

God wanted to teach his people an essential lesson: daily dependence. Not a confidence for the year, but for today. Not reserves to do without God, but a daily appointment with his faithfulness.

There is the story of George Müller, a pastor who in the nineteenth century in Bristol cared for thousands of orphans without ever asking anyone for money, only God. One morning there was nothing to eat for breakfast. Müller had the children sit at the table and thanked God for the food he would provide. Day 8. Forgive Us as We Forgive.

Today's reading : Matthew, chapter 18, verses 21 to 35.

Then Peter came and said to him, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?” Jesus said to him, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven. Therefore the Kingdom of Heaven is like a certain king who wanted to settle accounts with his servants. When he had begun to settle, one was brought to him who owed him ten thousand talents. But because he couldn’t pay, his lord commanded him to be sold, with his wife, his children, and all that he had, and payment to be made. The servant therefore fell down and knelt before him, saying, ‘Lord, have patience with me, and I will repay you all!’ The lord of that servant, being moved with compassion, released him and forgave him the debt. “But that servant went out and found one of his fellow servants who owed him one hundred denarii, and he grabbed him and took him by the throat, saying, ‘Pay me what you owe!’ “So his fellow servant fell down at his feet and begged him, saying, ‘Have patience with me, and I will repay you!’ He would not, but went and cast him into prison until he should pay back that which was due. So when his fellow servants saw what was done, they were exceedingly sorry, and came and told their lord all that was done. Then his lord called him in and said to him, ‘You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you begged me. Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?’ His lord was angry, and delivered him to the tormentors until he should pay all that was due to him. So my heavenly Father will also do to you, if you don’t each forgive your brother from your hearts for his misdeeds.”

Key verses.

Matthew, chapter 6, verses 14 to 15. “For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you don’t forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

Ephesians, chapter 4, verse 32. And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

The Context.

"Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors." This is the only phrase of the Lord's Prayer that Jesus comments on right after teaching it: "For if you forgive other people when they sin against you, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you do not forgive others their sins, your Father will not forgive your sins." (Matthew, chapter 6, verses 14 to 15)

Jesus knew this would be the hardest point. Receiving forgiveness is wonderful. Giving it is often a battle.

One day, Peter asks the question many are asking: "Lord, how many times shall I forgive my brother or sister who sins against me? Up to seven times?" He thinks he's being generous. Jesus answers: "up to seventy times seven," in other words, without counting. And he tells a parable.

What Jesus Teaches Us.

A servant owes his king ten thousand talents. It's an astronomical sum: a talent represented the wages of many years of work. This debt, he could never repay it, even in ten lives. The servant begs, and the king, moved with compassion, forgives him his entire debt. Then that same servant goes out, meets a fellow servant who owes him a hundred denarii, a few months' wages, seizes him by the throat and has him thrown in prison.

When the king learns of it, he is angry: "Then the master called the servant in. 'You wicked servant,' he said, 'I canceled all that debt of yours because you begged me to. Shouldn't you have had mercy on your fellow servant just as I had on you?'" (Matthew, chapter 18, verses 32 to 33)

The lesson is clear: when I refuse to forgive, I forget how much I have been forgiven. The cross of Jesus erased a debt I could never repay. The offenses done to me, even serious ones, are "hundred denarii" compared to it.

I want to be very clear: forgiving doesn't mean what was done to you wasn't serious. It doesn't mean excusing, forgetting, or necessarily trusting again or returning to a dangerous relationship. Forgiveness means giving up making the other person pay, and putting justice in God's hands.

Corrie ten Boom, a Dutch Christian who had hidden Jews during World War II, was deported to the Ravensbrück camp, where her sister Betsie died. After the war, while preaching forgiveness in Germany, a man came up to shake her hand at the end of the meeting. She recognized him: he was one of the cruelest guards in the camp. He told her he had become a Christian and asked for her forgiveness. Corrie said she felt nothing but anger. So she prayed silently: "Jesus, I cannot forgive him. Give me your forgiveness." She reached out her hand, and she felt God's love flow through her arm.

Forgiveness is not first a feeling, it's a decision. The feelings usually follow later.

Forgiveness is opening the door of a prison… and discovering that the prisoner was me.

For Your Life.

Is there a name that comes to mind as you read these lines? A parent, an ex, a friend who betrayed you, a church leader who hurt you, yourself perhaps?

Today, don't force your emotions, but make an act of will before God. You can pray like this: "Lord, I choose to forgive [name] for [what he did]. I give up making him pay. I entrust my wound to you and put justice in your hands. Heal my heart." You may need to say this several times: it's not a failure, it's the way.

And don't forget the first part of the phrase: "forgive us." You too need forgiveness today. Simply confess to him what weighs on your conscience, and receive his grace. "Be kind and compassionate to one another, forgiving each other, just as in Christ God forgave you." (Ephesians, chapter 4, verse 32)

Put it into practice.

One. Choose to Forgive. If a name comes to mind, pray out loud: "Lord, I choose to forgive... for... I give up making them pay. Heal my heart." You may need to say this again: that's normal.

Two. Forgiveness Doesn't Mean Accepting Everything. Forgiveness does not mean staying in a situation of violence or pretending nothing happened. If you are in danger or seriously hurt, protect yourself and ask for help from a leader or professional.

Three. Receive Forgiveness. Confess to God today what weighs on your conscience, simply, then read 1 John 1:9 out loud. If you have hurt someone, ask them for forgiveness this week.

To reflect on. What person do I still need to forgive, and what is holding me back from making this act of will before God?

Prayer. Our Father, forgive me my sins. Thank you for erasing a debt I could not pay. Today, by your grace, I choose to forgive those who have hurt me. I cannot do this alone: give me your forgiveness and heal my heart. Amen.

Key takeaway. Forgiveness is opening the door of a prison and discovering that the prisoner was me.

Day 9. Deliver Us from Evil.

Today's reading : Matthew, chapter 4, verses 1 to 11.

Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. When he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was hungry afterward. The tempter came and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread.” But he answered, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth.’” Then the devil took him into the holy city. He set him on the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you,’ and, ‘On their hands they will bear you up, so that you don’t dash your foot against a stone.’” Jesus said to him, “Again, it is written, ‘You shall not test the Lord, your God.’” Again, the devil took him to an exceedingly high mountain, and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. He said to him, “I will give you all of these things, if you will fall down and worship me.” Then Jesus said to him, “Get behind me, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only.’” Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and served him.

Key verses.

1 Corinthians, chapter 10, verse 13. No temptation has taken you except what is common to man. God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.

James, chapter 4, verse 7. Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.

The Context.

"Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil." This phrase can be surprising: does God push us toward evil? James answers clearly: "Let no one say when he is tempted, 'I am being tempted by God'; for God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one. But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire." (James, chapter 1, verses 13 to 14) God tempts no one. But he allows us to go through trials, and in those trials, the enemy seeks to make us fall. Jesus teaches us to pray: "Keep me from falling, and deliver me from the hands of the enemy."

Jesus himself went through this. Right after his baptism, he is led by the Spirit into the wilderness, where he fasts for forty days, and then he is tempted by the devil.

What Jesus Teaches Us.

Look at how the devil attacks Jesus: when he is hungry, the devil offers to turn stones into bread. He then tries to make him prove his identity: "If you are the Son of God..." Then he offers him all the kingdoms of the world in exchange for worship. The enemy always targets the same points: our needs, our identity, our ambition. And he often chooses our moments of weakness: tiredness, loneliness, discouragement.

And look at how Jesus responds. He does not argue, he does not negotiate. Three times, he says: "It is written." And the last time: "Jesus said to him, 'Away with you, Satan! For it is written, You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.'" (Matthew, chapter 4, verse 10) Jesus overcame temptation with the same weapon available to you: the Word of God, spoken with authority.

In Greek mythology, sirens attracted sailors with an irresistible song, and ships crashed on the rocks. Odysseus had himself tied to the mast so he would not give in. But Orpheus found another solution: when his ship passed by the sirens, he played music even more beautiful, and the sailors did not even hear their song. The best defense against temptation is not only to grit your teeth; it is to be filled with something more beautiful: God's presence, his Word, his love.

And God makes a promise to those who are tempted: "No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it." (1 Corinthians, chapter 10, verse 13) There is always a way out. Always.

Finally, Jesus has given you real authority over the enemy. James says it in one sentence: "Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you." (James, chapter 4, verse 7) Notice the order: first submit to God, then resist the devil. It is not our strength that makes the enemy flee; it is the name of Jesus and our submission to him.

Temptation knocks at the door; it is you who decides whether to open it.

For Your Life.

Know your weak points. What are the times, places, screens, and relationships where you fall most often? To pray "lead us not into temptation" also means making concrete decisions: not voluntarily putting yourself on the path of the trap.

Fill yourself with God's Word. Choose today one or two verses that directly answer your main temptation, and memorize them. The day the enemy attacks, you will be able to say like Jesus: "It is written."

And if you have fallen, do not stay on the ground. Deliver us from evil also means: "Lift me up, cleanse me, set me free." The God who teaches you to pray this phrase is the one who has already defeated the enemy at the cross.

Put it into practice.

One. Know Your Traps. Write down the times, places, screens, or relationships where you fall most often. Then make one concrete decision to avoid one of them (a filter, a rule, a schedule, an accountability partner).

Two. Arm Yourself with a Verse. Choose a verse that directly answers your main temptation and memorize it today. Write it on your phone so you have it on hand when the attack comes.

Three. If You Have Fallen. Do not stay on the ground. Confess, receive forgiveness, and get back up today. If it is a fall that keeps returning, talk to someone you trust: light sets free.

To reflect on. What is my main point of weakness when facing temptation, and what verse will I memorize to answer it?

Prayer. Our Father, do not lead me into temptation, and deliver me from evil. I submit myself to you. Fill me with your Word and your presence. In Jesus' name, I resist the enemy. Thank you for the way out you always give me. Amen.

Key takeaway. Temptation knocks at the door; it is me who decides whether to open it.

The best defense against temptation is not only to grit your teeth; it is to be filled with something more beautiful: God's presence, his Word, his love.

And God makes a promise to those who are tempted: "No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it." (1 Corinthians, chapter 10, verse 13) There is always a way out. Always.

Finally, Jesus has given you real authority over the enemy. James says it in one sentence: "Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you." (James, chapter 4, verse 7) Notice the order: first submit to God, then resist the devil. It is not our strength that makes the enemy flee; it is the name of Jesus and our submission to him.

Temptation knocks at the door; it is you who decides whether to open it.

For Your Life.

Know your weak points. What are the times, places, screens, and relationships where you fall most often? To pray "lead us not into temptation" also means making concrete decisions: not voluntarily putting yourself on the path of the trap.

Fill yourself with God's Word. Choose today one or two verses that directly answer your main temptation, and memorize them. The day the enemy attacks, you will be able to say like Jesus: "It is written."

And if you have fallen, do not stay on the ground. Deliver us from evil also means: "Lift me up, cleanse me, set me free." The God who teaches you to pray this phrase is the one who has already defeated the enemy at the cross.

Put it into practice.

One. Know Your Traps. Write down the times, places, screens, or relationships where you fall most often. Then make one concrete decision to avoid one of them (a filter, a rule, a schedule, an accountability partner).

Two. Arm Yourself with a Verse. Choose a verse that directly answers your main temptation and memorize it today. Write it on your phone so you have it on hand when the attack comes.

Three. If You Have Fallen. Do not stay on the ground. Confess, receive forgiveness, and get back up today. If it is a fall that keeps returning, talk to someone you trust: light sets free.

To reflect on. What is my main point of weakness when facing temptation, and what verse will I memorize to answer it?

Prayer. Our Father, do not lead me into temptation, and deliver me from evil. I submit myself to you. Fill me with your Word and your presence. In Jesus' name, I resist the enemy. Thank you for the way out you always give me. Amen.

Key takeaway. Temptation knocks at the door; it is me who decides whether to open it.

texte:
Day 10. Persevere in Prayer.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 18, verses 1 to 8.

He also spoke a parable to them that they must always pray and not give up, saying, “There was a judge in a certain city who didn’t fear God and didn’t respect man. A widow was in that city, and she often came to him, saying, ‘Defend me from my adversary!’ He wouldn’t for a while; but afterward he said to himself, ‘Though I neither fear God nor respect man, yet because this widow bothers me, I will defend her, or else she will wear me out by her continual coming.’” The Lord said, “Listen to what the unrighteous judge says. Won’t God avenge his chosen ones who are crying out to him day and night, and yet he exercises patience with them? I tell you that he will avenge them quickly. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?”

Key verses.

1 Thessalonians, chapter 5, verses 16 to 18. Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.

The Context.

The Lord's Prayer ends, in Matthew's version, with an explosion of praise: "For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, forever. Amen!" You begin by worshiping, and you end by worshiping. In between, you have trusted everything to God.

But Jesus knew there would be a trap: becoming discouraged when the answer is delayed. That is why he tells a parable with a very clear intention: "And he told them a parable, to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart." (Luke, chapter 18, verse 1)

What Jesus Teaches Us.

In a city, there is an unjust judge who does not fear God and does not care about people. And there is a widow, without power, without connections, without money, who comes to him repeatedly asking for justice. The judge refuses for a long time, then finally gives in, simply because she wears him out.

Attention: Jesus does not say that God resembles this judge. He says the opposite! If even an unjust judge eventually responds to persistence, how much more will your Father, who loves you, answer those who cry out to him day and night!

The prophet Elijah experienced this perseverance. After three and a half years of drought, God had promised rain. Elijah goes to the top of Mount Carmel, kneels down, his face between his knees, and prays. He sends his servant to look toward the sea. "There is nothing." He prays again. "There is nothing." Seven times. "And at the seventh time he said, 'Behold, a little cloud like a man's hand is rising from the sea.' And Elijah said, 'Go up, say to Ahab, "Prepare your chariot and go down, lest the rain stop you."'" (1 Kings, chapter 18, verse 44)

Elijah did not stop praying at the sixth time. How many prayers are abandoned just before the little cloud?

Persevering does not mean that God is deaf or that you have to convince him by force of words. Perseverance works mainly in us: it deepens our faith, purifies our motivations, teaches us to depend on him. And sometimes there is also invisible spiritual warfare, as Daniel discovered when the angel explained to him that his prayer had been heard on the first day, but he had been held back.

Paul sums up this life of prayer in three verbs: "Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you." (1 Thessalonians, chapter 5, verses 16 to 18) To pray without ceasing does not mean to stay on your knees twenty-four hours a day; it means to live in constant conversation with God, while driving, in the shower, at work, before sleeping.

God's delay is not a refusal; often, it is an appointment being prepared.

For Your Life.

During these ten days, you have gone through the entire Lord's Prayer: approaching God as a Father, contemplating his greatness, worshiping his name, seeking his kingdom, accepting his will, entrusting your needs to him, forgiving, resisting evil. You now have a framework for your entire life of prayer.

Today, I invite you to two things. First, go through the Lord's Prayer slowly, phrase by phrase, and at each phrase, add your own words, your own life. That is how it becomes your prayer.

Next, choose one or two prayers that you had stopped persevering in: a loved one who does not know God, a healing, a restoration, a calling. Write them down, date them, and take them up each day. And when you see the little cloud, do not forget to come back and give thanks.

Because to him belong the kingdom, the power, and the glory. Amen!

Put it into practice.

One. Pray the Lord's Prayer in Your Own Words. Go through the Lord's Prayer phrase by phrase and, after each phrase, add your own prayer: your loved ones, your concerns, your gratitude. It becomes your prayer.

Two. Your Prayer Journal. Write down one or two prayers that you had stopped persevering in. Date them. Take them up each day this week, and note the answers when they come.

Three. Keep Your Rhythm. This plan ends, but your appointment with God continues. Keep the same time slot tomorrow. If you can, find someone to pray with once a week, even by phone.

To reflect on. What prayer have I abandoned too soon, and am I ready to take it up again with perseverance, like Elijah on Mount Carmel?

Prayer. Our Father, for yours is the kingdom, the power, and the glory. Thank you for teaching me to pray. Give me Elijah's perseverance and the widow's faith. I take up again today the prayers I had abandoned, and I trust you for the time of your answer. Amen.

Key takeaway. God's delay is not a refusal; often, it is an appointment being prepared.

texte:
Day 1. God Came in Person.

Today's reading : John, chapter 1, verses 1 to 18.

In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it. There came a man sent from God, whose name was John. The same came as a witness, that he might testify about the light, that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but was sent that he might testify about the light. The true light that enlightens everyone was coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world didn’t recognize him. He came to his own, and those who were his own didn’t receive him. But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children, to those who believe in his name: who were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God. The Word became flesh and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only born Son of the Father, full of grace and truth. John testified about him. He cried out, saying, “This was he of whom I said, ‘He who comes after me has surpassed me, for he was before me.’” From his fullness we all received grace upon grace. For the law was given through Moses. Grace and truth were realized through Jesus Christ. No one has seen God at any time. The only born Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him.

Part 1: The King Arrives.

For 40 days, you're going to walk with Jesus. Not study him from a distance, like a character in history: walk with him, like Peter, John, Mary, or Zacchaeus. You'll see him born, call, heal, weep, die, and rise again. And at the end, I'm praying that you'll be able to say, like those who met him: "I knew of him by name. Now I know him."

John doesn't begin his Gospel with a manger, but with eternity: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made." (John, chapter 1, verses 1 to 3)

When God Becomes One of Us.

An old story tells of a farmer, one snowy winter evening. Frantic birds throw themselves against his windows, lost in the cold. He opens the barn door wide, lights the lamp, scatters seeds on the straw. Nothing works: the birds are afraid of him. He tries to shepherd them, but they flee. Then he sighs: "If only I could become a bird, for just a moment, I could speak to them in their language, and they'd follow me to the warmth." At that very moment, the bells of the nearby church ring out Christmas. And he understands.

That's exactly what God did: "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth." (John, chapter 1, verse 14)

God didn't send us a message. He came in person. He didn't shout from heaven: he took a body, a voice, carpenter's hands, feet that grew tired on the roads. He knew hunger, fatigue, tears, betrayal. The Creator of the universe lived in a neighborhood, with neighbors.

And if you want to know what God looks like, you no longer have to guess: "No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known." (John, chapter 1, verse 18) Everything you'll see of Jesus over these 40 days—his tenderness with the wounded, his firmness with the hypocrites, his compassion for the crowds—that's the face of God.

For Your Life.

John also warns us: the light has come, and many haven't received it. But he adds an incredible promise: "But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God, who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God." (John, chapter 1, verse 12)

Receiving Jesus isn't just believing that he existed. It's opening the door of your life to him, like the farmer opening his barn. Maybe you did that a long time ago, and you need to rekindle the flame. Maybe you've never really done it.

Today, before you begin this journey, just tell him: "Jesus, I want to know you, not just know things about you. Over these 40 days, show me who you are." He didn't come all the way from heaven to stay a stranger in your life.

Put it into practice.

One. Open the Door. Tell Jesus, in your own words: "I want to know you, not just know things about you." If you've never received him into your life, do it today (John, chapter 1, verse 12).

Two. Set Your 40-Day Appointment. Choose a specific time and place for these 40 days: when you wake up, during a break, in the evening. Set an alarm. A fixed appointment is better than a good intention.

Three. Find a Companion. Invite someone to do this plan with you (using the "plan together" feature or just a simple message each evening). You'll stick with it longer with a companion.

To reflect on. Do I know Jesus personally, or only by name? What am I expecting from these 40 days with him?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, eternal Word, thank you for coming to me. You didn't send a message—you came in person. I open the door of my life to you. Over these 40 days, show me your face, and help me know you truly. Amen.

Key takeaway. God didn't send us a message: he came in person.

texte:
Day 2. No Room at the Inn.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 2, verses 1 to 20.

Now in those days, a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be enrolled. This was the first enrollment made when Quirinius was governor of Syria. All went to enroll themselves, everyone to his own city. Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth, into Judea, to David’s city, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David, to enroll himself with Mary, who was pledged to be married to him as wife, being pregnant. While they were there, the day had come for her to give birth. She gave birth to her firstborn son. She wrapped him in bands of cloth and laid him in a feeding trough, because there was no room for them in the inn. There were shepherds in the same country staying in the field, and keeping watch by night over their flock. Behold, an angel of the Lord stood by them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were terrified. The angel said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy which will be to all the people. For there is born to you today, in David’s city, a Savior, who is Christ the Lord. This is the sign to you: you will find a baby wrapped in strips of cloth, lying in a feeding trough.” Suddenly, there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army praising God and saying, “Glory to God in the highest, on earth peace, good will toward men.” When the angels went away from them into the sky, the shepherds said to one another, “Let’s go to Bethlehem, now, and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.” They came with haste and found both Mary and Joseph, and the baby was lying in the feeding trough. When they saw it, they publicized widely the saying which was spoken to them about this child. All who heard it wondered at the things which were spoken to them by the shepherds. But Mary kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart. The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all the things that they had heard and seen, just as it was told them.

The Story.

A decree from Emperor Augustus, a census, a journey of over a hundred kilometers for a pregnant woman, a town packed to the brim. And this sentence, which says it all: "And she gave birth to her firstborn son and wrapped him in swaddling clothes and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn." (Luke, chapter 2, verse 7)

The King of kings isn't born in a palace, but in a place where animals are fed. His first cradle is a manger. No one had reserved a room for the Son of God.

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Look at who receives the first birth announcement. Not the emperor in Rome. Not the high priest in Jerusalem. Not the scholars. Shepherds, at night, in the fields. In those days, shepherds were looked down on: they were suspected of theft, their testimony wasn't worth much in court, and their work often kept them from going to the temple. Yet they're the ones God chooses: "And the angel said to them, 'Fear not, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.'" (Luke, chapter 2, verses 10 to 11)

"For all the people." For the shepherds as for the kings. For the one who smells like the stable as for the one who smells like perfume. From his birth, Jesus announces the agenda: no one is too small, too dirty, or too far away to be invited.

The first birth announcement of the Son of God wasn't sent to the palace, but to the shepherds in the night.

For Your Life.

There's a question running through this story: Is there room for Jesus? The innkeeper of Bethlehem probably wasn't cruel. He was simply full. Too many people, too much noise, too much to manage. He didn't turn Jesus away: he just had no room.

What if that's your situation? Your life isn't closed to God—it's just full. Full of work, worries, screens, notifications, projects. Jesus never forces his way in. But he makes do with little: a manger was enough for him. He's not asking you for a perfect life, neat and decorated. He's asking you for room.

Notice also the shepherds' reaction. They don't sit around discussing it: they go see, they tell others, and they leave praising God (Luke, chapter 2, verse 20). They came as shepherds, they left as witnesses. Nothing had changed in their job—their sheep were still waiting. But they had changed.

Today, ask yourself: what's cluttering my life so much that there's no room left for Jesus? And make room for him, concretely: a time, a place, a decision. Even a manger—he transforms it into a place of glory.

Put it into practice.

One. Make Room. Identify what fills your life so much that there's no room for Jesus (screens, work, busyness). Choose one thing to reduce this week and give that time to God.

Two. Think of Today's Shepherds. Who's left out around you (a lonely person, a coworker people avoid, an elderly neighbor)? Reach out to them this week: the good news is for them too.

Three. Tell What You've Seen. The shepherds left telling others. Share with someone today something God has done for you recently, even something simple.

To reflect on. What fills my life so much that I leave little room for Jesus? What will I change concretely?

Prayer. Jesus, King born in a manger, thank you for coming for the small, the forgotten, the night shepherds. Forgive me for sometimes being too full to make room for you. Today I open my heart, my time, and my priorities to you. Come and live in me. Amen.

Key takeaway. Jesus doesn't ask for a perfect life—he asks for room.

This is the sign to you: you will find a baby wrapped in strips of cloth, lying in a feeding trough.” Suddenly, there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army praising God and saying, “Glory to God in the highest, on earth peace, good will toward men.” When the angels went away from them into the sky, the shepherds said to one another, “Let’s go to Bethlehem, now, and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.” They came with haste and found both Mary and Joseph, and the baby was lying in the feeding trough. When they saw it, they publicized widely the saying which was spoken to them about this child. All who heard it wondered at the things which were spoken to them by the shepherds. But Mary kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart. The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all the things that they had heard and seen, just as it was told them.

The Story.

A decree from Emperor Augustus, a census, a journey of over a hundred kilometers for a pregnant woman, a town packed to the brim. And this sentence, which says it all: "And she gave birth to her firstborn son and wrapped him in swaddling clothes and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn." (Luke, chapter 2, verse 7)

The King of kings isn't born in a palace, but in a place where animals are fed. His first cradle is a manger. No one had reserved a room for the Son of God.

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Look at who receives the first birth announcement. Not the emperor in Rome. Not the high priest in Jerusalem. Not the scholars. Shepherds, at night, in the fields. In those days, shepherds were looked down on: they were suspected of theft, their testimony wasn't worth much in court, and their work often kept them from going to the temple. Yet they're the ones God chooses: "And the angel said to them, 'Fear not, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.'" (Luke, chapter 2, verses 10 to 11)

"For all the people." For the shepherds as for the kings. For the one who smells like the stable as for the one who smells like perfume. From his birth, Jesus announces the agenda: no one is too small, too dirty, or too far away to be invited.

The first birth announcement of the Son of God wasn't sent to the palace, but to the shepherds in the night.

For Your Life.

There's a question running through this story: Is there room for Jesus? The innkeeper of Bethlehem probably wasn't cruel. He was simply full. Too many people, too much noise, too much to manage. He didn't turn Jesus away: he just had no room.

What if that's your situation? Your life isn't closed to God—it's just full. Full of work, worries, screens, notifications, projects. Jesus never forces his way in. But he makes do with little: a manger was enough for him. He's not asking you for a perfect life, neat and decorated. He's asking you for room.

Notice also the shepherds' reaction. They don't sit around discussing it: they go see, they tell others, and they leave praising God (Luke, chapter 2, verse 20). They came as shepherds, they left as witnesses. Nothing had changed in their job—their sheep were still waiting. But they had changed.

Today, ask yourself: what's cluttering my life so much that there's no room left for Jesus? And make room for him, concretely: a time, a place, a decision. Even a manger—he transforms it into a place of glory.

Put it into practice.

One. Make Room. Identify what fills your life so much that there's no room for Jesus (screens, work, busyness). Choose one thing to reduce this week and give that time to God.

Two. Think of Today's Shepherds. Who's left out around you (a lonely person, a coworker people avoid, an elderly neighbor)? Reach out to them this week: the good news is for them too.

Three. Tell What You've Seen. The shepherds left telling others. Share with someone today something God has done for you recently, even something simple.

To reflect on. What fills my life so much that I leave little room for Jesus? What will I change concretely?

Prayer. Jesus, King born in a manger, thank you for coming for the small, the forgotten, the night shepherds. Forgive me for sometimes being too full to make room for you. Today I open my heart, my time, and my priorities to you. Come and live in me. Amen.

Key takeaway. Jesus doesn't ask for a perfect life—he asks for room.

Day 3. Prepare the Way.

Today's reading : Matthew, chapter 3, verses 1 to 12.

In those days, John the Baptizer came, preaching in the wilderness of Judea, saying, “Repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand!” For this is he who was spoken of by Isaiah the prophet, saying, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness, make the way of the Lord ready! Make his paths straight!” Now John himself wore clothing made of camel’s hair with a leather belt around his waist. His food was locusts and wild honey. Then people from Jerusalem, all of Judea, and all the region around the Jordan went out to him. They were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins. But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming for his baptism, he said to them, “You offspring of vipers, who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Therefore produce fruit worthy of repentance! Don’t think to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham for our father,’ for I tell you that God is able to raise up children to Abraham from these stones. Even now the ax lies at the root of the trees. Therefore every tree that doesn’t produce good fruit is cut down, and cast into the fire. “I indeed baptize you in water for repentance, but he who comes after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit. His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor. He will gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn up with unquenchable fire.”

The Story.

Before Jesus begins his ministry, God sends a strange man: John the Baptist. He lives in the desert, wears a garment of camel's hair, and eats locusts and wild honey. Not exactly an influencer profile. Yet crowds come from everywhere to listen to him. His message fits in one sentence: "In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judea, 'Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.' For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah when he said, 'The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.'" (Matthew, chapter 3, verses 2 to 3)

What This Reveals.

In ancient times, when a king was about to visit a region, a messenger was sent ahead. The inhabitants would repair the roads, fill in the holes, remove the stones, smooth out the bumps. You didn't receive a king on a torn-up road. Even today, when a head of state visits a city, sometimes they resurface the road the day before.

John is that messenger. And the way to be prepared isn't made of earth: it's the heart. The word "repent" frightens many people, but it's full of hope. To repent is to turn around. It's like your GPS saying "recalculating route": you took the wrong road, it's not the end of your journey, but you need to turn around.

John doesn't settle for fine words. To the religious people who come to be baptized as a habit, he says: "Bear fruit in keeping with repentance," (Matthew, chapter 3, verse 8) In other words: don't show me your tears, show me your life. Real repentance shows: in the way you speak, spend money, forgive, love.

And John knows his place. He, the star of the moment, says about Jesus: "I baptize you with water for repentance, but he who is coming after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire." (Matthew, chapter 3, verse 11) The greatest of the prophets calls himself unworthy to carry Jesus' sandals. That's the mark of a true servant: he prepares the way, then he steps aside.

For Your Life.

The King wants to come into every area of your life. But there may be holes to fill: wounds never healed, forgiveness never given. Mountains to level: pride, resentment, a habit you've been justifying for too long. Crooked paths to straighten: a lie, an unclear relationship, a deal that's not quite honest.

The good news is you're not preparing the way alone. John announces that Jesus will baptize "with the Holy Spirit and fire." The one asking you to turn around also gives you the strength to do it.

Today, take a moment of silence and ask: "Lord, what way should I prepare for you?" Then take one concrete step of repentance: an apology, a restitution, a decision. The King is just waiting for that to come in.

Put it into practice.

One. Ask What Way to Prepare. Take a moment of silence and ask: "Lord, what way should I prepare for you?" Write down what comes to mind: a grudge, a lie, a habit.

Two. One Concrete Fruit of Repentance. Choose a visible act this week: apologize, repay a debt, stop a dishonest practice, call someone you're at odds with.

Three. At Work or School. John told soldiers and tax collectors to change the way they worked (Luke, chapter 3, verses 12 to 14). Is there anything to straighten out in the way you work or study?

To reflect on. What "crooked path" of my life is the Lord asking me to straighten this week?

Prayer. Lord, I want to prepare the way for you. Show me the holes to fill, the mountains to level, the crooked paths to straighten. I turn around from where I've drifted from you. Come and reign in every area of my life. Amen.

Key takeaway. Repentance isn't the end of your journey—it's a recalculation of your route.

Day 4. My Beloved Son.

Today's reading : Matthew, chapter 3, verses 13 to 17.

Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him. But John would have hindered him, saying, “I need to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” But Jesus, answering, said to him, “Allow it now, for this is the fitting way for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he allowed him. Jesus, when he was baptized, went up directly from the water: and behold, the heavens were opened to him. He saw the Spirit of God descending as a dove, and coming on him. Behold, a voice out of the heavens said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.”

Key verses.

Mark, chapter 1, verse 11. A voice came out of the sky, “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

The Story.

Jesus is about thirty years old. He leaves the carpenter's workshop in Nazareth, walks to the Jordan, and gets in line in the middle of sinners coming to confess their sins. John is astonished: surely he should be baptized by Jesus! But Jesus insists. The one who never sinned stands in the place of sinners. The whole Gospel is already there.

Then the sky opens: "As soon as Jesus was baptized, he came up out of the water. And behold, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him. And behold, a voice from heaven said, 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.'" (Matthew, chapter 3, verses 16 to 17)

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Pay careful attention to when the Father speaks these words. Jesus hasn't healed anyone yet. He hasn't preached a sermon, multiplied bread, or cast out a demon. For thirty years, he was a carpenter in a village nobody talked about. Yet the Father says: "I am proud of you. You are my beloved Son."

The Father's love comes before performance. Jesus didn't serve to be loved; he served because he was loved.

Imagine a father in the stands at his child's first game. The whistle hasn't even blown, and he's already shouting: "That's my son!" He doesn't wait to see the score to be proud. He's proud because it's his child.

And right after this moment, what happens? Jesus is led into the wilderness to be tempted, and the enemy's first attack is: "If you are the Son of God..." (Matthew, chapter 4, verse 3). The enemy always attacks identity first. But Jesus holds firm, because he just heard his Father's voice.

For Your Life.

Many Christians live exhausted because they're trying to earn a love they already have. They serve, pray, give, commit... so God will love them a little more. But the Gospel turns it all around: in Christ, what the Father said about Jesus, he says about you. "He predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of his glorious grace, which he freely bestowed on us in the Beloved." (Ephesians, chapter 1, verses 5 to 6)

You don't have to earn your place at the table: you're family. Before your first achievement and after your worst failure, the Father looks at you with the same affection.

So today, before you do anything for God, take five minutes to simply receive. Close your eyes and listen to the Father tell you: "You are my beloved child." Then go serve, not to be loved, but because you're already loved. That changes everything: you no longer serve in fear of disappointing, but in the joy of being like your Father.

Put it into practice.

One. Receive Before You Give. Before you do anything for God today, take five minutes to listen to the Father tell you: "You are my beloved child." Begin your day with that.

Two. Change Your Motivation. Choose a service you do often out of fear of disappointing. This week, do it remembering: I do this because I'm loved, not to be loved.

Three. If You're a Parent. Tell your child today that you're proud of them for who they are, not for what they've achieved. You're giving them a glimpse of the Father's heart.

To reflect on. Am I serving God to be loved, or because I'm already loved? What does that change concretely?

Prayer. Father, thank you for loving me before I do anything for you. I receive today your word over my life: I am your beloved child. Free me from the need to earn your love, and let all my service flow from this assurance. Amen.

Key takeaway. Jesus didn't serve to be loved; he served because he was loved.

Day 5. It Is Written.

Today's reading : Matthew, chapter 4, verses 1 to 11.

Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. When he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was hungry afterward. The tempter came and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread.” But he answered, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth.’” Then the devil took him into the holy city. He set him on the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you,’ and, ‘On their hands they will bear you up, so that you don’t dash your foot against a stone.’” Jesus said to him, “Again, it is written, ‘You shall not test the Lord, your God.’” Again, the devil took him to an exceedingly high mountain, and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. He said to him, “I will give you all of these things, if you will fall down and worship me.” Then Jesus said to him, “Get behind me, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only.’” Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and served him.

Key verses.

Hebrews, chapter 4, verse 15. For we don’t have a high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin.

The Story.

Right after the voice from heaven comes the wilderness. Forty days without food. And when Jesus is hungry, when he's at his weakest, the tempter approaches. Satan never attacks when you're strong; he waits until you're tired, alone, starving.

Three temptations, and three doors the enemy still tries to open in our lives.

The first targets appetite: "Command these stones to become bread." Satisfy your need, right now, your way. The second targets spectacle: "Throw yourself down from the temple," do something sensational, show everyone who you are. The third targets the shortcut: "All these kingdoms I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me." The devil offers Jesus what the Father already promised him... but without the cross.

The devil always offers the crown without the cross.

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Each time, Jesus responds the same way: "It is written." He doesn't argue, doesn't debate, doesn't do a miracle to prove anything. He draws his sword: the Word. "Jesus answered, 'It is written: Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.'" (Matthew, chapter 4, verse 4)

Notice that all three of Jesus' answers come from the book of Deuteronomy. Jesus isn't quoting verses picked at random for the occasion: he knows Scripture because he's read it, meditated on it, memorized it long before the wilderness. You don't reach for your sword when the enemy strikes; you already have it in hand.

And Satan, he also knows how to quote the Bible (Matthew, chapter 4, verse 6). But he quotes it by cutting, twisting, taking it out of context. That's why Jesus responds: "Jesus said to him, 'It is also written: Do not put the Lord your God to the test.'" (Matthew, chapter 4, verse 7) A single sentence of the Bible ripped from its context can become a trap; the whole Scripture is a light.

For Your Life.

Jesus wasn't tempted so you'd admire his strength, but so he could understand you and come to your aid: "For we do not have a high priest who is unable to empathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who has been tempted in every way, just as we are—yet he did not sin." (Hebrews, chapter 4, verse 15)

He knows what it's like to be hungry, to be tired, to hear a small voice saying: "Take the shortcut, nobody will know." And he won because you could win in him.

What's your most frequent temptation? Appetite (sex, food, money, screens)? Spectacle (image, likes, the need to be seen)? The shortcut (lying, cheating, compromising)? Today, choose a verse that specifically answers that temptation. Write it down, memorize it, and the next time that voice comes, respond like your Master: "It is written."

Put it into practice.

One. Name Your Weak Door. Appetite, spectacle, or shortcut: which of these temptations touches you most? Write it down honestly.

Two. Arm Yourself With a Verse. Choose a verse that directly answers this temptation, memorize it, and make it your phone wallpaper. In the moment of attack, respond like Jesus: "It is written."

Three. Avoid the Pointless Wilderness. Identify when you're most vulnerable (tired, alone, late at night) and make a concrete decision for those times: go to bed earlier, call someone, leave your phone out of the bedroom.

To reflect on. What is my most frequent temptation, and what verse will I memorize to answer it?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you for conquering temptation for me. You know what I'm going through; you understand me. Give me a love for your Word so it's in my heart before the battle. When the voice of the shortcut comes, make me answer like you: it is written. Amen.

Key takeaway. You don't reach for your sword when the enemy strikes: you already have it in hand.

texte:
Day 6. Come and See.

Today's reading : John, chapter 1, verses 35 to 51.

Again, the next day, John was standing with two of his disciples, and he looked at Jesus as he walked, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God!” The two disciples heard him speak, and they followed Jesus. Jesus turned and saw them following, and said to them, “What are you looking for?” They said to him, “Rabbi” (which is to say, being interpreted, Teacher), “where are you staying?” He said to them, “Come and see.” They came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day. It was about the tenth hour. One of the two who heard John and followed him was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother. He first found his own brother, Simon, and said to him, “We have found the Messiah!” (which is, being interpreted, Christ). He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, “You are Simon the son of Jonah. You shall be called Cephas” (which is by interpretation, Peter). On the next day, he was determined to go out into Galilee, and he found Philip. Jesus said to him, “Follow me.” Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter. Philip found Nathanael, and said to him, “We have found him of whom Moses in the law and also the prophets, wrote: Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.” Nathanael said to him, “Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?” Philip said to him, “Come and see.” Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and said about him, “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom is no deceit!” Nathanael said to him, “How do you know me?” Jesus answered him, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.” Nathanael answered him, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are King of Israel!” Jesus answered him, “Because I told you, ‘I saw you underneath the fig tree,’ do you believe? You will see greater things than these!” He said to him, “Most certainly, I tell you all, hereafter you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”

Part 2: The Calling.

Day 7. The Best Wine at Last.

Today's reading : John, chapter 2, verses 1 to 11.

The third day, there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee. Jesus’ mother was there. Jesus also was invited, with his disciples, to the wedding. When the wine ran out, Jesus’ mother said to him, “They have no wine.” Jesus said to her, “Woman, what does that have to do with you and me? My hour has not yet come.” His mother said to the servants, “Whatever he says to you, do it.” Now there were six water pots of stone set there after the Jews’ way of purifying, containing two or three metretes apiece. Jesus said to them, “Fill the water pots with water.” So they filled them up to the brim. He said to them, “Now draw some out, and take it to the ruler of the feast.” So they took it. When the ruler of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and didn’t know where it came from (but the servants who had drawn the water knew), the ruler of the feast called the bridegroom and said to him, “Everyone serves the good wine first, and when the guests have drunk freely, then that which is worse. You have kept the good wine until now!” This beginning of his signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.

The Story.

Jesus' first miracle does not take place in a synagogue, nor before a crowd, but in the middle of a wedding celebration in a small village called Cana. And he doesn't heal a sick person: he saves a party.

Back then, a wedding could last several days. Running out of wine was a public shame for the family, a humiliation that would be talked about for a long time in the village. Mary notices this and comes to Jesus. Then she says to the servants a sentence that deserves to be posted in every home: "His mother said to the servants, 'Do whatever he tells you.'" (John, chapter 2, verse 5)

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Jesus cares about what touches you. Not just your big spiritual crises: also your party that's going wrong, your embarrassment, your lack. Nothing is too ordinary for him.

And look at how the miracle happens. Jesus doesn't snap his fingers. He asks for something very simple, almost mundane: fill six large stone jars with water. Each one held about a hundred liters. It took back-and-forth trips to the well, carrying, pouring. Physical work, with no glory. But the servants fill them "to the brim" (John, chapter 2, verse 7). Not halfway. To the brim.

The miracle came after obedience, not before. The servants poured water; as they carried it, it became wine.

And the result surprises everyone: "and said to him, 'Every man at the beginning sets out the good wine, and when the guests have well drunk, then the inferior. You have kept the good wine until now.'" (John, chapter 2, verse 10)

For Your Life.

Maybe your life looks like this party: the wine has run out. Joy, energy, love in your marriage, passion for your work, fervor in your faith… Only empty jars remain.

Here are three lessons from Cana.

Bring your need to Jesus, as Mary did. She doesn't tell him what to do; she simply presents the problem to him: "They have no wine."

Do what he tells you, even if it seems ordinary. Sometimes God's answer starts with something simple: opening your Bible, asking forgiveness, going back to church, serving. Water in jars. Fill them to the brim.

And believe that God keeps the best for what comes next. The world serves the good wine at the beginning, then the lesser wine. With Jesus, it's the opposite. What comes is better than what has passed.

Put it into practice.

One. Bring Your Need. Like Mary, present to Jesus what has run out in your life (joy, love in your marriage, energy, faith) in a simple sentence: "Lord, they have no wine here."

Two. Fill the Jar to the Brim. What simple thing is Jesus asking you to do? Read his Word, go back to church, ask forgiveness, serve. Do it this week, fully, not halfway.

Three. For Your Marriage or Family. If the "wine" is missing at home, plan a time of quality this week with your spouse or children, and pray together, even two minutes.

To reflect on. In what area of my life has the "wine" run out? What simple thing is Jesus asking me to do?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you see my empty jars: what has run out in my life. I present them to you. I will do everything you tell me, even if it seems ordinary. I believe you have kept the best for what comes next. Change my water into wine. Amen.

Key takeaway. With Jesus, the best wine is not behind you: it's ahead of you.
