Day 8. He Came by Night.

Today's reading : John, chapter 3, verses 1 to 21.

Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. He came to Jesus by night and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher who has come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do, unless God is with him.” Jesus answered him, “Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born anew, he can’t see God’s Kingdom.” Nicodemus said to him, “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?” Jesus answered, “Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born of water and Spirit, he can’t enter into God’s Kingdom. That which is born of the flesh is flesh. That which is born of the Spirit is spirit. Don’t marvel that I said to you, ‘You must all be born anew.’ The wind blows where it wants to, and you hear its sound, but don’t know where it comes from and where it is going. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.” Nicodemus answered him, “How can these things be?” Jesus answered him, “Are you the teacher of Israel, and don’t understand these things? Most certainly I tell you, we speak that which we know and testify of that which we have seen, and you don’t receive our witness. If I told you earthly things and you don’t believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things? No one has ascended into heaven but he who descended out of heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven. As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. For God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him. He who believes in him is not judged. He who doesn’t believe has been judged already, because he has not believed in the name of the only born Son of God. This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and men loved the darkness rather than the light, for their works were evil. For everyone who does evil hates the light and doesn’t come to the light, lest his works would be exposed. But he who does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be revealed, that they have been done in God.”

The Story.

Nicodemus is an important man: a Pharisee, a member of the Sanhedrin, the great Jewish council, and a recognized teacher. He has everything going for him: education, reputation, religion. Yet he comes to see Jesus… by night. Perhaps out of fear of what others will say, perhaps to have a real conversation in peace. He begins politely: "Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God." But Jesus gets right to the point: "Jesus answered and said to him, 'Most assuredly, I say to you, unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.'" (John, chapter 3, verse 3)

For Nicodemus, this is a shock. He thought he needed to improve; Jesus tells him he needs to start over. He thought he needed more religion; Jesus speaks to him of a new birth, of a life that comes from above.

What This Reveals About Jesus.

To help him understand, Jesus recalls a story that Nicodemus knows by heart: in the desert, when the people were bitten by serpents, Moses had lifted up a bronze serpent on a pole, and whoever looked at it lived (Numbers, chapter 21, verses 8 to 9). "And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have eternal life." (John, chapter 3, verses 14 to 15)

No need to heal the bite yourself. No need to earn healing. You simply had to look, with faith. And it is here that Jesus speaks perhaps the most well-known verse in all the Bible: "For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have everlasting life. For God did not send His Son into the world to condemn the world, but that the world through Him might be saved." (John, chapter 3, verses 16 to 17)

For Your Life.

The most beautiful part is the rest of Nicodemus' story. We find him twice more in John's Gospel. The first time, in the middle of the council, he dares to defend Jesus, timidly: "Does our law judge a man before it hears him and knows what he is doing?" (John, chapter 7, verses 50 to 51). The second time, after the crucifixion, when the disciples are hiding, Nicodemus comes in broad daylight with about a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes to bury Jesus' body (John, chapter 19, verses 39 to 40).

By night, then halfway, then in full light. Nicodemus' faith grew slowly, but it grew.

Maybe you are a Nicodemus. You believe, but in secret. You're afraid of what your family, your colleagues, your circle will say. Jesus doesn't reject you for that: he received Nicodemus by night. But he doesn't want to leave you in the night.

You can come to Jesus by night; he won't leave you in the night.

Today, ask yourself: what is the next step for me? Maybe to give your life to him for the first time, sincerely. Maybe to dare say around you that you believe in him. Take another step toward the light.

Put it into practice.

One. Your Next Step Toward the Light. Where are you at? By night, halfway, in full light? Choose a concrete step: give your life to Jesus, dare to say you're a Christian, get baptized, join a church.

Two. Look at the Cross. As the people looked at the bronze serpent, take a moment to look at Jesus crucified for you. Read John 3:16, putting your name in place of "the world."

Three. If You're Afraid of What Others Think. Choose just one trusted person to tell this week that you believe in Jesus. Courage grows step by step, as it did for Nicodemus.

To reflect on. Is there an area where I live my faith "by night," in secret? What step toward the light can I take this week?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you for welcoming me even when I come by night, with my questions and my fears. I look toward you, lifted up on the cross for me, and I receive eternal life. Make me born from above, and make my faith grow into the full light. Amen.

Key takeaway. You can come to Jesus by night; he won't leave you in the night.

Day 9. The Woman at the Well.

Today's reading : John, chapter 4, verses 5 to 30.

So he came to a city of Samaria called Sychar, near the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph. Jacob’s well was there. Jesus therefore, being tired from his journey, sat down by the well. It was about the sixth hour. A woman of Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.” For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food. The Samaritan woman therefore said to him, “How is it that you, being a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.) Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.” The woman said to him, “Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep. Day 10. The Spirit of the Lord Is Upon Me.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 4, verses 16 to 30.

He came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. He entered, as was his custom, into the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and stood up to read. The book of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him. He opened the book, and found the place where it was written, “The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent me to heal the broken hearted, to proclaim release to the captives, recovering of sight to the blind, to deliver those who are crushed, and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.” He closed the book, gave it back to the attendant, and sat down. The eyes of all in the synagogue were fastened on him. He began to tell them, “Today, this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” All testified about him and wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth; and they said, “Isn’t this Joseph’s son?” He said to them, “Doubtless you will tell me this proverb, ‘Physician, heal yourself! Whatever we have heard done at Capernaum, do also here in your hometown.’” He said, “Most certainly I tell you, no prophet is acceptable in his hometown. But truly I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the sky was shut up three years and six months, when a great famine came over all the land. Elijah was sent to none of them, except to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. There were many lepers in Israel in the time of Elisha the prophet, yet not one of them was cleansed, except Naaman, the Syrian.” They were all filled with wrath in the synagogue as they heard these things. They rose up, threw him out of the city, and led him to the brow of the hill that their city was built on, that they might throw him off the cliff. But he, passing through the middle of them, went his way.

The Story.

Jesus returns to Nazareth, the village where he grew up. On the Sabbath, he enters the synagogue, as he usually does. Someone hands him the scroll of the prophet Isaiah. He unrolls it, finds the passage, and reads it before those who knew him as a child: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me, Because He has anointed Me to preach the gospel to the poor; He has sent Me to heal the brokenhearted, To proclaim liberty to the captives, And recovery of sight to the blind, To set at liberty those who are oppressed, To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord." (Luke, chapter 4, verses 18 to 19)

Then he rolls up the book, sits down, and all eyes are fixed on him. He says simply: "Then He began to say to them, 'Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.'" (Luke, chapter 4, verse 21)

What This Reveals About Jesus.

This is Jesus' program, his manifesto. Look at who he addresses: the poor, the brokenhearted, the captives, the blind, the oppressed. Jesus didn't come for people who are doing well, but for people who are broken. He didn't come to decorate the lives of those who already have everything, but to lift up those who have nothing left.

And notice where the power of this ministry comes from: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me, because He has anointed Me." Even Jesus, the Son of God, exercised his ministry in the power of the Holy Spirit. If he needed it, how much more do we!

But the story takes a dark turn. At first, everyone is amazed. Then the questions come: "Is not this Joseph's son?" They know him too well. And when Jesus reminds them that God once blessed a foreign widow and a Syrian general rather than Israelites, the crowd becomes angry and wants to throw him off a cliff. Those who knew him best didn't recognize him.

For Your Life.

There are two lessons in this text.

First: if you feel poor, broken, captive, blind, or oppressed, this text is for you. You are exactly the kind of person Jesus came for. Your weakness is not an obstacle to his grace; it's the doorway in.

Second is a warning: familiarity is dangerous. The people of Nazareth were so used to Jesus that they saw nothing extraordinary in him anymore. It's a risk for those who grew up in church, who know all the stories by heart. You can know Jesus for so long that you stop marveling.

Today, ask the Lord to restore your sense of wonder. And reread this manifesto asking yourself: "Who around me is poor, broken, or captive?" Because what Jesus began, he continues to do today through his Church, filled with the same Spirit.

Put it into practice.

One. Rediscover Your Wonder. If Jesus has become too familiar, read Luke 4:18-19 slowly as if for the first time, and thank him for one specific thing he has done for you.

Two. You're Included Too. Poor, brokenhearted, captive, blind, oppressed: which of these descriptions fits you today? Bring it to Jesus: this text is for you.

Three. Continue His Mission. Choose one person around you who is poor, broken, or captive and do something concrete this week: a visit, a meal, help, a prayer.

To reflect on. Have I become too familiar with Jesus? Who around me needs to hear the good news of this manifesto?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you for coming for the poor, the brokenhearted, the captives. I bring to you what is broken in me. Forgive me when I've become too used to you. Restore my wonder, and fill me with your Spirit to continue your work around me. Amen.

Key takeaway. Jesus didn't come for people who are doing well, but for people who are broken.

Day 11. On Your Word.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 5, verses 1 to 11.

Now while the multitude pressed on him and heard the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret. He saw two boats standing by the lake, but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. He entered into one of the boats, which was Simon’s, and asked him to put out a little from the land. He sat down and taught the multitudes from the boat. When he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, “Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.” Simon answered him, “Master, we worked all night and caught nothing; but at your word I will let down the net.” When they had done this, they caught a great multitude of fish, and their net was breaking. They beckoned to their partners in the other boat, that they should come and help them. They came and filled both boats, so that they began to sink. But Simon Peter, when he saw it, fell down at Jesus’ knees, saying, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord.” For he was amazed, and all who were with him, at the catch of fish which they had caught; and so also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. Jesus said to Simon, “Don’t be afraid. From now on you will be catching people alive.” When they had brought their boats to land, they left everything, and followed him.

The Story.

Simon has spent the entire night on the Lake of Gennesaret. He knows his trade: night is the best time to fish, when the fish come to the surface. And yet, nothing. Not a single fish. Early in the morning, exhausted, he washes his nets on the shore. The day is finished before it has begun.

That's when Jesus gets into his boat, teaches the crowd, and then says to him: "Launch out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch." Imagine the scene: a carpenter telling a professional fisherman how to fish. In broad daylight, in deep water, after a night of failure. Everything in Simon's experience tells him it's useless. And yet: "Simon answered and said to Him, 'Master, we have toiled all night and caught nothing; nevertheless at Your word I will let down the net.'" (Luke, chapter 5, verse 5)

What This Reveals About Jesus.

"At Your word." That's the whole difference between experience and faith. Simon doesn't say, "I feel like this will work." He says, "I'm not so sure, but because it's you who says it, I'll do it." Faith isn't always a feeling; it's often a decision to obey.

The result exceeds everything: the nets begin to break, two boats are so full they start to sink. And Simon's reaction is surprising. He doesn't cry out for joy: he falls to Jesus' knees and says, "Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord!" Before Jesus' greatness, he sees his own smallness.

But Jesus doesn't leave. He answers him: "And so were also James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were Simon's partners. And Jesus said to Simon, 'Do not be afraid. From now on you will catch men.' So when they had brought their boats to land, they forsook all and followed Him." (Luke, chapter 5, verses 10 to 11)

For Your Life.

Your experience tells you "it's useless"; his word tells you "launch out into the deep."

Maybe you feel like you've worked all night without catching anything. You've prayed about this situation, you've tried, you've persevered, and the nets are still empty. Your experience tells you: give up, it's over. But Jesus might be getting into your boat right now.

Notice that Jesus didn't choose people who had succeeded. He chose people who had just failed. And he used their failure as the place of a miracle and a calling.

Notice too the end of the story: "they forsook all and followed Him." On the day of their greatest catch ever, they leave the fish on the beach. Because they understood that the one who gives the catch is worth more than the catch itself.

Today, what is Jesus' word that seems illogical to you? Forgive, give, start over, dare? Simply tell him: "Lord, I don't understand everything, but on your word, I will let down the net."

Put it into practice.

One. Your Night Without Fish. Write down the area where you feel like you've worked all night without catching anything. Bring it to Jesus just as it is.

Two. Obey Without Understanding Everything. What word of Jesus seems illogical in your situation (forgive, give, start over, wait)? Tell him: "On your word, I will do it," and take action this week.

Three. Get to Work. If your job discourages you, pray before you start your workday: "Lord, get in my boat." Invite him into what you do most ordinarily.

To reflect on. In what area have I "worked all night without catching anything"? What word of Jesus am I going to dare to obey, even without understanding?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you see my nights without results and my empty nets. Today I'm not relying on my experience, but on your word. On your word, I will let down the net. And if you call me to follow you, give me the strength to leave everything for you. Amen.

Key takeaway. Faith is not always a feeling: it's often a decision to obey.

Two. Obey Without Understanding Everything. What word of Jesus seems illogical in your situation (forgive, give, start over, wait)? Tell him: "On your word, I will do it," and take action this week.

Three. Get to Work. If your job discourages you, pray before you start your workday: "Lord, get in my boat." Invite him into what you do most ordinarily.

To reflect on. In what area have I "worked all night without catching anything"? What word of Jesus am I going to dare to obey, even without understanding?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you see my nights without results and my empty nets. Today I'm not relying on my experience, but on your word. On your word, I will let down the net. And if you call me to follow you, give me the strength to leave everything for you. Amen.

Key takeaway. Faith is not always a feeling: it's often a decision to obey.

Day 12. Four Friends and a Roof.

Today's reading : Mark, chapter 2, verses 1 to 12.

When he entered again into Capernaum after some days, it was heard that he was at home. Immediately many were gathered together, so that there was no more room, not even around the door; and he spoke the word to them. Four people came, carrying a paralytic to him. When they could not come near to him for the crowd, they removed the roof where he was. When they had broken it up, they let down the mat that the paralytic was lying on. Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven you.” But there were some of the scribes sitting there and reasoning in their hearts, “Why does this man speak blasphemies like that? Who can forgive sins but God alone?” Immediately Jesus, perceiving in his spirit that they so reasoned within themselves, said to them, “Why do you reason these things in your hearts? Which is easier, to tell the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven;’ or to say, ‘Arise, and take up your bed, and walk’? But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the paralytic— “I tell you, arise, take up your mat, and go to your house.” He arose, and immediately took up the mat and went out in front of them all, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying, “We never saw anything like this!”

The Story.

Jesus is in Capernaum, in a house. The news spreads, and the crowd is so large that there's no room left, even outside the door. Then four men arrive carrying a paralyzed man on a mat. It's impossible to get in.

Most people would have given up: "We tried, we'll come back another time." Not them. They go up on the flat roof of the house, dig a hole through the roof made of earth and branches, and lower their friend right in front of Jesus. Imagine the dust falling on the guests, the homeowner seeing his roof torn open, the crowd looking up.

What This Reveals About Jesus.

And here's the sentence that moves me every time: "When Jesus saw their faith, He said to the paralytic, 'Son, your sins are forgiven you.'" (Mark, chapter 2, verse 5)

"When Jesus saw their faith." Whose faith? The faith of the four friends. The paralyzed man said nothing, asked for nothing. It was his friends who believed for him, who carried him when he couldn't walk.

Then Jesus does something unexpected. Instead of healing the legs first, he forgives sins. He goes to the root, to the deepest need. The scribes are outraged: "Who can forgive sins but God alone?" They're right on one point: only God can forgive. And that's exactly what Jesus is revealing. So, to prove his invisible authority, he performs a visible miracle: "But that you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins"—He said to the paralytic, "I say to you, arise, take up your bed, and go to your house." Immediately he arose, took up the bed, and went out in the presence of them all, so that all were amazed and glorified God, saying, "We never saw anything like this!" (Mark, chapter 2, verses 10 to 12)

For Your Life.

Some days you carry the stretcher; other days you're the one on it.

If today you're on the stretcher, paralyzed by fear, depression, grief, or sin, let yourself be carried. Accept that others pray for you, believe for you, carry you to Jesus. It's not weakness; it's the beauty of the Church.

If today you're standing, look around you: who is on a stretcher? Who can't move forward alone? You may not have the power to heal them, but you can carry them in prayer, invite them, walk with them, hold their hand. And sometimes you'll need to be creative and persistent: make a hole in the roof when all the doors seem closed.

Each of us needs four friends like those. And each of us is called to be one of the four.

Today, think of someone who can't move forward alone. Carry them before Jesus in prayer, and do something concrete for them: a call, a visit, a message. Jesus sees the faith of those who carry.

Put it into practice.

One. If You're on the Stretcher. Accept being carried: ask two or three people to pray for you this week. Tell them specifically what you're going through.

Two. If You're Standing. Choose one person who can't move forward alone and carry them: a call, a visit, a meal, daily prayer for a week.

Three. Find Your Four Friends. Write the names of two or three people you could pray with regularly. Invite them for a prayer time this week, even over video call.

To reflect on. Am I the one carrying today or the one being carried? Who can I carry to Jesus this week?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you for seeing the faith of those who carry. Thank you for the people who have carried me in prayer. Give me the strength to be a friend who carries others to you, with persistence and creativity. And when I am weak, teach me to let myself be carried. Amen.

Key takeaway. Some days you carry the stretcher; other days you're the one on it.

texte:
Day 13. The Physician of Sinners.

Today's reading : Mark, chapter 2, verses 13 to 17.

He went out again by the seaside. All the multitude came to him, and he taught them. As he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax office. He said to him, “Follow me.” And he arose and followed him. He was reclining at the table in his house, and many tax collectors and sinners sat down with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many, and they followed him. The scribes and the Pharisees, when they saw that he was eating with the sinners and tax collectors, said to his disciples, “Why is it that he eats and drinks with tax collectors and sinners?” When Jesus heard it, he said to them, “Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”

The Story.

Levi, also called Matthew, is sitting at his tax booth. He is a tax collector: he collects taxes for the Romans, the hated occupier. Tax collectors were often wealthy because they collected more than necessary and kept the difference. To the people, they were traitors and thieves. They were lumped together with prostitutes.

And Jesus passes by this booth. He doesn't take a detour. He looks at Levi and says two words to him: "As Jesus passed by, he saw a man named Levi sitting at the tax booth. And he said to him, 'Follow me.' And he rose and followed him." (Mark, chapter 2, verse 14)

What This Reveals About Jesus.

No conditions first. Jesus doesn't tell him: "Pay back the money first, change jobs, go to the temple, and then we'll see." He calls him as he is, where he is. And Levi gets up, leaves everything, and follows him. A fisherman who leaves his boat can always go back to fishing; a tax collector who leaves his post will never get it back. Levi burns his bridges.

Then he throws a great feast at his house with all his friends: other tax collectors and people of ill repute. And Jesus sits at the table with them, eating, laughing, sharing. The religious leaders are scandalized: "Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?" Jesus answers: "When Jesus heard this, he said to them, 'Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.'" (Mark, chapter 2, verse 17)

Jesus presents himself as a doctor. A doctor doesn't run from the sick; he goes to them. Imagine a doctor who refused to enter a hospital because there were too many sick people. It would be absurd. Jesus goes where he is needed.

For Your Life.

This story has two messages, depending on where you find yourself.

If you feel like Levi, with a heavy past, a damaged reputation, things you're ashamed of, hear this: Jesus passes by your booth, and he calls you. Not when you become perfect: now. He doesn't ask you to be healthy to come to the doctor.

If you feel more like the religious leaders, ask yourself: do I see the Church as a museum for respectable people, or as a hospital for the wounded? Do I spend time with people who don't know Jesus, or do I stay only among Christians? Jesus wasn't afraid to be seen at the table with sinners. He didn't adopt their sin, but he shared their table.

Levi did the only thing he knew how to do: he invited his friends to meet Jesus over a good meal. And you? What table can you open this week so that someone might meet Jesus?

Put it into practice.

One. If You Feel Like Levi. Your past doesn't disqualify Jesus's call. Tell him today: "Here I am, just as I am." Then take one concrete step to follow him.

Two. Open Your Table. Like Levi, invite someone to your home or to a restaurant—someone who doesn't know Jesus. You don't need to preach: share a meal, listen, and let the conversation come naturally.

Three. Look at Your Church. How do you welcome newcomers or those with a difficult past? This week, go greet someone who is alone at church or in your group.

To reflect on. Do I see the Church as a museum for respectable people, or as a hospital for the wounded? What table can I open this week?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, physician of my soul, thank you for calling me as I was. I had nothing to offer you, and you said: follow me. Give me your eyes for those far from you, and the courage to share their table so I can speak to them about you. Amen.

Key takeaway. Jesus doesn't ask you to be healthy to come to the doctor.

Day 14. Salt and Light.

Today's reading : Matthew, chapter 5, verses 1 to 16.

Seeing the multitudes, he went up onto the mountain. When he had sat down, his disciples came to him. He opened his mouth and taught them, saying, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Blessed are the gentle, for they shall inherit the earth. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled. Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God. Blessed are those who have been persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven. “Blessed are you when people reproach you, persecute you, and say all kinds of evil against you falsely, for my sake. Rejoice, and be exceedingly glad, for great is your reward in heaven. For that is how they persecuted the prophets who were before you. “You are the salt of the earth, but if the salt has lost its flavor, with what will it be salted? It is then good for nothing, but to be cast out and trodden under the feet of men. “You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden. Neither do you light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house. Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

Part 3: His Word and His Power.

Jesus goes up on a mountain, sits down, and begins the most famous sermon in history: the Sermon on the Mount. For several days, we will hear what he teaches and see what he does.

The World Upside Down.

Jesus's first words must have surprised the crowd: "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted." (Matthew, chapter 5, verses 3 to 4)

Blessed are the poor, those who weep, the meek, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, those who are persecuted... The world says: blessed are the rich, the strong, those who never cry, those who crush others. Jesus says exactly the opposite. His kingdom is a world upside down, or rather, our world is upside down, and Jesus comes to set it right.

The Beatitudes are not a to-do list to earn blessing. They are declarations of happiness over people the world considers losers. If you're crying today, Jesus doesn't tell you "stop crying"; he tells you "you will be comforted."

Salt and Light.

Then Jesus looks at this crowd of simple people, peasants, fishermen, the sick, and says to them: "You are the salt of the earth." Not: "you will become," but: "you are."

Before the invention of refrigeration, salt was used to preserve meat and fish. Without salt, everything rotted in a few days. Salt also gave flavor. To be salt is to prevent decay around you and to give flavor to others' lives.

But salt is useless in the saltshaker. It must be spread, mixed, in contact. A Christian who stays only at church is salt in a saltshaker.

Then Jesus continues: "You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden; nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house. Let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven." (Matthew, chapter 5, verses 14 to 16)

For Your Life.

A light doesn't need to shout to be noticed. A lighthouse makes no noise; it shines, simply, and ships avoid the rocks because of it.

Notice the purpose of this light: so that people see your good works and "give glory to your Father." Not you. Your light isn't there to draw attention to yourself, but to show the way to God.

Where has God placed you? Your work, your school, your neighborhood, your family: that's where you must be salt and light. Today, ask yourself this question: if Christians disappeared from my surroundings, would anyone notice the difference? And choose one concrete act of kindness, honesty, or generosity so that someone sees the light of your Father.

Put it into practice.

One. Get Out of the Saltshaker. Where has God placed you (work, school, neighborhood, family)? Choose one specific place where you want to be salt this week.

Two. A Light in the Darkness. Do one concrete act of kindness, honesty, or generosity that people will notice, so they glorify your Father, not you.

Three. If You're Crying. If you're going through a season of tears, reread Matthew 5:4 and write down what you expect from God's comfort. He doesn't ask you to hide your tears.

To reflect on. Where has God placed me to be salt and light? What concrete action will I take this week so my Father is glorified?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you for saying I am the salt of the earth and the light of the world. Help me get out of the saltshaker. Where you've placed me, may my life prevent decay, give flavor, and show the way to you. May people see your works and glorify our Father. Amen.

Key takeaway. Salt is useless in the saltshaker.

texte:
Day 15. Seek First His Kingdom.

Today's reading : Matthew, chapter 6, verses 19 to 34.

“Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth, where moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal; but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal; for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness! “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon. Therefore I tell you, don’t be anxious for your life: what you will eat, or what you will drink; nor yet for your body, what you will wear. Isn’t life more than food, and the body more than clothing? See the birds of the sky, that they don’t sow, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns. Your heavenly Father feeds them. Aren’t you of much more value than they? “Which of you by being anxious, can add one moment to his lifespan? Why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They don’t toil, neither do they spin, yet I tell you that even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today exists and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, won’t he much more clothe you, you of little faith? “Therefore don’t be anxious, saying, ‘What will we eat?’, ‘What will we drink?’ or, ‘With what will we be clothed?’ For the Gentiles seek after all these things; for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. But seek first God’s Kingdom and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well. Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient.

The Story.

Jesus continues his teaching and addresses a subject that concerns us all: worry. Money, food, clothes, the future. He begins with a question of the heart: "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." (Matthew, chapter 6, verse 21)

What you consider your treasure will always end up capturing your heart. Your bank statement and your calendar often say more about your faith than your prayers.

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Then Jesus invites the crowd to look around them. He points to the birds flying over the mountain: "Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they?" (Matthew, chapter 6, verse 26)

A bird makes no reserves for winter, doesn't worry about crisis, doesn't calculate retirement. It lives under the eye of the Creator, day after day. And Jesus adds: you are worth much more than them.

Then he shows them the lilies of the field, these wild flowers that no one planted: even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of them. If God clothes the grass of the field like this, which is here today and burned tomorrow, will he not care for you?

And Jesus asks a very practical question: "And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?" Worry has never solved anything. A phrase often attributed to Corrie ten Boom says it this way: "Worry does not empty tomorrow of its sorrow; it empties today of its strength."

For Your Life.

Jesus's remedy is not "think of nothing," but "think of something else first": "But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble." (Matthew, chapter 6, verses 33 to 34)

"First." Everything is in that word. It's not that your needs don't matter; Jesus even says the Father knows you need them. But order matters. When God is first, everything else finds its place.

It's like the buttons on a shirt: if you get the first one wrong, all the others will be misaligned. Put God on the first button, and the rest will follow.

And Jesus adds very practical wisdom: live one day at a time. God gives grace for today, not for imaginary problems three years from now.

Today, make a list of your worries. For each one, ask yourself: can I do something about this today? If yes, do it. If no, give it to the Father in prayer. Then make one concrete decision to seek God first: the first moment of your day, the first part of your money, the first place in your choices.

Put it into practice.

One. The List of Worries. Write down your worries. For each one: can I do something about this today? If yes, do it. If no, give it to the Father in prayer.

Two. The First Button. Choose one concrete way to seek God first: the first moment of your day, the first part of your money, the first place in a decision.

Three. One Day at a Time. Tonight, before bed, thank God for three provisions of your day, and leave tomorrow to him. Do this every evening this week.

To reflect on. What worry occupies my mind the most right now? How can I concretely seek God "first" this week?

Prayer. Father, you feed the birds and clothe the flowers of the field: you will care for me. I give you my worries, one by one. I choose to seek you first, you and your kingdom. Give me the grace to live today, one day at a time, under your gaze. Amen.

Key takeaway. Worry does not empty tomorrow of its sorrow; it empties today of its strength.

Isn’t life more than food, and the body more than clothing? See the birds of the sky, that they don’t sow, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns. Your heavenly Father feeds them. Aren’t you of much more value than they? “Which of you by being anxious, can add one moment to his lifespan? Why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They don’t toil, neither do they spin, yet I tell you that even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today exists and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, won’t he much more clothe you, you of little faith? “Therefore don’t be anxious, saying, ‘What will we eat?’, ‘What will we drink?’ or, ‘With what will we be clothed?’ For the Gentiles seek after all these things; for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. But seek first God’s Kingdom and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well. Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient.

The Story.

Jesus continues his teaching and addresses a subject that concerns us all: worry. Money, food, clothes, the future. He begins with a question of the heart: "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." (Matthew, chapter 6, verse 21)

What you consider your treasure will always end up capturing your heart. Your bank statement and your calendar often say more about your faith than your prayers.

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Then Jesus invites the crowd to look around them. He points to the birds flying over the mountain: "Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they?" (Matthew, chapter 6, verse 26)

A bird makes no reserves for winter, doesn't worry about crisis, doesn't calculate retirement. It lives under the eye of the Creator, day after day. And Jesus adds: you are worth much more than them.

Then he shows them the lilies of the field, these wild flowers that no one planted: even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of them. If God clothes the grass of the field like this, which is here today and burned tomorrow, will he not care for you?

And Jesus asks a very practical question: "And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?" Worry has never solved anything. A phrase often attributed to Corrie ten Boom says it this way: "Worry does not empty tomorrow of its sorrow; it empties today of its strength."

For Your Life.

Jesus's remedy is not "think of nothing," but "think of something else first": "But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble." (Matthew, chapter 6, verses 33 to 34)

"First." Everything is in that word. It's not that your needs don't matter; Jesus even says the Father knows you need them. But order matters. When God is first, everything else finds its place.

It's like the buttons on a shirt: if you get the first one wrong, all the others will be misaligned. Put God on the first button, and the rest will follow.

And Jesus adds very practical wisdom: live one day at a time. God gives grace for today, not for imaginary problems three years from now.

Today, make a list of your worries. For each one, ask yourself: can I do something about this today? If yes, do it. If no, give it to the Father in prayer. Then make one concrete decision to seek God first: the first moment of your day, the first part of your money, the first place in your choices.

Put it into practice.

One. The List of Worries. Write down your worries. For each one: can I do something about this today? If yes, do it. If no, give it to the Father in prayer.

Two. The First Button. Choose one concrete way to seek God first: the first moment of your day, the first part of your money, the first place in a decision.

Three. One Day at a Time. Tonight, before bed, thank God for three provisions of your day, and leave tomorrow to him. Do this every evening this week.

To reflect on. What worry occupies my mind the most right now? How can I concretely seek God "first" this week?

Prayer. Father, you feed the birds and clothe the flowers of the field: you will care for me. I give you my worries, one by one. I choose to seek you first, you and your kingdom. Give me the grace to live today, one day at a time, under your gaze. Amen.

Key takeaway. Worry does not empty tomorrow of its sorrow; it empties today of its strength.

Day 16. The House on the Rock.

Today's reading : Matthew, chapter 7, verses 13 to 29.

“Enter in by the narrow gate; for the gate is wide and the way is broad that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter in by it. How narrow is the gate and the way is restricted that leads to life! There are few who find it. “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves. By their fruits you will know them. Do you gather grapes from thorns or figs from thistles? Even so, every good tree produces good fruit, but the corrupt tree produces evil fruit. A good tree can’t produce evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree produce good fruit. Every tree that doesn’t grow good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. Therefore by their fruits you will know them. “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. Many will tell me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, didn’t we prophesy in your name, in your name cast out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?’ Then I will tell them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity.’ “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine and does them, I will liken him to a wise man who built his house on the rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock. Everyone who hears these words of mine and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house; and it fell—and its fall was great.” When Jesus had finished saying these things, the multitudes were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them with authority, and not like the scribes.

The Story.

Jesus concludes his great sermon with a little story that every Sunday school child knows. Two men build a house. From the outside, you might see no difference: the same facade, the same walls, the same roof. The difference is hidden underground, in the foundations. "Therefore, whoever hears these sayings of Mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man who built his house on the rock. And the rain descended, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house; and it did not fall, for it was founded on the rock." (Matthew, chapter 7, verses 24 to 25)

"But everyone who hears these sayings of Mine, and does not do them, will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. And the rain descended, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house; and it fell. And great was its fall." (Matthew, chapter 7, verses 26 to 27)

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Notice this carefully: both men heard Jesus' words. They were both at the same sermon, maybe sitting side by side. The difference isn't between those who hear and those who don't hear, but between those who put it into practice and those who just listen.

And notice this too: the storm hits both houses. The rain, the floods, the winds. Jesus doesn't promise that the house on the rock will be spared from the storm. He promises that it will stand firm.

The Leaning Tower of Pisa is known throughout the world because it tilts. Why? Not because its walls are built poorly—its arches and columns are magnificent. But its foundations are shallow, laid on soil that's too soft. From the first floors upward, it began to lean. Beautiful construction never makes up for bad foundations.

For Your Life.

The storm doesn't create the cracks—it reveals them.

Sooner or later, a storm will come into your life: an illness, a loss, a betrayal, a financial crisis, a failure. This is not the moment to start digging foundations. Foundations are built in good weather, day by day, when everything is fine and it seems unnecessary.

Building on the rock isn't just reading the Bible, going to church, or listening to good messages. It's putting it into practice. Forgiving when Jesus says to forgive. Giving when he says to give. Being honest when no one is watching. Every act of obedience is another stone in your foundations.

Just before this story, Jesus speaks of two gates: a wide one that many take, and a narrow one that leads to life. Ease attracts crowds; truth demands courage.

Today, choose just one thing that you've heard in the Sermon on the Mount that you're not yet putting into practice. Not ten: one. And put it into practice this week. That's how you build a house that will stand in the storm.

Put it into practice.

One. Just One Word to Practice. Choose just one thing from the Sermon on the Mount that you're not yet putting into practice (forgiving, not judging, praying in secret, giving) and practice it this week.

Two. Dig While the Weather Is Good. If things are going well right now, this is the best time to strengthen your foundations: choose a spiritual habit to build before the next storm comes.

Three. Check Your Cracks. If a storm is here, ask yourself without shame: what crack is it revealing? Talk about it with God and with a mature believer.

To reflect on. Which word of Jesus am I hearing without putting it into practice? What step of obedience will I take this week?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you are my rock. I don't just want to hear your words; I want to put them into practice. Show me the cracks in my foundations, and help me build my life on you, day by day, so that I stand firm when the storm comes. Amen.

Key takeaway. The storm doesn't create the cracks—it reveals them.

Day 17. Say Only One Word.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 7, verses 1 to 10.

After he had finished speaking in the hearing of the people, he entered into Capernaum. A certain centurion’s servant, who was dear to him, was sick and at the point of death. When he heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and save his servant. When they came to Jesus, they begged him earnestly, saying, “He is worthy for you to do this for him, for he loves our nation, and he built our synagogue for us.” Jesus went with them. When he was now not far from the house, the centurion sent friends to him, saying to him, “Lord, don’t trouble yourself, for I am not worthy for you to come under my roof. Therefore I didn’t even think myself worthy to come to you; but say the word, and my servant will be healed. For I also am a man placed under authority, having under myself soldiers. I tell this one, ‘Go!’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come!’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him, and turned and said to the multitude who followed him, “I tell you, I have not found such great faith, no, not in Israel.” Those who were sent, returning to the house, found that the servant who had been sick was well.

The Story.

A Roman centurion lives in Capernaum. An officer of the occupying army, commanding a hundred soldiers. Normally, a man like him was despised by the Jews. But this one is different: he loves the Jewish people, and has even built their synagogue. And he has a servant whom he loves deeply, who is about to die.

He sends Jewish elders to beg Jesus to come. Jesus sets out. But as he approaches the house, the centurion sends friends to tell him: "Jesus went with them. Now when he was already not far from the house, the centurion sent friends to him, saying to him, 'Lord, do not trouble Yourself, for I am not worthy that You should enter under my roof. Therefore I did not even think myself worthy to come to You. But say the word, and my servant will be healed.'" (Luke, chapter 7, verses 6 to 7)

What This Reveals About Jesus.

The centurion understands something that many religious leaders have not grasped: Jesus' authority has no limit of distance. He explains: "For I also am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me. And I say to one, 'Go,' and he goes; and to another, 'Come,' and he comes; and to my servant, 'Do this,' and he does it." In the military, an order given by the one in authority is carried out, even if the officer is not present. The centurion has understood that sickness itself obeys Jesus.

And Jesus is amazed: "When Jesus heard these things, He marveled at him, and turned around and said to the crowd that followed Him, 'I say to you, I have not found such great faith, not even in Israel.'" (Luke, chapter 7, verse 9)

There are only two times in the Gospels when it's said that Jesus is astonished: here, before the faith of a foreigner, and in Nazareth, before the unbelief of his own village (Mark, chapter 6, verse 6). Jesus marvels at the faith of a man who did not grow up in religion, but who understood who Jesus was.

For Your Life.

Notice two things in the heart of this man.

First, humility: "I am not worthy." The elders had said of him: "He deserves that You do this for him." But he says: "I am not worthy." Faith is not built on our merit, but on Jesus' authority.

Second, trust in the word: "Say the word." No need to see, to touch, to feel. One word from Jesus is enough. The servant is healed from a distance, at that very hour.

Maybe you're praying for someone who is far away: a child who has drifted from God, a parent who is sick in another country, a friend in a desperate situation. You cannot be there. But Jesus' word has no limit of distance. No ocean, no hospital wall, no closed door can stop it.

Today, pray for a person who is far from you, with the faith of the centurion: "Lord, I am not worthy, but say only one word, and she will be healed, he will be saved, she will be set free."

Put it into practice.

One. Pray for Someone Far Away. Choose a person who is distant (a child who has left, a parent who is sick in another country, a friend in crisis) and pray for them with the centurion's faith: "Say only one word."

Two. Humility and Faith. Begin your prayer with: "Lord, I am not worthy," then present your request with confidence. The two go together.

Three. For a Coworker or Neighbor. The centurion interceded for his servant. Is there someone for whom you have responsibility and whom you could pray for this week?

To reflect on. For which person far from me will I pray with the centurion's faith?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, I am not worthy that You should enter under my roof, but I know that Your word has all authority. No distance can stop it. Say only one word for those I love who are far from me. Give me faith that will amaze You. Amen.

Key takeaway. Jesus' word has no limit of distance.

Day 18. Do You See This Woman?.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 7, verses 36 to 50.

One of the Pharisees invited him to eat with him. He entered into the Pharisee’s house and sat at the table. Behold, a woman in the city who was a sinner, when she knew that he was reclining in the Pharisee’s house, brought an alabaster jar of ointment. Standing behind at his feet weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears, and she wiped them with the hair of her head, kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment. Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw it, he said to himself, “This man, if he were a prophet, would have perceived who and what kind of woman this is who touches him, that she is a sinner.” Jesus answered him, “Simon, I have something to tell you.” He said, “Teacher, say on.” “A certain lender had two debtors. The one owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. When they couldn’t pay, he forgave them both. Which of them therefore will love him most?” Simon answered, “He, I suppose, to whom he forgave the most.” He said to him, “You have judged correctly.” Turning to the woman, he said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? I entered into your house, and you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears, and wiped them with the hair of her head. You gave me no kiss, but she, since the time I came in, has not ceased to kiss my feet. You didn’t anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment. Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But one to whom little is forgiven, loves little.” He said to her, “Your sins are forgiven.” Those who sat at the table with him began to say to themselves, “Who is this who even forgives sins?” He said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you. Go in peace.”

The Story.

Simon, a Pharisee, invites Jesus to dinner. In those days, guests reclined on cushions, with their feet turned outward, and homes often remained open—people from the village could come in to listen to conversations.

Suddenly, a woman enters. Everyone knows her: she's a sinner of the city, perhaps a prostitute. She approaches Jesus from behind, at his feet, and begins to weep. Her tears fall on Jesus' feet. She wipes them with her hair, kisses them, and pours precious perfume on them.

The silence must be terrible. Simon thinks to himself: "If this Man were a prophet, He would know who and what manner of woman this is who is touching Him, for she is a sinner."

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Jesus has understood very well what Simon is thinking. He tells him a little parable: two men owe a creditor a debt, one owes five hundred denarii, the other fifty. The creditor forgives both debts. Which one will love him more? Simon answers: "I suppose the one whom he forgave more."

Then Jesus turns toward the woman and says to Simon: "So He turned to the woman and said to Simon, 'Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has washed my feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head.'" (Luke, chapter 7, verse 44)

"Do you see this woman?" What a question! Of course Simon sees her. But he sees only her past, her reputation, her label. Simon saw her past; Jesus saw her love.

Jesus makes a list: Simon offered no water for his feet, no kiss of greeting, no oil for his head. The most basic courtesies. She gave everything. And Jesus concludes: "Therefore I say to you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But to whom little is forgiven, the same loves little.' Then He said to her, 'Your sins are forgiven.'" (Luke, chapter 7, verses 47 to 48)

For Your Life.

Simon's problem is not that he had sinned less. It's that he thought he needed less forgiveness. And the one who thinks he needs little forgiveness loves little.

The more you become aware of what Jesus has forgiven you, the greater your love for him grows. It's no accident that those who come from far away often have the most passionate praise.

And if you feel like this woman, rejected, judged, reduced to your past, listen to what Jesus says to her at the end: "Your faith has saved you; go in peace." He lifts her up in front of everyone. He restores her dignity publicly, in the very place where she had been humiliated publicly.

Today, take a moment to remember all that Jesus has forgiven you. Not to sink into guilt, but to let gratitude rise up. Then ask yourself: is there someone I'm looking at the way Simon looked at this woman? Ask Jesus to give you his gaze.

Put it into practice.

One. Remember Your Debt. Write down everything Jesus has forgiven you, without staying locked in it. Then thank him, aloud or in song. Gratitude nourishes love.

Two. Change Your Gaze. Is there someone you're looking at the way Simon looked at this woman? Ask Jesus for his gaze and make a gesture of respect toward that person.

Three. If You Feel Judged. Reread Luke 7:50 and receive Jesus' word for you: "Your faith has saved you; go in peace." Your past does not have the final word.

To reflect on. Am I aware of all that has been forgiven me? Is there someone I reduce to their past?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank You for all You have forgiven me. My debt was immense, and You erased it. May my love for You be measured by this forgiveness. Give me Your gaze on others, so that I see not their past, but what Your grace can do in them. Amen.

Key takeaway. Simon saw his past; Jesus saw her love.

Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw it, he said to himself, “This man, if he were a prophet, would have perceived who and what kind of woman this is who touches him, that she is a sinner.” Jesus answered him, “Simon, I have something to tell you.” He said, “Teacher, say on.” “A certain lender had two debtors. The one owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. When they couldn’t pay, he forgave them both. Which of them therefore will love him most?” Simon answered, “He, I suppose, to whom he forgave the most.” He said to him, “You have judged correctly.” Turning to the woman, he said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? I entered into your house, and you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears, and wiped them with the hair of her head. You gave me no kiss, but she, since the time I came in, has not ceased to kiss my feet. You didn’t anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment. Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But one to whom little is forgiven, loves little.” He said to her, “Your sins are forgiven.” Those who sat at the table with him began to say to themselves, “Who is this who even forgives sins?” He said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you. Go in peace.”

The Story.

Simon, a Pharisee, invites Jesus to dinner. In those days, guests reclined on cushions, with their feet turned outward, and homes often remained open—people from the village could come in to listen to conversations.

Suddenly, a woman enters. Everyone knows her: she's a sinner of the city, perhaps a prostitute. She approaches Jesus from behind, at his feet, and begins to weep. Her tears fall on Jesus' feet. She wipes them with her hair, kisses them, and pours precious perfume on them.

The silence must be terrible. Simon thinks to himself: "If this Man were a prophet, He would know who and what manner of woman this is who is touching Him, for she is a sinner."

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Jesus has understood very well what Simon is thinking. He tells him a little parable: two men owe a creditor a debt, one owes five hundred denarii, the other fifty. The creditor forgives both debts. Which one will love him more? Simon answers: "I suppose the one whom he forgave more."

Then Jesus turns toward the woman and says to Simon: "So He turned to the woman and said to Simon, 'Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has washed my feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head.'" (Luke, chapter 7, verse 44)

"Do you see this woman?" What a question! Of course Simon sees her. But he sees only her past, her reputation, her label. Simon saw her past; Jesus saw her love.

Jesus makes a list: Simon offered no water for his feet, no kiss of greeting, no oil for his head. The most basic courtesies. She gave everything. And Jesus concludes: "Therefore I say to you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But to whom little is forgiven, the same loves little.' Then He said to her, 'Your sins are forgiven.'" (Luke, chapter 7, verses 47 to 48)

For Your Life.

Simon's problem is not that he had sinned less. It's that he thought he needed less forgiveness. And the one who thinks he needs little forgiveness loves little.

The more you become aware of what Jesus has forgiven you, the greater your love for him grows. It's no accident that those who come from far away often have the most passionate praise.

And if you feel like this woman, rejected, judged, reduced to your past, listen to what Jesus says to her at the end: "Your faith has saved you; go in peace." He lifts her up in front of everyone. He restores her dignity publicly, in the very place where she had been humiliated publicly.

Today, take a moment to remember all that Jesus has forgiven you. Not to sink into guilt, but to let gratitude rise up. Then ask yourself: is there someone I'm looking at the way Simon looked at this woman? Ask Jesus to give you his gaze.

Put it into practice.

One. Remember Your Debt. Write down everything Jesus has forgiven you, without staying locked in it. Then thank him, aloud or in song. Gratitude nourishes love.

Two. Change Your Gaze. Is there someone you're looking at the way Simon looked at this woman? Ask Jesus for his gaze and make a gesture of respect toward that person.

Three. If You Feel Judged. Reread Luke 7:50 and receive Jesus' word for you: "Your faith has saved you; go in peace." Your past does not have the final word.

To reflect on. Am I aware of all that has been forgiven me? Is there someone I reduce to their past?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank You for all You have forgiven me. My debt was immense, and You erased it. May my love for You be measured by this forgiveness. Give me Your gaze on others, so that I see not their past, but what Your grace can do in them. Amen.

Key takeaway. Simon saw his past; Jesus saw her love.

Day 19. Let's Cross to the Other Side.

Today's reading : Mark, chapter 4, verses 35 to 41.

On that day, when evening had come, he said to them, “Let’s go over to the other side.” Leaving the multitude, they took him with them, even as he was, in the boat. Other small boats were also with him. A big wind storm arose, and the waves beat into the boat, so much that the boat was already filled. He himself was in the stern, asleep on the cushion; and they woke him up and asked him, “Teacher, don’t you care that we are dying?” He awoke and rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” The wind ceased and there was a great calm. He said to them, “Why are you so afraid? How is it that you have no faith?” They were greatly afraid and said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”

The Story.

It's evening, after a long day of teaching. Jesus says to his disciples: "That day, when evening came, he said to his disciples, 'Let us go over to the other side.'" (Mark, chapter 4, verse 35) They get into the boat. Jesus, exhausted, falls asleep at the stern, his head on a pillow.

Then the storm breaks out. The Sea of Galilee is known for its sudden storms: it's surrounded by hills, and the wind can rush through with terrible violence. Waves fill the boat. And those who are afraid are not tourists: they are experienced fishermen who know this lake by heart. If they panic, it's because the situation is truly grave.

They wake Jesus: "And he was in the stern, asleep on a pillow. And they woke him and said to him, 'Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?' And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, 'Peace! Be still!' And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm." (Mark, chapter 4, verses 38 to 39)

What This Reveals About Jesus.

"Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?" That's maybe the question you're asking God right now. "Does this matter to you? Why are you sleeping while I'm drowning?"

But look at Jesus's response. He gets up, and he speaks to the wind and the sea the way you'd speak to a barking dog: "Peace! Be still!" And everything stops. Not gradually: immediately, a great calm.

Then he turns to his disciples: "And he said to them, 'Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?' And they were filled with great fear, and said to one another, 'Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?'" (Mark, chapter 4, verses 40 to 41)

Their fear changes its object. They were afraid of the storm; now they're in awe before the One who commands the storm. They're beginning to understand who is in their boat.

For Your Life.

There's a story about an airplane caught in severe turbulence. The passengers are terrified, some are screaming, others are praying. Only a little girl remains calm and keeps playing. After landing, someone asks her: "Weren't you afraid?" She answers: "No, my dad's the pilot."

Notice one essential detail: before the storm, Jesus had said "let us go over to the other side." Not "let's go into the middle of the lake to sink." His word already contained the destination. The storm didn't cancel his promise.

If Jesus is in your boat, the storm can shake the boat, but it cannot sink it.

What's the storm in your life today? Rather than letting fear speak, remember the word God has given you. And bring him your storm. He can calm it with a word. And if he doesn't calm it right away, he can calm your heart in the middle of it. Either way, you'll make it to the other side.

Put it into practice.

One. Name Your Storm. Write down the storm you're going through. Just below it, write a promise from God that applies to your situation. Read it again when fear rises.

Two. Wake Jesus in Prayer. Like the disciples, cry out to him honestly. Then finish with: "I believe you're leading me to the other side."

Three. Be Calm for Someone Else. Think of someone who's panicking right now. Call them, listen to them, and pray with them: your presence can be Jesus's calm for them.

To reflect on. What storm am I going through right now? What promise from God will I hold on to in the middle of it?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you're in my boat. You see the waves and the wind that frighten me. You command the storm: speak to mine too. Calm the waters, or calm my heart in the middle of them. I believe you're leading me to the other side. Amen.

Key takeaway. If Jesus is in your boat, the storm won't sink it.

Day 20. Sitting, Clothed, and in His Right Mind.

Today's reading : Mark, chapter 5, verses 1 to 20.

They came to the other side of the sea, into the country of the Gadarenes. When he had come out of the boat, immediately a man with an unclean spirit met him out of the tombs. He lived in the tombs. Nobody could bind him any more, not even with chains, because he had been often bound with fetters and chains, and the chains had been torn apart by him, and the fetters broken in pieces. Nobody had the strength to tame him. Always, night and day, in the tombs and in the mountains, he was crying out, and cutting himself with stones. When he saw Jesus from afar, he ran and bowed down to him, and crying out with a loud voice, he said, “What have I to do with you, Jesus, you Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, don’t torment me.” For he said to him, “Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!” He asked him, “What is your name?” He said to him, “My name is Legion, for we are many.” He begged him much that he would not send them away out of the country. Now on the mountainside there was a great herd of pigs feeding. All the demons begged him, saying, “Send us into the pigs, that we may enter into them.” At once Jesus gave them permission. The unclean spirits came out and entered into the pigs. The herd of about two thousand rushed down the steep bank into the sea, and they were drowned in the sea. Those who fed the pigs fled, and told it in the city and in the country. The people came to see what it was that had happened. They came to Jesus, and saw him who had been possessed by demons sitting, clothed, and in his right mind, even him who had the legion; and they were afraid. Those who saw it declared to them what happened to him who was possessed by demons, and about the pigs. They began to beg him to depart from their region. As he was entering into the boat, he who had been possessed by demons begged him that he might be with him. He didn’t allow him, but said to him, “Go to your house, to your friends, and tell them what great things the Lord has done for you and how he had mercy on you.” He went his way, and began to proclaim in Decapolis how Jesus had done great things for him, and everyone marveled.

The Story.

After the storm on the lake, Jesus arrives on the other side, in the country of the Gerasenes. And as soon as he steps out of the boat, a man comes to meet him. A terrifying man: he lives in the tombs, naked, crying out day and night and cutting himself with stones. They've tried to chain him, but he breaks the chains. No one can control him. He's a man inhabited by a multitude of demons, who call themselves "Legion."

Notice one thing: Jesus crossed a storm at night to come to this one man. The entire journey had a purpose: one man, lost in the tombs.

What This Reveals About Jesus.

The demons tremble before Jesus. They beg him, they bargain. Jesus has total authority: he drives them out, and they enter a herd of about two thousand pigs that rush down into the sea.

Then the people of the town arrive, and here's what they see: "And they came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man, the one who had had the legion, sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid." (Mark, chapter 5, verse 15)

Sitting: the one who wandered day and night has found rest. Clothed: the one who lived naked has regained his dignity. In his right mind: the one who was tormented has regained peace of mind. That's what Jesus does with a life that everyone had given up on.

But the reaction of the townspeople is sad: they beg Jesus to leave their region. They've lost pigs, and that matters more to them than a man set free. Sometimes, someone's freedom disturbs the economy and comfort of others.

For Your Life.

The freed man wants to follow Jesus. But Jesus tells him: "Jesus did not permit him, but said to him, 'Go home to your own people and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.'" (Mark, chapter 5, verse 19)

He becomes the first missionary of this pagan region. He hasn't attended Bible school, he doesn't know much. But he has a story: "Here's what Jesus did for me." And the man goes and proclaims throughout the Decapolis all that Jesus has done for him (Mark, chapter 5, verse 20). And when Jesus comes back to this region later, people will bring him the sick and the news will spread everywhere (Mark, chapter 7, verses 31 to 37).

No one is too far, too chained, too broken for Jesus. The chains that no one could break, he breaks them. The man that everyone avoided, he crosses a storm to meet him.

Maybe you know someone who seems unreachable: addictions, violence, occultism, torment. Don't lose hope: Jesus has authority over all powers. Pray for this person with faith.

And your story? You don't need a complicated speech. Simply tell, in your own home, to those close to you, what the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.

Put it into practice.

One. What Have You Been Set Free From?. Write down what Jesus has broken in your life, even partially. Then tell someone close to you about it this week, simply.

Two. Pray for Someone Unreachable. Choose one person who seems too far gone (addiction, violence, occultism) and pray for them every day this week, with faith in Jesus's authority.

Three. Don't Prefer the Pigs. Is there a comfort or interest you're putting before someone's freedom? Ask God to give you his heart for people.

To reflect on. What has Jesus set me free from? Who will I tell this week what the Lord has done for me?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you for crossing the storm to come find me. You broke chains that no one could break. I pray for those still in chains: show your authority in their lives. And give me the courage to tell those close to me what you have done for me. Amen.

Key takeaway. No one is too far, too chained, or too broken for Jesus.
