Day 21. Don't Fear, Only Believe.

Today's reading : Mark, chapter 5, verses 21 to 43.

When Jesus had crossed back over in the boat to the other side, a great multitude was gathered to him; and he was by the sea. Behold, one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name, came; and seeing him, he fell at his feet and begged him much, saying, “My little daughter is at the point of death. Please come and lay your hands on her, that she may be made healthy, and live.” He went with him, and a great multitude followed him, and they pressed upon him on all sides. A certain woman who had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and had suffered many things by many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better, but rather grew worse, having heard the things concerning Jesus, came up behind him in the crowd and touched his clothes. For she said, “If I just touch his clothes, I will be made well.” Immediately the flow of her blood was dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of her affliction. Immediately Jesus, perceiving in himself that the power had gone out from him, turned around in the crowd and asked, “Who touched my clothes?” His disciples said to him, “You see the multitude pressing against you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” He looked around to see her who had done this thing. But the woman, fearing and trembling, knowing what had been done to her, came and fell down before him, and told him all the truth. He said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace, and be cured of your disease.” While he was still speaking, people came from the synagogue ruler’s house, saying, “Your daughter is dead. Why bother the Teacher any more?” But Jesus, when he heard the message spoken, immediately said to the ruler of the synagogue, “Don’t be afraid, only believe.” He allowed no one to follow him except Peter, James, and John the brother of James. He came to the synagogue ruler’s house, and he saw an uproar, weeping, and great wailing. When he had entered in, he said to them, “Why do you make an uproar and weep? The child is not dead, but is asleep.” They ridiculed him. But he, having put them all out, took the father of the child, her mother, and those who were with him, and went in where the child was lying. Taking the child by the hand, he said to her, “Talitha cumi!” which means, being interpreted, “Girl, I tell you, get up!” Immediately the girl rose up and walked, for she was twelve years old. They were amazed with great amazement. He strictly ordered them that no one should know this, and commanded that something should be given to her to eat.

The Story.

Jairus is a respected man: a synagogue official. But that day, his title is useless to him. His twelve-year-old daughter is dying. He falls at Jesus's feet and begs him to come. Jesus goes with him. Every minute counts.

And suddenly, everything stops. In the crowd pressing around Jesus, a woman touches him. For twelve years, she's been suffering from constant bleeding. She's spent everything on doctors, and her condition has only gotten worse. According to the law, her illness made her unclean: she couldn't touch anyone or go to the temple. Twelve years without touch, without a hug, without community. She says to herself: "If I just touch his clothes, I will be made well." She touches him, and she's healed instantly.

Jesus stops: "Who touched my clothes?" The disciples think the question is absurd: everyone's touching him! But Jesus knows the difference between a crowd jostling him and faith touching him.

What This Reveals About Jesus.

The woman comes forward trembling and tells him everything. Jesus could have let her go healed in body. But he wanted to heal her heart too, before everyone: "And he said to her, 'Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your affliction.'" (Mark, chapter 5, verse 34)

"Daughter." No one had called her that in twelve years. She came looking for healing; she leaves with an identity.

But meanwhile, Jairus is waiting. And the news comes: "Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher anymore?" Imagine this father. That delay cost him his daughter. It's then that Jesus says to him: "But Jesus, overhearing what they said, said to the ruler of the synagogue, 'Don't be afraid, only believe.'" (Mark, chapter 5, verse 36)

Jesus arrives at the house, takes the child's hand, and says to her: "Talitha koum," "Little girl, I say to you, get up." And she gets up.

For Your Life.

Jesus's delays are not refusals.

Twelve years of sickness for the woman, twelve years of life for the girl. The one is starting to live again at the moment the other seemed to be losing her life. And Jesus took care of both, in the right order, in his time.

Maybe you're like Jairus. You've prayed, and Jesus seems to have stopped for someone else. Others are answered, and you're waiting. And now you're being told: "It's too late. Don't trouble the Teacher anymore." Listen to Jesus's voice louder than the voice of bad news: "Don't be afraid, only believe."

Maybe you're like that woman, exhausted, alone, after trying everything. Dare to reach out. Dare to make your way through the crowd. Jesus feels the difference between the crowd and faith.

Today, bring before Jesus what seems too late or too long to you. And repeat his word: "Don't be afraid, only believe."

Put it into practice.

One. Set Down What Seems Too Late. Write the situation where you hear: "It's too late, don't trouble the Teacher anymore." Then repeat Jesus's word: "Don't be afraid, only believe."

Two. Dare to Reach Out. If you're exhausted like the woman, take a step toward Jesus today: a moment of prayer, attending a service, asking someone to pray for you.

Three. When Someone Else Gets Their Answer First. If others are answered and you're not, rejoice for them and trust your waiting to Jesus. His delays are not refusals.

To reflect on. In what situation do I feel like it's "too late"? How can I reach out to Jesus today?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you feel the difference between the crowd and faith. I reach out to you today. When bad news says it's too late, help me hear your voice: don't be afraid, only believe. I trust you for your timing. Amen.

Key takeaway. Jesus's delays are not refusals.

Jesus arrives at the house, takes the child's hand, and says to her: "Talitha koum," "Little girl, I say to you, get up." And she gets up.

For Your Life.

Jesus's delays are not refusals.

Twelve years of sickness for the woman, twelve years of life for the girl. The one is starting to live again at the moment the other seemed to be losing her life. And Jesus took care of both, in the right order, in his time.

Maybe you're like Jairus. You've prayed, and Jesus seems to have stopped for someone else. Others are answered, and you're waiting. And now you're being told: "It's too late. Don't trouble the Teacher anymore." Listen to Jesus's voice louder than the voice of bad news: "Don't be afraid, only believe."

Maybe you're like that woman, exhausted, alone, after trying everything. Dare to reach out. Dare to make your way through the crowd. Jesus feels the difference between the crowd and faith.

Today, bring before Jesus what seems too late or too long to you. And repeat his word: "Don't be afraid, only believe."

Put it into practice.

One. Set Down What Seems Too Late. Write the situation where you hear: "It's too late, don't trouble the Teacher anymore." Then repeat Jesus's word: "Don't be afraid, only believe."

Two. Dare to Reach Out. If you're exhausted like the woman, take a step toward Jesus today: a moment of prayer, attending a service, asking someone to pray for you.

Three. When Someone Else Gets Their Answer First. If others are answered and you're not, rejoice for them and trust your waiting to Jesus. His delays are not refusals.

To reflect on. In what situation do I feel like it's "too late"? How can I reach out to Jesus today?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you feel the difference between the crowd and faith. I reach out to you today. When bad news says it's too late, help me hear your voice: don't be afraid, only believe. I trust you for your timing. Amen.

Key takeaway. Jesus's delays are not refusals.

Day 22. Five Loaves and Two Fish.

Today's reading : John, chapter 6, verses 1 to 15.

After these things, Jesus went away to the other side of the sea of Galilee, which is also called the Sea of Tiberias. A great multitude followed him, because they saw his signs which he did on those who were sick. Jesus went up into the mountain, and he sat there with his disciples. Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand. Jesus therefore, lifting up his eyes and seeing that a great multitude was coming to him, said to Philip, “Where are we to buy bread, that these may eat?” He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do. Philip answered him, “Two hundred denarii worth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may receive a little.” One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him, “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are these among so many?” Jesus said, “Have the people sit down.” Now there was much grass in that place. So the men sat down, in number about five thousand. Jesus took the loaves, and having given thanks, he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to those who were sitting down, likewise also of the fish as much as they desired. When they were filled, he said to his disciples, “Gather up the broken pieces which are left over, that nothing be lost.” So they gathered them up, and filled twelve baskets with broken pieces from the five barley loaves, which were left over by those who had eaten. When therefore the people saw the sign which Jesus did, they said, “This is truly the prophet who comes into the world.” Jesus therefore, perceiving that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, withdrew again to the mountain by himself.

The Story.

A massive crowd follows Jesus: about five thousand men, not counting the women and children. The day is wearing on, there's nothing to eat, and they're far from any villages. Jesus turns to Philip: "Where can we buy bread for these people to eat?" He already knew what he was going to do; he wanted to test him.

Philip does the math: two hundred denarii of bread—that's roughly eight months' wages for a worker—wouldn't even be enough. Philip sees the problem.

Then Andrew steps forward: "Here is a boy with five small barley loaves and two small fish, but how far will they go among so many?" (John, chapter 6, verse 9)

Barley loaves: the bread of the poor. Two tiny fish. A child's meal. And Andrew himself says it: "How far will they go among so many?"

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Jesus has the crowd sit down on the grass. Then: "Jesus then took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated; so also the fish, as much as they wanted. When they had all had enough to eat, he told his disciples, 'Gather the pieces that are left over. Let nothing be wasted.'" (John, chapter 6, verses 11 to 12)

Jesus takes what's given to him, he gives thanks, he distributes it. He doesn't despise the small basket. He doesn't say, "It's too little, I'll do without it." He could have made bread fall from heaven, like the manna in the desert. But he chooses to start with a child's meal.

And at the end, they gather twelve baskets of leftovers. More than they started with. God doesn't just give enough; he gives abundantly.

For Your Life.

What you give to Jesus is never too small; what he does with it is never small.

We're often like Philip: we calculate, we see the problem, we measure everything that's missing. Or like Andrew: we see a few resources, but we think they won't help. "What good is my little talent, my little time, my little gift, my little prayer, in the face of such a great need?"

The boy didn't calculate anything. He gave what he had. We don't even know his name. But two thousand years later, we're still talking about his meal.

Jesus doesn't ask you for what you don't have. He asks you for what you do have. Moses had a staff. David had a slingshot. The widow of Zarephath had a little flour and oil. This boy had five loaves and two fish. And you—what do you have in your hands?

Today, identify your "basket": a talent, some time, a skill, money, a house, a voice. Maybe it seems ridiculous compared to the world's needs. Give it to Jesus anyway. Let him take it, bless it, and multiply it. You'll be amazed at the leftovers.

Put it into practice.

One. Identify Your Basket. Write down what you have in your hands: a talent, time, a skill, money, a house, a voice. Nothing is too small.

Two. Give It This Week. Choose a concrete way to put it at His service: serve in your church, help a neighbor, give to a mission, lend your house for a group.

Three. Before the Numbers, Prayer. Face a need that's too big (finances, a project, family), do what Jesus did: take what you have, give thanks, and start with that.

To reflect on. What do I have "in my basket" that I could give to Jesus, even if it seems too small?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, I don't have much, but I give you what I have. My time, my talents, my resources, my life. Take them, bless them, and multiply them to feed many others. I don't want to keep counting what's missing—I want to trust you with what I have. Amen.

Key takeaway. Jesus doesn't ask you for what you don't have: he asks you for what you do have.

Day 23. Get Out of the Boat.

Today's reading : Matthew, chapter 14, verses 22 to 33.

Immediately Jesus made the disciples get into the boat and go ahead of him to the other side, while he sent the multitudes away. After he had sent the multitudes away, he went up into the mountain by himself to pray. When evening had come, he was there alone. But the boat was now in the middle of the sea, distressed by the waves, for the wind was contrary. In the fourth watch of the night, Jesus came to them, walking on the sea. When the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were troubled, saying, “It’s a ghost!” and they cried out for fear. But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, “Cheer up! It is I! Don’t be afraid.” Peter answered him and said, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the waters.” He said, “Come!” Peter stepped down from the boat and walked on the waters to come to Jesus. But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, “Lord, save me!” Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” When they got up into the boat, the wind ceased. Those who were in the boat came and worshiped him, saying, “You are truly the Son of God!”

The Story.

After the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus has his disciples get into a boat and go ahead of him to the other side of the lake while he goes up on a mountainside by himself to pray. During the night, the boat is battered by the waves; the wind is against them. Between three and six in the morning, in the fourth watch of the night, Jesus comes to them... walking on the water.

The disciples cry out in fear: "It's a ghost!" And Jesus says to them: "Jesus immediately said to them: 'Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid!'" (Matthew, chapter 14, verse 27)

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Peter has a crazy idea: "Lord, if it's you, tell me to come to you on the water." And Jesus answers with one word: "Come!" "And he said, 'Come.' Then Peter got down out of the boat, walked on the water and came toward Jesus. But when he saw the wind, he was afraid and, beginning to sink, cried out, 'Lord, save me!' Immediately Jesus reached out his hand and caught him. 'You of little faith,' he said, 'why did you doubt?'" (Matthew, chapter 14, verses 29 to 31)

We often talk about Peter sinking. But don't forget: Peter walked on water. He's the only human being besides Jesus to have done it. Eleven disciples stayed safe in the boat. Only one got out.

A Christian author, John Ortberg, wrote a book with a title that says it all: "If You Want to Walk on Water, You've Got to Get Out of the Boat." Miracles rarely happen in the comfort zone.

And what happened when Peter began to sink? The wind hadn't changed. The waves were the same as when he stepped out of the boat. What had changed was where he was looking: he looked at the wind instead of looking at Jesus.

And even then, Jesus doesn't let him sink. "Immediately," the text says, he reached out his hand and caught him. The rebuke comes after the rescue, not before.

For Your Life.

Better to sink after walking on water than to stay dry without ever trying.

What's your boat? What makes you feel secure but limits you? Maybe Jesus is saying "come" to you: for a calling, a service, a difficult conversation, a project, a step of faith. You're afraid of sinking. That's normal. But Jesus is on the water, and he's reaching out his hand.

And if you've already started to sink because you looked at the wind, circumstances, criticism, your weaknesses, it's not too late. Do what Peter did: cry out, "Lord, save me!" His hand is faster than the waves.

Today, spot one thing that's turning your eyes away from Jesus, a "wind" that impresses you. Then fix your eyes on him again, through his Word and worship. And dare to take a step out of the boat.

Put it into practice.

One. Name Your Boat. Write down the comfort zone that protects you but limits you. What is Jesus saying "come" to? Write it down.

Two. One Step Out of the Boat. Take a small step of faith this week: a difficult conversation, serving, signing up, witnessing. Start small, but get out.

Three. Change Your Focus. Spot the "wind" that impresses you most (circumstances, criticism, numbers). Each morning, before you look at it, read a psalm and fix your eyes on Jesus.

To reflect on. What is my "boat," my comfort zone? What is Jesus saying "come" to right now?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you're walking on the waters that frighten me. If it's you calling me, I want to get out of the boat. Keep my eyes fixed on you, not on the wind. And when I start to sink, reach out and catch me by the hand. I trust you. Amen.

Key takeaway. Miracles rarely happen in the comfort zone.

texte:
Day 24. Who Do You Say I Am?.

Today's reading : Matthew, chapter 16, verses 13 to 28.

Now when Jesus came into the parts of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, saying, “Who do men say that I, the Son of Man, am?” They said, “Some say John the Baptizer, some, Elijah, and others, Jeremiah or one of the prophets.” He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Jesus answered him, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. I also tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it. I will give to you the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will have been bound in heaven; and whatever you release on earth will have been released in heaven.” Then he commanded the disciples that they should tell no one that he was Jesus the Christ. From that time, Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and the third day be raised up. Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying, “Far be it from you, Lord! This will never be done to you.” But he turned and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men.” Then Jesus said to his disciples, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, and whoever will lose his life for my sake will find it. For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his life? Or what will a man give in exchange for his life? For the Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will give to everyone according to his deeds. Most certainly I tell you, there are some standing here who will in no way taste of death until they see the Son of Man coming in his Kingdom.”

The Story.

Jesus takes his disciples far north to Caesarea Philippi, a city filled with pagan temples. In the midst of all these gods, he asks them a question: "Who do people say the Son of Man is?"

Answers come flying: John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, one of the prophets. Respectful answers, even flattering. But all wrong. Today too, many say: "Jesus was a great teacher, a good prophet, a master of morality." That's nice, but it's not enough.

Then Jesus looks his disciples in the eye: "But what about you?" he asked. "Who do you say I am? Simon Peter answered, 'You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.'" (Matthew, chapter 16, verses 15 to 16)

What This Reveals About Jesus.

What others say about Jesus won't save you; what you say about him changes everything.

Peter doesn't answer with an opinion, but with a revelation. And Jesus tells him: it's not flesh and blood that revealed this to you, but my Father. Then he adds: "And I tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not overcome it."

But right after, the same Peter goes too far. When Jesus announces that he must suffer, die, and rise again, Peter takes him aside and rebukes him: "Never, Lord! This shall never happen to you!" And Jesus answers him harshly: "Get behind me, Satan!" Just a few verses separate Peter's greatest declaration from his greatest error. You can have a true revelation and, the next moment, refuse the cross.

For Your Life.

And Jesus continues, speaking to all of them: "Then Jesus said to his disciples, 'If any of you wants to be my follower, you must give up your own way, take up your cross, and follow me. If you try to hang on to your life, you will lose it. But if you give up your life for my sake, you will save it.'" (Matthew, chapter 16, verses 24 to 25)

Taking up your cross isn't about dealing with a bad back or a difficult coworker. In those days, the person who carried their cross was walking to their death. Jesus is talking about dying to yourself: to your ego, your rights, your own will, so you can live for him.

It's the paradox of the Gospel: those who cling to their life lose it; those who give it away find it. Like a seed: as long as it stays in the packet, it remains alone. Planted in the ground, it bears fruit.

Today, Jesus is asking you personally: "And you—who do you say I am?" Not what your parents, your pastor, or your church say. You. Take time to answer, write it down if you can. Then ask yourself: is there a cross I'm refusing to carry, an area where I say like Peter, "this won't happen to me"?

Put it into practice.

One. Your Personal Answer. Write your answer to the question: "And you—who do you say I am?" Not what others say: your answer.

Two. The Cross You're Refusing. Is there an area where you say like Peter: "This won't happen to me"? An obedience that costs, a surrender. Give it back to Jesus.

Three. Carry Your Cross Daily. Choose an act of self-denial this week: give up your place, serve without being seen, don't need the last word in an argument.

To reflect on. If Jesus asked me today, "And you—who do you say I am?" what would I answer, honestly?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you are the Messiah, the Son of the living God. You're not just a wise man or a prophet: you are my Lord and my Savior. I choose to deny myself, take up my cross, and follow you. I lose my life to find it in you. Amen.

Key takeaway. What others say about Jesus won't save you; what you say about him changes everything.

And Jesus continues, speaking to all of them: "Then Jesus said to his disciples, 'If any of you wants to be my follower, you must give up your own way, take up your cross, and follow me. If you try to hang on to your life, you will lose it. But if you give up your life for my sake, you will save it.'" (Matthew, chapter 16, verses 24 to 25)

Taking up your cross isn't about dealing with a bad back or a difficult coworker. In those days, the person who carried their cross was walking to their death. Jesus is talking about dying to yourself: to your ego, your rights, your own will, so you can live for him.

It's the paradox of the Gospel: those who cling to their life lose it; those who give it away find it. Like a seed: as long as it stays in the packet, it remains alone. Planted in the ground, it bears fruit.

Today, Jesus is asking you personally: "And you—who do you say I am?" Not what your parents, your pastor, or your church say. You. Take time to answer, write it down if you can. Then ask yourself: is there a cross I'm refusing to carry, an area where I say like Peter, "this won't happen to me"?

Put it into practice.

One. Your Personal Answer. Write your answer to the question: "And you—who do you say I am?" Not what others say: your answer.

Two. The Cross You're Refusing. Is there an area where you say like Peter: "This won't happen to me"? An obedience that costs, a surrender. Give it back to Jesus.

Three. Carry Your Cross Daily. Choose an act of self-denial this week: give up your place, serve without being seen, don't need the last word in an argument.

To reflect on. If Jesus asked me today, "And you—who do you say I am?" what would I answer, honestly?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you are the Messiah, the Son of the living God. You're not just a wise man or a prophet: you are my Lord and my Savior. I choose to deny myself, take up my cross, and follow you. I lose my life to find it in you. Amen.

Key takeaway. What others say about Jesus won't save you; what you say about him changes everything.

Day 25. Jesus Alone.

Today's reading : Matthew, chapter 17, verses 1 to 9.

After six days, Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John his brother, and brought them up into a high mountain by themselves. He was changed before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light. Behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them talking with him. Peter answered and said to Jesus, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.” When the disciples heard it, they fell on their faces, and were very afraid. Jesus came and touched them and said, “Get up, and don’t be afraid.” Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone. As they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying, “Don’t tell anyone what you saw, until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.”

The Story.

Six days later, Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain. And there, before them, he is transfigured: his face shines like the sun, his clothes become white as light. Moses and Elijah appear and talk with him. Moses, who represents the Law; Elijah, who represents the prophets. All of Israel's history is there, gathered around Jesus.

Peter, who can never seem to stay silent, suggests: "Lord, it is good for us to be here; if you wish, I will make three shelters here—one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah." He wants to extend the moment, to hold it, to put Jesus on the same level as these two great men.

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Before Peter even finishes speaking, a bright cloud covers them: "While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them; and suddenly a voice came out of the cloud, saying, 'This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Hear Him!'" (Matthew, chapter 17, verse 5)

It's the same voice as at his baptism, with an addition: "Hear Him!" Moses and Elijah were great, but Jesus is unique. He is not a prophet among others—he is the Son.

The disciples fall facedown, gripped by great fear. Then: "But Jesus came and touched them and said, 'Arise, and do not be afraid.' When they had lifted up their eyes, they saw no one but Jesus only." (Matthew, chapter 17, verses 7 to 8)

Jesus alone. Moses and Elijah have vanished. The shelters will not be built. Only Jesus remains, touching them and saying: do not be afraid.

For Your Life.

You don't build shelters on the mountain; you take the light there and bring it back down into the valley.

There are moments of the mountain in the Christian life: a worship service where God's presence was so strong, a retreat, a camp, an encounter that shook you. And you want to stay there forever. But look what waits for the disciples at the foot of the mountain: a desperate father and a child tormented by a demon (Matthew, chapter 17, verses 14 to 18). The mountain prepares you for the valley.

If you're in the valley today, remember the mountain. The glory you saw was not an illusion. The Jesus of the summit is the same one who walks with you down below.

And hold onto two words from this story. "Hear Him": among all the voices, opinions, advice, and influences, only one voice must have the final word. "Jesus alone": it's possible to stay attached to people, to experiences, to traditions—even good ones—to the point that they take Jesus' place.

Today, take ten minutes of silence simply to listen. Don't speak, don't ask—just listen. Open your Bible, read slowly, and ask: "Lord, what do you want to tell me?" Then go back down into your valley carrying his light.

Put it into practice.

One. Ten Minutes of Listening. Take ten minutes of silence, Bible open, asking for nothing. Read slowly and ask: "Lord, what do you want to tell me?" Write down what touches your heart.

Two. Jesus Alone. Is there a person, a tradition, or an experience that has taken Jesus' place? Restore it to its rightful place in prayer.

Three. Go Back Down Into the Valley. After a powerful moment with God, choose one person who is suffering and serve them this week. The mountain prepares you for the valley.

To reflect on. What voices have taken up too much space in my life? How can I better listen to Jesus, and Jesus alone, this week?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you are the Father's beloved Son. I want to listen to you, above all other voices. Let nothing and no one take your place. Thank you for my mountaintop moments. Give me the strength to come back down into my valley with your light, to serve those who are suffering. Amen.

Key takeaway. The mountain prepares you for the valley.

Day 26. Who Is My Neighbor?.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 10, verses 25 to 37.

Behold, a certain lawyer stood up and tested him, saying, “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” He said to him, “What is written in the law? How do you read it?” He answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself.” He said to him, “You have answered correctly. Do this, and you will live.” But he, desiring to justify himself, asked Jesus, “Who is my neighbor?” Jesus answered, “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who both stripped him and beat him, and departed, leaving him half dead. By chance a certain priest was going down that way. When he saw him, he passed by on the other side. In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side. But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion, came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him. On the next day, when he departed, he took out two denarii, gave them to the host, and said to him, ‘Take care of him. Whatever you spend beyond that, I will repay you when I return.’ Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?” He said, “He who showed mercy on him.” Then Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”

Part 4: On the Road to Jerusalem.

Jesus sets his face firmly toward Jerusalem, where the cross awaits him. During this journey, he will tell some of his most beautiful stories.

The Story.

A teacher of the law wants to test Jesus: "What must I do to inherit eternal life?" Jesus turns the question back to him, and the man answers very well: "He answered, 'You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind'; and 'your neighbor as yourself.'" (Luke, chapter 10, verse 27)

But he wants to justify himself, so he asks: "And who is my neighbor?" In other words: how far must I go? Whom must I love, and whom can I ignore?

Jesus answers with a story. A man is going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, a road nearly twenty miles long, notorious for bandits. He is attacked, stripped, and left half dead. A priest comes by, sees him... and passes on the other side. A Levite does the same. Then comes a Samaritan—an enemy, despised by the Jews. He stops, bandages his wounds, puts him on his own beast, takes him to an inn, pays for him, and promises to return.

What This Reveals About Jesus.

The evening before his death, on April 3, 1968, Martin Luther King commented on this story in his final speech. He imagined that the priest and the Levite had asked themselves: "If I stop to help this man, what will happen to me?" The Samaritan, however, reversed the question: "If I do not stop to help this man, what will happen to him?"

That's exactly what Jesus does. The teacher was asking: "Who is my neighbor?"—that is, "Who deserves my love?" Jesus turns the question around: "Which of these three do you think was neighbor to him who fell among the thieves?" And he said, "He who showed mercy on him." Then Jesus said to him, "Go and do likewise." (Luke, chapter 10, verses 36 to 37)

The question is no longer: "Who is my neighbor?" but: "Whose neighbor will I become?"

For Your Life.

The priest and the Levite weren't necessarily mean people. They probably had good reasons: a service at the temple, fear of becoming unclean by touching a half-dead man, fear of the bandits, their schedule. We too always have good reasons to pass on the other side of the road.

Love according to Jesus costs something: time (the Samaritan changes his plans), money (two denarii and the promise to pay more), and commitment (he will return). And it crosses barriers: a Samaritan helping a Jew.

And don't forget that in this story, Jesus is the first good Samaritan. We were wounded on the roadside, and he stopped, he paid the price, and he promised to return.

Today, ask God to open your eyes to someone "on the roadside": a lonely neighbor, a colleague in difficulty, a stranger in need. Don't pass on the other side. Do something concrete, even if it costs you a little.

Put it into practice.

One. Open Your Eyes. Ask God to show you someone "on the roadside" this week: a lonely neighbor, a struggling colleague, a stranger in need.

Two. Accept That It Costs Something. Set aside time, money, or energy for a concrete act of love. The Samaritan's love changed his plans.

Three. Cross a Barrier. Do an act of kindness toward someone different from you (different culture, opinion, generation, or someone you're in conflict with).

To reflect on. Who is "on the roadside" in my life right now? What concrete action will I take to become their neighbor?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you stopped for me when I was wounded on the roadside. Forgive me for the times I've passed on the other side. Open my eyes to those suffering around me, and give me a love that stops, that cares for wounds, and that pays the price. Amen.

Key takeaway. The question is not "who is my neighbor?" but "whose neighbor will I become?"

texte:
Day 27. One Thing Is Necessary.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 10, verses 38 to 42.

As they went on their way, he entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house. She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus’ feet and heard his word. But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she came up to him, and said, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me.” Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”

The Story.

On the road to Jerusalem, Jesus stops in a village at the home of two sisters: Martha and Mary. Martha welcomes him into her house. Receiving Jesus and his disciples means welcoming at least thirteen hungry men at once. There's food to prepare, serving to do, cleaning up. Martha rushes around in all directions.

And Mary? "She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus' feet and heard His word. But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she approached Him and said, 'Lord, do You not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Therefore tell her to help me.'" (Luke, chapter 10, verses 39 to 40)

What This Reveals About Jesus.

In that time, sitting "at the feet" of a teacher was the position of a disciple. And it wasn't the usual place for a woman. Mary takes a place that culture didn't give her, and Jesus welcomes her there.

Martha, on the other hand, is exhausted. She even reproaches Jesus: "Do You not care?" And Jesus answers her with great tenderness, repeating her name: "And Jesus answered and said to her, 'Martha, Martha, you are worried and troubled about many things. But one thing is needed, and Mary has chosen that good part, which will not be taken away from her.'" (Luke, chapter 10, verses 41 to 42)

Jesus doesn't criticize Martha's service. The meal was necessary, the hospitality was beautiful. The problem wasn't what Martha was doing, but what it was doing to her: she was "worried and troubled." And in her anxiety, she ended up accusing her sister and doubting Jesus.

For Your Life.

You can be so busy serving Jesus that you forget to be with him.

That's the trap for many committed Christians. You do things for God, so many things, good things. Meetings, service, projects, phones ringing, notifications without end. And one day you realize you haven't spent real time alone with him in weeks. You serve the Master of the house, but you never sit at his feet anymore.

Imagine a wife whose husband works all the time to give her a beautiful house, but never spends an evening with her. She would eventually say: "I don't want your gifts—I want you." God doesn't first look for exhausted servants, but for present children.

Service must flow from presence. Martha without Mary is exhaustion. Mary sitting forever without getting up is spiritual selfishness. But Mary first, then Martha—that's balance.

Today, set a specific, protected time—even if it's short—when you'll sit at Jesus' feet. Phone on airplane mode, Bible open, heart available. That's "the good part," and no one can take it from you.

Put it into practice.

One. Protected Time. Set a time each day at Jesus' feet, even if it's short: phone on airplane mode, Bible open. Put it on your calendar.

Two. Martha or Mary?. Write down what makes you "worried and troubled" in your service or life. Give it to Jesus before you keep serving.

Three. As a Family. If you're a busy parent, take five minutes with your children to read a verse and pray together. The good part can be shared as a family too.

To reflect on. Do I tend to be more like Martha or more like Mary? What protected time will I set aside to sit at Jesus' feet?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, forgive me for the times I've been so busy serving you that I forgot to be with you. I choose the good part. Teach me to sit at your feet, to listen to you, and then to serve with a heart at peace. Amen.

Key takeaway. You can be so busy serving Jesus that you forget to be with him.

Day 28. The Father Who Ran.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 15, verses 11 to 32.

He said, “A certain man had two sons. The younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me my share of your property.’ So he divided his livelihood between them. Not many days after, the younger son gathered all of this together and traveled into a far country. There he wasted his property with riotous living. When he had spent all of it, there arose a severe famine in that country, and he began to be in need. He went and joined himself to one of the citizens of that country, and he sent him into his fields to feed pigs. He wanted to fill his belly with the pods that the pigs ate, but no one gave him any. But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough to spare, and I’m dying with hunger! I will get up and go to my father, and will tell him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no more worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants.”’ “He arose and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him. The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ “But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring out the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet. Bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let’s eat and celebrate; for this, my son, was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found.’ Then they began to celebrate. “Now his elder son was in the field. As he came near to the house, he heard music and dancing. He called one of the servants to him and asked what was going on. He said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and healthy.’ But he was angry and would not go in. Therefore his father came out and begged him. But he answered his father, ‘Behold, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a commandment of yours, but you never gave me a goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this your son came, who has devoured your living with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him.’ “He said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But it was appropriate to celebrate and be glad, for this, your brother, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found.’”

The Story.

It may be the most beautiful story ever told. A father had two sons. The younger said to him, "Father, give me the share of the property that falls to me." In the culture of that time, many commentators point out, asking for your inheritance while your father is alive was almost like saying, "I wish you were dead."

The father agrees. The son goes to a distant country and squanders everything in wild living. Then comes the famine. He ends up keeping pigs, the unclean animal par excellence for a Jew, and he even envies their food. He has hit bottom.

That's when he "comes to himself." He prepares a speech: "I am no longer worthy to be called your son; treat me like one of your hired servants." And he takes the road home.

What This Reveals About God.

"And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him." (Luke, chapter 15, verse 20)

"While he was still a long way off, his father saw him." That means the father was watching the road. Maybe every day. He had never stopped waiting.

And he runs. In that culture, an elderly, respected man did not run in public—he would have to lift his robe, and it was beneath his dignity. But this father doesn't care. He runs, throws his arms around his son, kisses him. The son starts his speech, but the father won't even let him finish. He calls his servants: the best robe, a ring on his finger, sandals on his feet, the fattened calf. A celebration.

The Father wasn't waiting for your speech; he was waiting for your return.

For Your Life.

But the story isn't over. There's a second son. The one who stayed, who always obeyed. When he hears the music, he gets angry and refuses to go in. "All these years I have been serving you…" He was at home, but his heart was just as far away as his brother's. He served his father like an employee, not like a son.

And the father comes out to him too: "My child," the father said to him, "you have always been with me, and all that is mine is yours. But it was fitting to celebrate and be glad, because this your brother was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found." (Luke, chapter 15, verses 31 to 32)

There are two ways to be far from the Father: by leaving home, or by staying at home with a hard heart. The first son loses himself in sin, the second in religion. And the Father runs toward both.

If you're the son who left, the road back is open. You don't need a perfect speech. The Father is already running toward you.

If you're the older son, ask yourself: Am I serving God with joy, like a son, or with bitterness, like an employee counting his hours? Do I rejoice when someone comes back, even if they've done anything wrong?

Today, come to yourself, no matter which son you are. And let yourself be embraced by the Father.

Put it into practice.

One. Come to Yourself. Which son are you right now—the one who left or the one who stayed with a hard heart? Tell the Father honestly.

Not many days after, the younger son gathered all of this together and traveled into a far country. There he wasted his property with riotous living. When he had spent all of it, there arose a severe famine in that country, and he began to be in need. He went and joined himself to one of the citizens of that country, and he sent him into his fields to feed pigs. He wanted to fill his belly with the pods that the pigs ate, but no one gave him any. But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough to spare, and I’m dying with hunger! I will get up and go to my father, and will tell him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no more worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants.”’ “He arose and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him. The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ “But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring out the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet. Bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let’s eat and celebrate; for this, my son, was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found.’ Then they began to celebrate. “Now his elder son was in the field. As he came near to the house, he heard music and dancing. He called one of the servants to him and asked what was going on. He said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and healthy.’ But he was angry and would not go in. Therefore his father came out and begged him. But he answered his father, ‘Behold, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a commandment of yours, but you never gave me a goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this your son came, who has devoured your living with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him.’ “He said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But it was appropriate to celebrate and be glad, for this, your brother, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found.’”

The Story.

It may be the most beautiful story ever told. A father had two sons. The younger said to him, "Father, give me the share of the property that falls to me." In the culture of that time, many commentators point out, asking for your inheritance while your father is alive was almost like saying, "I wish you were dead."

The father agrees. The son goes to a distant country and squanders everything in wild living. Then comes the famine. He ends up keeping pigs, the unclean animal par excellence for a Jew, and he even envies their food. He has hit bottom.

That's when he "comes to himself." He prepares a speech: "I am no longer worthy to be called your son; treat me like one of your hired servants." And he takes the road home.

What This Reveals About God.

"And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him." (Luke, chapter 15, verse 20)

"While he was still a long way off, his father saw him." That means the father was watching the road. Maybe every day. He had never stopped waiting.

And he runs. In that culture, an elderly, respected man did not run in public—he would have to lift his robe, and it was beneath his dignity. But this father doesn't care. He runs, throws his arms around his son, kisses him. The son starts his speech, but the father won't even let him finish. He calls his servants: the best robe, a ring on his finger, sandals on his feet, the fattened calf. A celebration.

The Father wasn't waiting for your speech; he was waiting for your return.

But the story isn't over. There's a second son. The one who stayed, who always obeyed. When he hears the music, he gets angry and refuses to go in. "All these years I have been serving you…" He was at home, but his heart was just as far away as his brother's. He served his father like an employee, not like a son.

And the father comes out to him too: "My child," the father said to him, "you have always been with me, and all that is mine is yours. But it was fitting to celebrate and be glad, because this your brother was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found." (Luke, chapter 15, verses 31 to 32)

Today, come to yourself, no matter which son you are. And let yourself be embraced by the Father.

Day 29. Roll Away the Stone.

Today's reading : John, chapter 11, verses 17 to 44.

So when Jesus came, he found that he had been in the tomb four days already. Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away. Many of the Jews had joined the women around Martha and Mary, to console them concerning their brother. Then when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary stayed in the house. Therefore Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died. Even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.” Jesus said to her, “Your brother will rise again.” Martha said to him, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day.” Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies. Whoever lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?” She said to him, “Yes, Lord. I have come to believe that you are the Christ, God’s Son, he who comes into the world.” When she had said this, she went away and called Mary, her sister, secretly, saying, “The Teacher is here and is calling you.” When she heard this, she arose quickly and went to him. Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was in the place where Martha met him. Then the Jews who were with her in the house and were consoling her, when they saw Mary, that she rose up quickly and went out, followed her, saying, “She is going to the tomb to weep there.” Therefore when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell down at his feet, saying to him, “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died.” When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews weeping who came with her, he groaned in the spirit and was troubled, and said, “Where have you laid him?” They told him, “Lord, come and see.” Jesus wept. The Jews therefore said, “See how much affection he had for him!” Some of them said, “Couldn’t this man, who opened the eyes of him who was blind, have also kept this man from dying?” Jesus therefore, again groaning in himself, came to the tomb. Now it was a cave, and a stone lay against it. Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha, the sister of him who was dead, said to him, “Lord, by this time there is a stench, for he has been dead four days.” Jesus said to her, “Didn’t I tell you that if you believed, you would see God’s glory?” So they took away the stone from the place where the dead man was lying. Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, “Father, I thank you that you listened to me. I know that you always listen to me, but because of the multitude standing around I said this, that they may believe that you sent me.” When he had said this, he cried with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!” He who was dead came out, bound hand and foot with wrappings, and his face was wrapped around with a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Free him, and let him go.”

The Story.

Lazarus, the friend of Jesus, brother of Martha and Mary, is gravely ill. The sisters send a message: "Lord, the one you love is sick." And Jesus… stays where he is for two more days. When he finally arrives in Bethany, Lazarus has been dead for four days.

Martha runs toward him: "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died." Then Mary arrives, falls at his feet, and says exactly the same thing. They must have repeated it for four days: "If only you had come…"

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Jesus knew he was going to raise Lazarus. He had even announced it to his disciples. And yet, before the tomb, in the midst of weeping: "Jesus wept. So the Jews said, 'See how he loved him.'" (John, chapter 11, verses 35 to 36)

It's the shortest verse in the Bible, and one of the most profound. Jesus weeps. He's not rushed to move on to the miracle. He doesn't say, "Stop weeping, you'll see!" He enters into the grief of his friends. He weeps with those who weep.

Your sorrow is not indifferent to Jesus. He knows the end of your story, and yet he weeps with you in the middle.

Then he gives an order: "Jesus said, 'Roll away the stone.' Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, 'Lord, by this time there is a stench, for he has been dead four days.' Jesus said to her, 'Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?'" (John, chapter 11, verses 39 to 40)

Martha has a very logical objection: "He already stinks." Everyone knows that after four days, it's over. But Jesus asks her to do her part: roll away the stone. He could have done it with a word. But he wants human hands to roll it.

Then he cries out: "Lazarus, come out!" And the dead man comes out, his feet and hands wrapped with burial strips. And Jesus gives one final order to the witnesses: "Unbind him, and let him go."

For Your Life.

Jesus can raise the dead, but he asks you to roll away the stone.

Maybe there's something in your life that has been dead for "four days": a dream, a marriage, a relationship, a calling, your joy. Everyone says, "It's over, it already stinks." And maybe you repeat, "Lord, if you had been here…"

Jesus weeps with you. But he also tells you: "Roll away the stone." The stone might be bitterness, refusal to forgive, a closed door, fear of believing again. He's not asking you to raise the dead; that's his job. He's asking you to roll the stone.

And look at the last word: "Unbind him." Lazarus was alive, but still wrapped in his burial cloths. It's the role of the community: to help those whom Jesus has brought back to life to free themselves from what still wraps them.

Today, name your "stone," and dare to roll it away before Jesus.

Put it into practice.

One. Name Your Stone. Write down what's preventing God from acting in a situation that seems dead: bitterness, refusal to forgive, a closed door, fear of believing again.

Two. Roll It Away. Take a concrete step this week: forgive, make a first move, reach out again, dare to pray about this matter once more.

Three. Help Someone Be Unbound. Think of someone who has known Jesus but remains trapped by their "burial cloths" (shame, habits, wounds). Walk alongside them: listen, pray, offer concrete help.

To reflect on. What "stone" is Jesus asking me to roll away today so he can act?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you for weeping with me. You know what has died in my life and what everyone thinks is lost. I roll away the stone before you: my bitterness, my doubts, my closed doors. Cry out life again. And help me to unbind others. Amen.

Key takeaway. Jesus can raise the dead, but he asks you to roll away the stone.

Day 30. I Must Stay at Your House.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 19, verses 1 to 10.

He entered and was passing through Jericho. There was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector, and he was rich. He was trying to see who Jesus was, and couldn’t because of the crowd, because he was short. He ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was going to pass that way. When Jesus came to the place, he looked up and saw him, and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.” He hurried, came down, and received him joyfully. When they saw it, they all murmured, saying, “He has gone in to lodge with a man who is a sinner.” Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.” Jesus said to him, “Today, salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.”

The Story.

Jericho. Zacchaeus is not just a tax collector: he is the chief tax collector, and he is rich. In other words, he has grown wealthy by collaborating with the occupier and collecting more than required. The whole city hates him.

He wants to see Jesus, but there are two problems: the crowd, and his height. He is short. So he does something very undignified for a wealthy man: he runs ahead and climbs a sycamore tree. Imagine a bank manager perched in a tree in a suit.

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Jesus arrives at the tree. He stops, looks up, and calls him by name: "And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him, 'Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.'" (Luke, chapter 19, verse 5)

Jesus knows his name. He doesn't say to him, "Come down, so I can lecture you." He says, "I must stay at your house today." "I must": as if it were the most important appointment of his journey.

The crowd murmurs, "He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner." But Jesus won't let public opinion dictate his friendships.

And yet, Jesus asks nothing of Zacchaeus. No list of conditions, no sermon on honesty. Zacchaeus himself stands up: "And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, 'Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.' And Jesus said to him, 'Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.'" (Luke, chapter 19, verses 8 to 10)

For Your Life.

Zacchaeus was seeking to see Jesus; he discovered that Jesus was seeking him.

Notice the order: first, Jesus welcomes Zacchaeus. Then, Zacchaeus changes. Change is not the condition for Jesus's love; it is the fruit of that love. No one forced Zacchaeus to give back the money. Grace did what shame and the reproach of an entire city had never been able to do.

And his repentance is concrete. He doesn't just say "I'm sorry." He gives half his possessions to the poor, and restores four times what he stole. The true encounter with Jesus always touches the wallet, relationships, and habits.

Maybe you feel small too: small because of your past, your reputation, what others say about you. Maybe the crowd is hiding Jesus from you. Do what Zacchaeus did: run ahead, climb a tree, do what it takes to see him. And you will discover that he stops under your tree, and that he knows your name.

And if Jesus comes to your house today, what needs to change? Is there something to repair, to restore, to give back? Grace doesn't ask it as a price to pay. It gives you the desire to do it.

Put it into practice.

One. Climb Your Tree. Make a concrete effort to see Jesus this week: wake up earlier, go to a prayer meeting, read an entire Gospel.

Two. What Needs to Be Repaired. If Jesus came to your house today, what would need to change? A debt to repay, an apology, a wrong to make right? Do it, with joy.

Three. Your Generosity. Zacchaeus gave to the poor. Choose a concrete gift this week, within your means: money, a meal, your time.

To reflect on. If Jesus came to my house today, what would need to change or be made right?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you for stopping under my tree and calling me by my name. I receive you with joy in my house and in my life. May your grace produce true change in me. Show me what I need to repair, and give me the joy of doing it. Amen.

Key takeaway. Zacchaeus was seeking to see Jesus; he discovered that Jesus was seeking him.

Day 31. The King on a Donkey.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 19, verses 28 to 44.

Having said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. When he came near to Bethsphage and Bethany, at the mountain that is called Olivet, he sent two of his disciples, saying, “Go your way into the village on the other side, in which, as you enter, you will find a colt tied, which no man has ever sat upon. Untie it and bring it. If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ say to him: ‘The Lord needs it.’” Those who were sent went away and found things just as he had told them. As they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, “Why are you untying the colt?” They said, “The Lord needs it.” Then they brought it to Jesus. They threw their cloaks on the colt and sat Jesus on them. As he went, they spread their cloaks on the road. As he was now getting near, at the descent of the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works which they had seen, saying, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest!” Some of the Pharisees from the multitude said to him, “Teacher, rebuke your disciples!” He answered them, “I tell you that if these were silent, the stones would cry out.” When he came near, he saw the city and wept over it, saying, “If you, even you, had known today the things which belong to your peace! But now, they are hidden from your eyes. And think of Jesus' tears. He still weeps today over cities that do not recognize Him. Over your city, your neighborhood, your family.

Today, do two things. Ask yourself whether your faith is that of a fan or that of a disciple. Then pray for your city as Jesus wept over Jerusalem: that it may recognize the time of its visitation.

Put it into practice.

One. Fan or Disciple?. Write honestly what shows that you follow Jesus even when it costs something, and what shows that you follow Him only when everything is going well.

Two. The Lord Needs It. Ask God what He wants to use in you (your time, your car, your home, your talent) and say yes to Him this week.

Three. Pray for Your City. Take ten minutes to pray for your city, walking if possible: its leaders, its families, those who don't know Jesus.

Day 32. The King with a Towel.

Today's reading : John, chapter 13, verses 1 to 17.

Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his time had come that he would depart from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. During supper, the devil having already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him, Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God and was going to God, arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist. Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him. Then he came to Simon Peter. He said to him, “Lord, do you wash my feet?” Jesus answered him, “You don’t know what I am doing now, but you will understand later.” Peter said to him, “You will never wash my feet!” Jesus answered him, “If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me.” Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head!” Jesus said to him, “Someone who has bathed only needs to have his feet washed, but is completely clean. You are clean, but not all of you.” For he knew him who would betray him; therefore he said, “You are not all clean.” So when he had washed their feet, put his outer garment back on, and sat down again, he said to them, “Do you know what I have done to you? You call me, ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord.’ You say so correctly, for so I am. If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you. Most certainly I tell you, a servant is not greater than his lord, neither is one who is sent greater than he who sent him. If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.

Part 5: The Cross.

We enter the last days of Jesus before the cross. John devotes almost half his Gospel to this final week. Slow down, read carefully: this is the heart of everything.

The Story.

"Before the Feast of Passover, Jesus, knowing that His hour had come that He should depart from this world to the Father, having loved His own who were in the world, He loved them to the end." (John, chapter 13, verse 1)

"He loved them to the end." And how? With a gesture no one expected. During the meal, Jesus rises, removes His outer garments, takes a towel, pours water into a basin, and begins to wash His disciples' feet.

In that culture, roads were dusty, people wore sandals, and feet were dirty. Washing guests' feet was the task of the lowest slave. Even a disciple was not required to wash his master's feet. That evening there was no slave, and none of the disciples offered to do it. Luke even tells us that during this meal they were arguing about who was the greatest (Luke, chapter 22, verse 24).

So while they argue over first place, Jesus takes last place.

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Peter refuses: "You shall never wash my feet." He cannot accept that his Lord would humble Himself this way. But Jesus answers him: "If I do not wash you, you have no part with Me." Before serving, you must accept being served by Jesus, being washed by Him. Pride can also hide in the refusal to receive.

And there is a detail that takes your breath away: Jesus knows that Judas will betray Him (John, chapter 13, verse 2, 11). Yet He also washes his feet. He kneels before the one who will hand Him over for thirty pieces of silver, takes his feet in His hands, and washes them.

Then Jesus puts His outer garments back on and explains: "If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet. For I have given you an example, that you should do as I have done to you." (John, chapter 13, verses 14 to 15)

For Your Life.

The greatest is not the one who has the most people serving him, but the one who serves the most people.

In the world, greatness is measured by how many people are under your command. In the kingdom of God, it is measured by how many people you serve. Jesus didn't say, "Blessed are you if you know these things," but "Blessed are you if you practice them" (John, chapter 13, verse 17).

Washing feet today may not be with a basin and water. It's doing the task no one wants to do. It's serving someone who can give you nothing in return. It's even serving someone who has hurt you, as Jesus did with Judas.

Today, take a towel, literally or figuratively. Find a humble, invisible service that no one will notice. And do it for Jesus.

Put it into practice.

One. Take a Towel. Find a humble and invisible service this week (dishes, cleaning at church, helping a neighbor) and do it for Jesus.

Two. Let Yourself Be Served. If you struggle to receive help, accept someone's assistance this week without making excuses. Receiving is also a form of humility.

Three. Serve the One Who Hurt You. Think of a person who has hurt you. Without putting yourself in danger, do a small act of kindness toward them, as Jesus did with Judas.

To reflect on. What humble and invisible service can I render this week? Is there someone who has hurt me whom I could serve?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, You, the Master, took the towel and washed the feet of Your disciples, even the feet of Judas. Wash me first, and cleanse my heart of all pride. Then teach me to serve as You do, without seeking first place, even those who have hurt me. Amen.

Key takeaway. While they argued over first place, Jesus took last place.

texte:
Day 33. Do This in Remembrance of Me.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 22, verses 14 to 30.

When the hour had come, he sat down with the twelve apostles. He said to them, “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer, for I tell you, I will no longer by any means eat of it until it is fulfilled in God’s Kingdom.” He received a cup, and when he had given thanks, he said, “Take this and share it among yourselves, for I tell you, I will not drink at all again from the fruit of the vine, until God’s Kingdom comes.” He took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body which is given for you. Do this in memory of me.” Likewise, he took the cup after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you. But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. The Son of Man indeed goes as it has been determined, but woe to that man through whom he is betrayed!” They began to question among themselves which of them it was who would do this thing. A dispute also arose among them, which of them was considered to be greatest. He said to them, “The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called ‘benefactors.’ But not so with you. Rather, the one who is greater among you, let him become as the younger, and one who is governing, as one who serves. For who is greater, one who sits at the table, or one who serves? Isn’t it he who sits at the table? But I am among you as one who serves. “But you are those who have continued with me in my trials. I confer on you a kingdom, even as my Father conferred on me, that you may eat and drink at my table in my Kingdom. You will sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

The Story.

It is the evening of Passover. For more than a thousand years, every Jewish family has celebrated this meal to remember the night when God freed Israel from Egypt. The blood of the lamb on the doorposts, the angel of death passing over, the exodus from slavery. Each element of the meal tells this story.

And that evening, Jesus says to His disciples a phrase full of emotion: "I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer." Then He takes the bread and the cup and gives them new meaning: "And He took bread, gave thanks and broke it, and gave it to them, saying, 'This is My body which is given for you; do this in remembrance of Me.' Likewise He also took the cup after supper, saying, 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is shed for you.' " (Luke, chapter 22, verses 19 to 20)

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Jesus is saying: "Tonight, a new liberation is beginning, and I am the Lamb." The broken bread is His body that will be broken on the cross. The cup is His blood that will be shed. Not for Israel alone: "for you," for all who believe.

He speaks of a "new covenant." A covenant is more than a contract. A contract says, "I'll do my part if you do yours." A covenant says, "I give myself to you." Like in a marriage. Jesus seals this covenant with His own blood.

Yet at the same table there is Judas' betrayal, and right after, an argument over who is the greatest. Jesus answers them: "Let it not be so among you; on the contrary, he who is greatest among you, let him be as the younger, and he who governs as he who serves. For who is greater, he who sits at the table, or he who serves? Is it not he who sits at the table? Yet I am among you as the One who serves." (Luke, chapter 22, verses 26 to 27)

Even on His last evening, the disciples don't understand. And Jesus doesn't reject them. He continues to love them, to teach them, to share bread with them.

For Your Life.

When you take communion, you're not just remembering—you're proclaiming a covenant.

When you take the bread and the cup, you are saying: "Jesus died for me. His body was broken in my place. His blood paid my debt. I am in the covenant." Paul adds that every time you do this, you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes (1 Corinthians, chapter 11, verse 26). This is a proclamation looking to the past, but also to the future.

It's possible to take communion out of habit, thinking about something else, as if reciting a formula. This text invites us to rediscover it as a meal of love. Jesus "eagerly desired" this moment with His disciples. He desires it also with you.

Today, even if you're not taking communion, take a moment to remember. Thank Jesus for His broken body and shed blood, given precisely for you. And the next time you share the bread and cup at church, do it with awareness: you are proclaiming the covenant.

Put it into practice.

One. Remember. Take a moment to thank Jesus for His broken body and shed blood, given precisely for you. Write a prayer of thanksgiving.

Two. Prepare Your Next Communion. The next time you take it, prepare your heart the day before: confess what weighs on you, forgive, and live it as the proclamation of the covenant.

Three. A Meal That Gathers. Organize a meal with brothers and sisters this week or with your family, and take a moment to remember what Jesus did.

To reflect on. How do I live communion: out of habit, or as the proclamation of a covenant? What could change?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you for Your broken body and shed blood given for me. Thank you for this new covenant, sealed by Your love. Forgive me for the times I took this meal without thinking about it. I remember You, and I proclaim Your death until You come. Amen.

Key takeaway. Communion is not just a memory—it's the proclamation of a covenant.
